finding.measure: Readability of generated dialogue materials used for speaking/listening practice (Flesch Reading Ease, Dale-Chall, McAlpine EFLAW)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT-generated dialogues may reduce boredom by increasing dialogue variety and may lower anxiety compared with more difficult or less natural materials. This is framed as supporting sustained practice, confidence, and motivation to continue using the chatbot repeatedly, though these are inferred from readability and design considerations rather than measured with a learner survey or experiment.
finding.measure: Inferred suitability for repeated practice, variety, and learner confidence/motivation based on readability profiles

finding.finding_summary: The authors claim that using ChatGPT to generate reference dialogues can reduce the time and cost of creating chatbot dialogue content compared with human-authored materials. They also note that deterministic dialogue flow with reusable alternative replies is computationally lighter for mobile devices than a complex question-answer generation system, but no direct efficiency benchmark is reported.
finding.measure: Perceived development and runtime efficiency of generating reusable chatbot dialogue content

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how artificial intelligence (AI) has been studied and applied in higher education, with particular attention to how the field is developing, what kinds of AI uses are most common, and what ethical or pedagogical issues are discussed. The review was motivated by the authors’ observation that AI in education is growing quickly, but educators may not have a clear picture of where the research stands or how to use these tools meaningfully.

The authors conducted a systematic review of peer-reviewed English and Spanish journal articles published between 2007 and November 2018. From 2,656 initial records, 146 studies on AI in higher education were included. The review covered AI applications across the student life cycle, including profiling and prediction, assessment and evaluation, adaptive systems and personalisation, and intelligent tutoring systems. Most studies were quantitative and came primarily from computer science and STEM fields, with relatively little contribution from education researchers.

Across the reviewed literature, the main uses of AI were predictive analytics for admissions, drop-out/retention, and student modelling; automated assessment and grading; adaptive learning systems; and intelligent tutoring systems that deliver content, hints, or feedback. The review found that studies usually involved undergraduate students and focused on academic support services rather than broader institutional governance. The authors conclude that the field is expanding, but critical reflection on ethics, privacy, and implementation risks is rare, and there is a need for stronger pedagogical grounding and more educator involvement in AI-in-education research.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review with explicit search and coding procedures, but it is not a meta-analysis and the included studies are a mix of descriptive, correlational, and quasi-experimental work. The paper synthesizes the field rather than testing one intervention under controlled conditions.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests potentially meaningful benefits for efficiency and some learner support functions, but the evidence is heterogeneous, largely preliminary, and not summarized with pooled effect sizes. Impacts are therefore promising but unclear at the general-population level.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of AI applications in higher education, covering intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive systems, assessment/feedback tools, and predictive analytics rather than evaluating a single deployed tool

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that AI applications were commonly framed as reducing staff workload and improving efficiency in higher education, especially for admission decisions, course planning, grading, feedback, and early-warning functions. However, this is a synthesis of 146 mostly descriptive/quantitative studies rather than a pooled estimate, so no single effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Documented functions and reported performance/efficiency claims across included studies

finding.finding_summary: Assessment and evaluation applications were reported to operate at high accuracy and efficiency levels, especially automated grading and feedback systems. Examples in the review include computer-human grading agreement of 94.6%-98.2% for postgraduate medical essays, but the paper does not conduct a meta-analysis.
finding.measure: Automated grading agreement, feedback generation performance, and evaluation task efficiency

finding.finding_summary: A small number of studies examined engagement, motivation, and self-regulation, generally suggesting that AI-supported systems can help monitor and sometimes improve learner engagement or self-regulatory processes. The review also notes at least one negative result in which the support was not well matched to more advanced learners, but no pooled effect size is provided.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, self-regulation indicators

paper_profiles.title: Co-Designing a Real-Time Classroom Orchestration Tool to Support Teacher–AI Complementarity
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to design real-time classroom orchestration support for teachers working in AI-enhanced K–12 classrooms. The central problem is that intelligent tutoring systems and other adaptive learning tools can improve student practice, but they also make it harder for teachers to monitor students, interpret what is happening in real time, and intervene effectively. The authors argue that classroom AI tools should complement, rather than replace, teachers, and that designing such tools requires deep stakeholder co-design and new prototyping methods.

The intervention studied is Lumilo, a wearable mixed-reality tool implemented as smart glasses that surface real-time learning analytics to teachers. Across a series of formative studies, lo-fi and mid-fi prototypes, and replay-based enactments, the researchers worked with middle-school math teachers to identify useful analytics, test display concepts, and refine how information should be presented during live class sessions. The work focused on equation-solving ITS classrooms, especially on what teachers want to see about students’ reasoning, struggle, off-task behavior, misconceptions, and progress.

The study involved middle-school math teachers in multiple schools and districts in the United States, with classroom-based prototyping and piloting in authentic school settings. The main conclusions are that teachers prefer simple, glanceable indicators; want analytics that explain why a signal appears; value access to raw student work alongside automated inferences; and generally want tools that support teacher judgment without taking away autonomy. The paper also concludes that some seemingly attractive automation concepts, such as explicit time-management nudges, may be rejected if they undermine teacher control, and that selective sharing and the ability to override or customize the system are important implementation features.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative/case-study paper using interviews, card sorting, speed dating, prototyping, and classroom piloting, but it is not a controlled efficacy study and reports no causal student-outcome estimates. The evidence is credible for design requirements and implementation insights, but weaker for impact claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for teacher workflow and classroom orchestration, but it does not provide measurable effect sizes on student learning. Impact is therefore promising but unclear from an outcomes-evidence perspective.

interventions.use_case: real-time classroom analytics for middle-school math teachers to detect students’ knowledge, struggle, off-task behavior, misconceptions, and recent progress while students work in an ITS; delivered via wearable mixed-reality smart glasses (Lumilo) and class-level displays to support orchestration decisions

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not report student achievement effects from an intervention trial; instead, it studies how real-time analytics can support middle-school mathematics instruction in ITS classrooms. The relevant mathematical content is equation solving, and the main evidence is qualitative design feedback from 10 teachers in needs-finding studies and 16 teachers in prototyping sessions (plus classroom piloting), showing that teachers wanted support for diagnosing students’ solution paths, misconceptions, and areas of struggle, but were wary of inaccurate or non-actionable inferences.
finding.measure: Qualitative teacher judgments about equation-solving analytics, solution-path visibility, and usefulness of class/student-level mathematical indicators
finding.study_size: n=26 teachers across design studies and prototyping sessions

finding.finding_summary: Teachers strongly valued analytics about student frustration, motivation, and engagement, but also expressed discomfort with automated judgments about motivation such as labeling students as 'careless.' The study therefore suggests potential benefits for timely support of affective and motivational needs, alongside risks of misclassification and stigmatizing inferences.
finding.measure: Qualitative reactions to real-time affect/motivation indicators and concerns about student frustration/carelessness
finding.study_size: n=26 teachers across design studies and prototyping sessions

finding.finding_summary: A central finding is that teachers wanted analytics to improve their real-time metacognitive and decision-making work: prioritizing attention, interpreting why students are stuck, and deciding when to intervene versus hold back. At the same time, they rejected designs that overly automated teacher judgment or undermined autonomy, indicating that the learning benefit depends on preserving teacher agency and actionable interpretation.
finding.measure: Qualitative teacher feedback on decision support, prioritization, diagnosis, and autonomy in classroom orchestration
finding.study_size: n=26 teachers across design studies and prototyping sessions

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s strongest substantive contribution is showing that wearable real-time analytics may reduce teacher orchestration burden by helping teachers monitor many students at once, identify who needs help, and surface actionable class-level patterns without constantly scanning the room. Across formative studies with 10 teachers and prototyping with 16 teachers, participants repeatedly described benefits such as prioritizing help, detecting off-task behavior, and supporting one-to-many attention, while also emphasizing that the interface must avoid distraction and information overload.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported workload, orchestration burden, and perceived usefulness of real-time analytics displays for monitoring and intervention
finding.study_size: n=26 teachers across design studies and prototyping sessions

paper_profiles.title: The Future of Embodied Design for Mathematics Teaching and Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper surveys and synthesizes major research programs on embodied cognition as they apply to mathematics teaching and learning. Rather than testing a single intervention, it asks how embodied design, action–cognition transduction, gesture and multimodality, graspable math, playful learning, and embodied teacher education can inform future mathematics education research and practice.

The paper draws on a wide range of prior empirical studies, many of them design-based and often involving middle-school and some high-school students, to illustrate how technology-mediated tasks can connect physical action, gesture, perception, and mathematical reasoning. Examples include perception-based embodied tasks for probability and slope, action-based tasks such as the Mathematics Imagery Trainer for proportion, and AI-embedded or game-based systems that provide real-time prompts and track movement and gesture.

Across these programs, the authors argue that meaningful mathematical learning can emerge when students first act or perceive in intuitive, sensorimotor ways and only then formalize those experiences using symbols, grids, language, and other disciplinary representations. The paper concludes that embodied mathematics learning is most powerful when actions are conceptually relevant, when gestures and multimodal interaction are used to build common ground, and when technology is designed to support collaboration, explanation, and reflection. It also emphasizes that not all movement is beneficial; only mathematically grounded actions and collaborative embodiment appear to improve intuition, insight, proof, and problem solving.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed theoretical and design-synthesis article that summarizes multiple prior empirical studies, but it is not itself a primary experimental evaluation. The paper provides some quantitative results from cited studies, yet the methodology is heterogeneous and largely secondary rather than a single well-controlled design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The article suggests potentially meaningful benefits for mathematics reasoning and collaboration, with several cited effects at or above moderate magnitude. However, because the paper is primarily a framework/synthesis and not a direct intervention trial, the impact for K-12 practice is promising but still indirect and somewhat uncertain.

interventions.use_case: Embodied mathematics learning environments and interactive simulations, including the Mathematics Imagery Trainer and the Hidden Village game, where students use movement, gesture, and on-screen feedback to explore ratios, proportion, slope, probability, and geometric transformations.

An AI-embedded embodied tutor ('Maria') with naturalistic speech-and-gesture capabilities that responds to students’ actions with prompts, attention-directing feedback, encouragement, and challenges inside the Mathematics Imagery Trainer.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed embodied-design and action-cognition studies, mathematically relevant movement and gesture were associated with improved mathematical reasoning, proof, and generalization. Reported results include higher similarity understanding for directed body movements than non-body-based activities (F(1,162)=56.4, p<0.05, η²=0.04), geometry proof performance gains in n=120 (d=0.62, p<0.05), and gesture-based prediction/insight effects in geometry (d=0.44 and d=0.65) with dynamic depictive gestures strongly predicting valid proofs (d=1.40, p<0.001).
finding.measure: Mathematical reasoning, similarity understanding, geometry proof performance, intuition/insight, generalization tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that embodied and playful mathematics activities can motivate learning by engaging students in challenging, technology-based tasks and by making reasoning more accessible through action. However, this is mainly a synthesis claim rather than a single causal estimate, so the evidence is suggestive rather than definitive.
finding.measure: Engagement/motivation inferred from task participation and design rationale

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that gesture and collaborative embodiment support collaboration, common ground, and multimodal co-construction of meaning. In collaborative settings, jointly enacted gestures helped students copy, extend, correct, and revise one another’s ideas, suggesting benefits for communication and collaborative problem solving rather than only content learning.
finding.measure: Collaborative gesture use, multimodal co-construction, common-ground building

paper_profiles.title: Learning Is Moving in New Ways: The Ecological Dynamics of Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how embodied and interactive technologies can support mathematics learning, and argues that existing theories of learning are not well equipped to explain how students move from sensorimotor action to mathematical reasoning. The authors develop an ecological dynamics perspective for mathematics education, drawing on sports science, ecological psychology, dynamical systems theory, and related approaches to explain how students learn through guided interaction with technology.

The paper centers on the Mathematical Imagery Trainer for Proportion (MIT-P), an experimental embodied-interaction environment in which students manipulate hand positions to make a screen turn green when a target ratio is achieved. The main empirical material comes from qualitative case studies and vignettes of Grade 4–6 students working individually or in pairs in semistructured clinical interviews. The authors analyze how students first discover sensorimotor control strategies, then form attentional anchors such as the interval between the hands, and finally incorporate symbolic artifacts like grids and numerals as frames of reference for proportional reasoning.

The paper concludes that mathematical concepts can emerge through a process in which students solve embodied control problems, then mathematize those action schemes through interaction with instructional artifacts and teacher guidance. The authors argue that ecological dynamics and the construct of attentional anchors help explain how environmental constraints, feedback, and symbolic supports shape learning. They also suggest that this perspective offers design principles for action-based mathematics instruction, especially for creating fields of promoted action that encourage discovery and the development of robust motor-action routines.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: Peer-reviewed qualitative/theoretical paper with case-based empirical vignettes, but no experimental comparison or quantitative effect estimate. The evidence is useful for mechanism-building and design insight, yet it does not meet RCT/QED standards for causal inference.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for proportional reasoning in a priority K-12 population, but it provides no measured effect size. Impact is therefore plausible but unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: embodied-interaction mathematics learning with the Mathematical Imagery Trainer for Proportion (MIT-P), a touchscreen/computer-based activity where students manipulate cursors/hands to discover proportional relationships

finding.finding_summary: This is a theoretical/qualitative design paper about an embodied mathematics learning environment, not a controlled outcomes study. It reports that Grade 4–6 students using the Mathematical Imagery Trainer for Proportion (n=22) developed sensorimotor schemes for proportional reasoning, such as recognizing that the interval between hands changes with the task and that the right hand must be higher for a 1:2 ratio.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of task performance, student talk, and interaction behaviors in task-based semistructured clinical interviews

paper_profiles.title: Classroom dialogue and digital technologies: A scoping review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how digital technologies have been used to support classroom dialogue and what benefits and challenges are associated with that use. Rather than testing a single intervention, it conducts a scoping review and thematic synthesis of empirical research linking dialogue, dialogic pedagogy, and digital technology in school settings.

The review included 72 peer-reviewed studies published between 2000 and 2016, covering learners aged 4 to 18 and conducted across 18 countries. The studies involved a range of technologies, especially computer-mediated communication tools, interactive whiteboards, tablet computers, blogs/microblogs, wikis, and subject-specific tools. Most studies were qualitative or mixed-methods and took place in primary, secondary, or both school contexts.

The review concludes that digital technologies can enhance productive classroom dialogue through several mechanisms: supporting knowledge co-construction, exposing learners to alternative perspectives, enabling metacognition, scaffolding peer and teacher interaction, creating shared dialogic spaces, and improving participation, atmosphere, and motivation. At the same time, the paper identifies recurring risks and constraints, including students’ technical skills, uneven access, distraction, pace pressures, classroom management issues, and teacher pedagogical and technical challenges. Overall, the paper argues that technology benefits depend heavily on the surrounding pedagogy, classroom culture, and implementation conditions.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic scoping review using transparent search and thematic synthesis methods, but it does not estimate causal effects and includes mostly qualitative and mixed-methods studies. It therefore provides useful mapping evidence, but limited credibility for impact estimation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review reports generally positive patterns in dialogue, collaboration, engagement, and learning environments, but these are synthesized qualitatively without pooled effect sizes or a single intervention test. The practical impact is promising but remains unclear in magnitude and causal certainty.

finding.finding_summary: This scoping review synthesizes 72 studies on classroom dialogue and digital technology and finds recurring evidence that technology can support collaboration, metacognition, reasoning, and knowledge co-construction. Reported benefits include more productive dialogue, shared cognition, and opportunities to scaffold understanding, but the paper is descriptive rather than estimating a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Qualitative synthesis of reported classroom dialogue, collaboration, reasoning, and metacognitive outcomes across included studies

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, digital technologies were often associated with higher motivation, engagement, inclusion, and participation in classroom dialogue. The review reports 15 studies linking technology use to motivation/engagement and 13 studies linking it to learner inclusion/participation, but no pooled effect size was calculated.
finding.measure: Observed motivation, engagement, participation, and inclusion in classroom dialogue settings
finding.study_size: n=72 studies (15 studies on motivation/engagement; 13 on inclusion/participation)

paper_profiles.title: Recent developments in using digital technology in mathematics education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews selected significant recent developments in the use of digital technology in mathematics education over roughly the previous five years. The authors aim to synthesise important trends and concerns rather than evaluate a single intervention. Their review spans STEAM and critical making, changing classroom spaces, computer algebra systems and dynamic geometry, student collaboration through online environments and social media, artificial intelligence including hyper-personalisation, multimodality and video, the effects of COVID-19, and the epistemology of digital technology through the notion of humans-with-media.

The paper is a narrative review drawing on recent high-impact journal articles and conference proceedings in mathematics education. It does not focus on one participant population or one country; instead, it discusses classroom, online, and blended contexts across school and university settings, with examples such as flipped classrooms, GeoGebra-based activities, social media learning communities, AI-supported personalised learning, and emergency remote teaching during the pandemic. ChatGPT is mentioned as part of the broader discussion of generative AI, but no empirical study of ChatGPT implementation is reported.

The main conclusions are that digital technologies are reshaping how mathematics is taught and learned, with a shift from routine calculation toward mathematical thinking, collaboration, and personalised learning. The authors also stress important risks: inequitable access, overreliance on technology, possible reduction in conceptual understanding, distraction, ethical issues, and the need for stronger teacher preparation. They argue that future research should examine long-term outcomes, effectiveness for different technologies and populations, assessment, and how AI such as ChatGPT will alter mathematical activity and pedagogical relationships.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review and theoretical synthesis, not an empirical evaluation of ChatGPT in middle school mathematics. It does not report a primary study design, causal identification, or outcome data specific to the retrieved topic.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that ChatGPT and related AI tools may reshape mathematics learning through personalization and human-with-media interaction, but it provides no measured effect sizes or direct evidence of impact. The likely influence is conceptually important, yet the empirical impact remains unclear from this article.

interventions.use_case: Discussion of ChatGPT as a generative AI tool that may support mathematics learning through collectives of student-teachers-with-ChatGPT, including personalized explanations, hints, and adaptive support for mathematical tasks.
Discussion of AI-driven adaptive platforms that model learner goals, preferences, and knowledge to personalize mathematics instruction, pacing, and practice.

Examples of interactive online mathematics platforms and digital tools used for practice and instruction, including adaptive exercises and instant feedback features (e.g., Khan Academy, IXL-like platforms).

paper_profiles.title: From Design to Implementation to Practice: a Learning by Teaching System: Betty’s Brain
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews a decade of research on Betty’s Brain, a computer-based learning environment built around the learning-by-teaching paradigm. The authors ask how the system’s design evolved from an initial proof-of-concept into a classroom-oriented open-ended learning environment, and what the accumulated evidence reveals about student learning, task difficulties, and the role of scaffolding.

Betty’s Brain asks middle school students to learn science content by constructing causal maps and teaching that knowledge to a virtual agent, Betty. Students read hypertext resources, build and revise their causal maps, quiz Betty, inspect her answers, and use feedback from Betty and a mentor agent, Mr. Davis, to improve their models. The paper emphasizes how interface redesigns, conversational feedback, and later coherence analysis were used to better understand students’ behavior and support more adaptive scaffolding.

The paper reports that the system can motivate students and support science learning, but also that many learners struggle with the interconnected tasks of reading, translating text into causal relations, using quiz feedback, and deciding how to revise their maps. More successful students showed higher coherence in their actions, better map accuracy, and stronger science gains. The authors conclude that open-ended learning environments need stronger task-specific and metacognitive scaffolds, and that behavioral analytics such as coherence analysis can help diagnose difficulty and guide support.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed overview/reflection paper synthesizing findings from multiple prior classroom and pull-out studies, but it is not itself a single controlled evaluation with a clearly reported experimental design in this article. Much of the evidence is descriptive, correlational, or drawn from previously published studies, so only one credibility criterion is clearly met.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful learning and engagement benefits for some students, but the effects are uneven and often not quantified with effect sizes in this article. Overall impact appears modest and context-specific rather than broadly demonstrated at a medium/large level.

interventions.use_case: Teachable-agent learning-by-teaching environment (Betty’s Brain) for middle school science, where students build causal maps, ask a virtual agent questions, and quiz the agent to learn domain content and monitor understanding.
Virtual pedagogical agent and mentor agent interaction (Betty and Mr. Davis) used as conversational support and feedback channels inside the learning environment.

finding.finding_summary: Across 10 years of classroom and pull-out studies, the Betty’s Brain environment generally supported science learning, but student success varied substantially by how they used the system. The paper reports that more successful students showed significantly higher science learning gains and better causal map accuracy; in one 40-student study, 18 students made very little progress, while 22 taught a correct or nearly correct map, and 6 made meaningful progress.
finding.measure: Science learning gains; causal map accuracy / map scores; task performance in teaching Betty
finding.study_size: multiple studies; one cited classroom study n=40 and one clustering study n=98

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the learning-by-teaching design increased engagement and motivation, with students showing the protégé effect and social responsibility toward Betty. However, many students also experienced frustration and disengagement when they could not interpret feedback or use the causal modeling tools effectively.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, frustration/disengagement observations, time disengaged
finding.study_size: multiple studies; one analysis reported 77% of feedback ignored and a clustering study with n=98

finding.finding_summary: A major substantive focus of the paper is students’ metacognitive and self-regulated learning behaviors in an open-ended environment. The authors report that more successful students used more systematic, coherent sequences of reading, editing, and quizzing, while struggling students often ignored feedback; in one video-based study, 77% of feedback from Betty and Mr. Davis was ignored.
finding.measure: Coherence metrics, sequence mining, metacognitive strategy use, feedback uptake
finding.study_size: one clustering study n=98; one video analysis study (n not reported); one cited study n=40

finding.finding_summary: The redesigned interface and coherence analysis framework improved the system’s ability to track what students were doing and to support more targeted scaffolding decisions. The paper reports that coherence-analysis metrics predicted task performance and learning gains and distinguished behavior profiles beyond what learning gains or map correctness alone could capture, though no numeric effect sizes are given.
finding.measure: Predictive validity of coherence-analysis metrics; behavior profiling; support for scaffolding decisions
finding.study_size: n=98 for the clustering analysis; recent classroom study referenced in Segedy et al. 2015

paper_profiles.title: In search of attributes that support self-regulation in blended learning environments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what attributes of blended learning environments support learners’ self-regulation. The authors argue that blended learning can place high demands on learners’ cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational regulation, yet the literature had not clearly identified which design features help learners succeed or struggle in these environments.

To answer this question, the paper conducts a systematic literature review of 95 empirical studies published between 1985 and 2015. The review focuses on blended learning settings that combine online and classroom-based interventions, and examines how specific design attributes relate to self-regulation. The paper is theoretical in scope rather than an intervention study: it synthesizes prior research across adult and postsecondary learning contexts, with emphasis on course-level learning tasks.

The review identifies seven attributes that support self-regulation: authenticity, personalization, learner control, scaffolding, interaction, reflection cues, and calibration cues. The authors conclude that these attributes shape task definition, goal-setting, planning, and self-monitoring by influencing learners’ cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational processes. They also argue that these attributes are not unique to blended learning but are central to effective learning environments more broadly, and that the main contribution of the paper is a design framework for supporting self-regulated learning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic literature review, but it synthesizes heterogeneous studies rather than reporting a single well-controlled experiment or meta-analytic effect estimate. The evidence base includes many correlational, survey, and qualitative studies, so causal credibility is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests meaningful design principles for supporting self-regulation in blended learning, but it does not provide a quantified overall effect size or a direct test of student impact. The practical impact is therefore important but still somewhat indirect and unclear in magnitude.

finding.finding_summary: This systematic literature review (n=95 publications) identifies seven blended-learning attributes that support self-regulation: authenticity, personalization, learner control, scaffolding, interaction, reflection cues, and calibration cues. The paper does not estimate a single effect size, but synthesizes evidence that these design features generally support metacognition and self-regulated learning, while also noting risks such as cognitive overload for novices and reduced effectiveness when learner control is high without sufficient scaffolding.
finding.measure: Systematic synthesis of empirical studies on self-regulated learning in blended learning environments; outcomes included cognition, metacognition, motivation, and self-regulatory behaviors

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that several blended-learning design attributes—especially interaction, personalization, and authenticity—are associated with higher motivation, satisfaction, and engagement. However, the direction is mixed for some learners: low prior knowledge or low self-regulatory ability can make high learner control frustrating, and lack of social interaction can increase dropout risk and decrease satisfaction.
finding.measure: Motivation, satisfaction, engagement, dropout risk, and related self-regulatory indicators across the reviewed studies

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the application of ChatGPT in ESL/EFL education and related research issues: a systematic review of empirical studies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapid emergence of ChatGPT in English as a second language (ESL) and English as a foreign language (EFL) education and the lack of a comprehensive synthesis of empirical evidence. The authors systematically reviewed 70 empirical studies published within 1.5 years of ChatGPT’s release, aiming to map where and how ChatGPT has been used, what research methods have been employed, and what major research issues have been examined.

The review is organized using the Technology-based Learning Model, which frames analysis around application domains, research methods, and research issues. The included studies covered a range of contexts, but were concentrated in higher education and in East Asia and the Middle East. Most studies focused on writing, with far fewer on speaking and reading and none specifically on listening. The review also identified four broad methodological types: ChatGPT evaluation, AI detection, human observation, and human intervention, with most intervention studies being short-term and often based on surveys and interviews.

Overall, the paper concludes that ChatGPT shows clear affordances for language learning, especially in supporting idea generation, feedback, lesson planning, and learner motivation, while also raising concerns about inaccurate information, privacy, academic dishonesty, over-reliance, and reduced real-life communication. The review argues that future research should include longer-term, more rigorous designs, more objective outcome measures, and broader coverage of under-studied skills and K–12 contexts to better understand both the benefits and risks of ChatGPT in ESL/EFL education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review using PRISMA methods, but it synthesizes mostly qualitative, observational, and short-term intervention studies rather than a set of high-credibility randomized or quasi-experimental studies. The review is useful for mapping evidence, but it does not itself provide a causal estimate of impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests moderate practical promise for ChatGPT in language learning and teacher support, especially for writing and motivation, but the underlying evidence is heterogeneous and often lacks effect sizes. Because benefits and risks are both substantial and the evidence is mostly short-term, the overall impact is best judged as unclear-to-modest rather than large.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of empirical studies on ChatGPT/GPT-4/GPT-4o use in ESL/EFL education, including students using the chatbot for writing help, speaking practice, reading support, and general language-learning assistance; also includes teacher use for lesson planning and feedback generation.

finding.finding_summary: Across 70 empirical studies, ChatGPT was most often used for writing. The review reports that it can help students generate ideas, organize texts, improve spelling/grammar and vocabulary, and that several comparison studies found significant gains in writing performance and motivation (e.g., p=0.00 across multiple higher-education studies), but other studies found inaccuracy, weak feedback quality, and inconsistent AI-detection performance.
finding.measure: Writing performance, syntactic complexity, vocabulary range, coherence/cohesion, grammatical accuracy, writing motivation, and writing assessment quality
finding.study_size: n=70 review; writing-focused studies n=30; comparison studies n=6

finding.finding_summary: Few studies addressed speaking, but those that did found ChatGPT could generate dialogue materials, act as a speaking partner, and support speech assessment. Benefits were reported for confidence and speaking skill, while limitations included inaccurate outputs, prompt difficulties, and technical problems; no pooled effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Speaking task performance, learner confidence, perceived task competence, and speech pause assessment

finding.finding_summary: Several studies reported that students generally perceived ChatGPT as useful and satisfying, and some comparison studies found higher motivation in ChatGPT-assisted writing conditions than in traditional instruction. The review notes these motivation gains but also reports concerns about over-reliance and diminished real-life communication.
finding.measure: Motivation surveys, satisfaction/self-report, perceived usefulness
finding.study_size: motivation/satisfaction studies across the review; comparison studies n=2 for motivation

finding.finding_summary: The review highlights that ChatGPT may support idea generation, organization, and feedback-seeking, but teachers and students also worried it could weaken critical thinking and creativity through over-reliance. These durable-skill effects were mainly drawn from qualitative and survey evidence rather than controlled designs.
finding.measure: Perceived critical thinking, creativity, and feedback-seeking behavior
finding.study_size: multiple observational studies; exact pooled n not reported

finding.finding_summary: The review found clear evidence that ChatGPT can reduce teacher workload by generating lesson plans, exercises, and writing feedback, and by producing more feedback than human teachers in some studies. However, teachers also flagged concerns about feedback quality, relevance, and the need for professional judgment.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, lesson-planning support, feedback generation, and writing-assessment efficiency
finding.study_size: multiple studies; exact pooled n not reported

finding.finding_summary: Across the review, teachers and students raised institutional concerns about incorrect information, privacy leakage, academic dishonesty, and the need for updated assessment policies and AI literacy. The paper argues these risks shape how schools can govern ChatGPT adoption, but it does not report a pooled quantitative institutional effect.
finding.measure: Perceptions of academic integrity, privacy, policy needs, and teacher professional development requirements
finding.study_size: teacher and student perspective studies n=14 and n=11 on general perspectives

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Quantitative Decline: Conceptual Shifts in Adolescents' Development of Interest in Mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether adolescents' mathematics interest changes not only in amount but also in meaning. The authors ask whether the construct of interest becomes structurally different across adolescence, and whether younger and older students think about mathematics interest in qualitatively different ways. The motivation is to move beyond the common finding that average interest declines during adolescence and to investigate whether the internal meaning of interest shifts over time.

The paper uses two complementary studies. Study 1 reanalyzes longitudinal survey data from a large German mathematics project (PALMA) with 3,193 students followed annually from Grades 5 to 9. Using latent variable modeling and tests of measurement invariance, the authors assess whether the six-item mathematics interest scale functions the same way across time. Study 2 interviews 70 students in Grades 5 and 9 using cognitive validation procedures to examine how they interpret the same items and which components of interest they mention spontaneously.

The main findings are that mathematics interest is not psychometrically invariant across Grades 5 to 9 and that students' concepts of interest shift with age. Younger students more often frame interest in affective terms such as enjoyment, while older students more often mention cognitive and self-directed aspects such as wanting to know more, autonomy, and sustained engagement. The authors conclude that developmental research should account for qualitative changes in constructs over time, not just quantitative declines, and that cognitive validation can help reveal changes in item meaning across age groups.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical study using longitudinal modeling and qualitative interviews, but it is not an intervention evaluation and does not test a technology or AI treatment. The design is observational/psychometric, so it fits a lower-evidence qualitative/correlational tier for intervention purposes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not evaluate any AI or educational technology intervention, so there is no demonstrated intervention impact on learning or implementation outcomes. Its findings are about construct development in mathematics interest, not about effectiveness of ChatGPT or similar tools.

finding.finding_summary: This paper studies developmental changes in mathematics interest among adolescents rather than an AI intervention. In Study 1 (n=3,193), longitudinal latent variable modeling found significant noninvariance in item intercepts, structural weights, and error variances from Grade 5 to Grade 9, indicating structural change in interest over time. In Study 2 (n=70), cognitive validation interviews showed a shift from affect-laden associations in Grade 5 to more cognitively oriented concepts in Grade 9; the age-group differences were small-to-medium and reported as medium in size (e.g., emotional experiences more frequent in Grade 5, thirst for knowledge/autonomy/behavioral engagement more frequent in Grade 9).
finding.measure: Mathematics interest scale measurement invariance; cognitive validation interview coding of interest components; frequencies of affective/cognitive statements
finding.std_deviation: Grade 5/9 interview SDs for age were 0.60 years; other SDs not_reported

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT-Based Simulation Helps to Develop the Pre-Service Mathematics Teachers’ Critical Thinking
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can be used as a simulation tool in pre-service mathematics teacher preparation and whether working with ChatGPT-generated solutions develops critical thinking. The authors frame ChatGPT as a digital platform that can generate student-like answers to mathematics problems, including plausible but incorrect solutions, which pre-service teachers can analyze, critique, and correct.

The study was conducted in 2023 at Sumy State Pedagogical University in Ukraine with 32 pre-service mathematics teachers: 14 bachelor’s students and 18 master’s students. Participants completed tasks based on the topic of mathematical induction. They first examined ChatGPT-generated proofs, identified mistakes, corrected them, and asked ChatGPT to respond to their corrections. The authors also measured critical thinking twice, a month apart, using a rubric based on analytical reasoning, identifying inconsistencies, correcting errors, and seeking rational problem-solving approaches.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT can generate sufficiently plausible student-like answers, although it frequently produces mathematical errors, weak justifications, and incomplete or incorrect alternative proofs. The pre-service teachers were generally able to detect many of these errors, and their performance improved on the second round of work. A Wilcoxon test indicated a significant gain in the authors’ critical-thinking measure. The authors argue that ChatGPT can support simulation-based teacher training, but they also emphasize risks and tradeoffs: output quality depends on prompt wording and language, ChatGPT often fails to correct its own mistakes, and its use requires careful, balanced grading and instructor oversight.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small single-group pedagogical experiment without a control/comparison condition, so causal inference is limited. The study is peer-reviewed and uses a pre-post nonparametric test, but it is best characterized as qualitative/quasi-experimental evidence with substantial concerns.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are confined to a small sample of pre-service mathematics teachers and concern critical thinking rather than student achievement. No effect size is reported, and the evidence suggests a modest/unclear impact beyond the study context.

interventions.use_case: Using ChatGPT as a simulation of secondary-school pupil responses in math problem solving, where pre-service mathematics teachers prompt the model, inspect generated proofs, and try to correct its errors

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that repeated work with ChatGPT-based math-answer simulation improved pre-service mathematics teachers' critical thinking. On the Wilcoxon test, 18 of 32 participants improved and 22 changed their score from the first to the second task set; the authors report T=243 and reject the null hypothesis in favor of improvement.
finding.measure: Critical thinking task score (0-8) based on ability to analyze information, identify inconsistencies, rectify mistakes, and seek rational solutions; compared across two administrations one month apart

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective paper examines the opportunities and risks of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) for human learning. Rather than reporting a single empirical study, it synthesizes ideas from learning sciences, educational technology, and human-computer interaction to argue that GenAI can reshape how learning is supported, how resources are created, how feedback is delivered, and how assessment is designed.

The paper discusses GenAI as a learning support tool (including examples such as ChatGPT and Khanmigo), a resource-generation tool for instructional materials, a feedback provider, and a basis for more adaptive assessment systems. It frames these possibilities within human-centered theories such as Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development, constructivism, and inquiry-based learning, and argues that educators should retain control over pedagogical decisions while using GenAI to scale support and diversify learning experiences.

The paper’s main conclusions are cautionary and forward-looking. It emphasizes that GenAI can improve personalization, efficiency, and accessibility, but it also raises serious concerns about hallucinations, bias, privacy, equity, overreliance, and assessment validity. The authors call for AI literacy, evidence-based decision-making, and stronger methodological rigor in future research, noting that current evidence is still limited and that rigorous studies are needed to determine when GenAI genuinely improves learning versus when it creates only an illusion of performance gains.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed perspective article, not an empirical study. It synthesizes prior literature and argues for future research but reports no original intervention evaluation or causal design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report any measured learning effects, effect sizes, or direct evidence of impact on student outcomes. Its claims are conceptual and speculative rather than demonstrated empirical impacts.

interventions.use_case: A perspective discussion of ChatGPT/Khanmigo-style generative AI tutors used for personalized, adaptive learning support, including guided questioning, step-by-step instruction, and conversational tutoring in mathematics and other subjects.

paper_profiles.title: Visual Instruction Tuning
paper_profiles.venue: 37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces visual instruction tuning, an approach for extending instruction tuning from text-only large language models to multimodal vision-language models. The central problem is the lack of large-scale multimodal instruction-following data, which limits the ability of models to act as general-purpose visual assistants that can follow human instructions over images. To address this, the authors propose a pipeline that uses ChatGPT/GPT-4 to transform existing image-text pairs into instruction-following training examples by generating questions, conversations, detailed descriptions, and reasoning prompts from symbolic image representations such as captions and bounding boxes.

The proposed model, LLaVA, combines a frozen CLIP vision encoder with a Vicuna language model and is trained in two stages: first, a feature-alignment pretraining stage on filtered image-caption pairs; second, end-to-end fine-tuning on 158K generated multimodal instruction-following samples. The paper evaluates the method on a multimodal chatbot benchmark and on ScienceQA, a multimodal science reasoning dataset, showing strong gains in instruction following and competitive or state-of-the-art performance on science question answering when combined with GPT-4 judging/ensembling.

The work does not study students or classrooms; rather, it is a model-development paper focused on multimodal AI capabilities. The authors also discuss risks and tradeoffs including hallucination, inherited bias from base models, misuse risks, and evaluation challenges, and they note that performance can degrade on tasks requiring high-resolution perception, broad knowledge, or robust grounding. Overall, the paper argues that synthetic instruction data generated by strong language models can effectively bootstrap multimodal assistants, but also highlights limitations in grounding and reliable visual understanding.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed machine learning systems paper, but it is not an education intervention study and does not evaluate student learning outcomes, experimental schooling conditions, or K-12 instructional impact. The reported evidence is model benchmark performance rather than educational effectiveness evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct educational impact is demonstrated for students, classrooms, or middle school mathematics achievement. The paper reports benchmark gains on multimodal reasoning and chat ability, which are not interpretable as instructional impact for the requested topic.

interventions.use_case: A multimodal chat assistant built by visual instruction tuning, using GPT-4/ChatGPT-generated instruction data to make LLaVA follow user questions about images and provide conversational, descriptive, and reasoning-based responses.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that visual instruction tuning improves multimodal reasoning on ScienceQA, reaching 90.92% accuracy for LLaVA versus 85.19% for LLaMA-Adapter and 91.68% for the prior SoTA MM-CoTLarge. In the authors' own ensemble, LLaVA + GPT-4 (judge) achieved 92.53% accuracy, the new best reported result in their table. This is evidence of improved scientific question answering and reasoning, not K-12 student learning.
finding.measure: ScienceQA multiple-choice accuracy
finding.study_size: n=21,208 total questions in ScienceQA; split 12,726 train / 4,241 validation / 4,241 test

paper_profiles.title: A large-scale comparison of human-written versus ChatGPT-generated essays
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can generate argumentative essays that humans rate as equal or better than student-written essays, and whether the two ChatGPT versions studied (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 via the ChatGPT web interface) differ in quality and linguistic profile. The authors motivate the work as an independent, rigorous assessment of generative AI in an educational writing task, responding to concerns that current vendor benchmarks are not sufficiently transparent or methodologically sound.

The intervention/approach is not a classroom teaching intervention but a comparative content-generation and rating study. The authors took 90 argumentative essay prompts from an existing corpus of high-school-level essays, prompted ChatGPT-3 and ChatGPT-4 in a zero-shot setting to write about 200-word essays, and compared these outputs with one human-written essay per topic from an online forum frequented by German high-school students. Six essays were rated by each participating teacher, using seven essay-quality criteria (topic/completeness, logic/composition, expressiveness, language mastery, complexity, vocabulary/text linking, language constructs). The study also computed linguistic markers such as lexical diversity, syntactic complexity, nominalization, modals, epistemic markers, and discourse markers.

The evaluation was completed by 111 secondary-school teachers in Germany during a two-hour online training session about ChatGPT; 90 topics produced 270 essays in total (human, ChatGPT-3, ChatGPT-4), with high inter-rater agreement. The paper reports that both ChatGPT versions outperformed the human-written essays on all seven rating criteria, with GPT-4 outperforming GPT-3.5 on several dimensions, especially logical structure, vocabulary/text linking, and complexity. The authors conclude that current generative models can write strong argumentative essays and may require educators to rethink homework and assessment; however, they also note notable tradeoffs, including rigid formulaic structure, fewer discourse markers in GPT-4, and the fact that the study’s human essays came from non-native speakers, limiting generalizability to some other student populations.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed observational comparison study with human expert ratings and within-subject design, but it is not an intervention trial and does not evaluate student learning outcomes directly. The evidence is methodologically solid for benchmarking essay quality, yet it does not meet RCT/QED standards for educational effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests potentially large effects on writing quality for AI-generated essays, but the impact is on essay generation quality rather than demonstrated learning gains for students. It also highlights risks and tradeoffs—formulaic structure, dependence on language proficiency, and possible homework/assessment disruption—without measuring downstream educational benefits.

interventions.use_case: zero-shot prompting of ChatGPT-3 and ChatGPT-4 to generate argumentative student essays for comparison against human-written essays

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT-generated essays were rated significantly higher than human-written student essays on all essay-quality criteria, with the largest gains for ChatGPT-4. Across the seven-point rubric, human vs ChatGPT-3 showed medium-to-large effects (d=0.52 to 1.15), and human vs ChatGPT-4 showed large-to-very-large effects (d=0.88 to 1.43); overall mean ratings were 3.69 for humans, 4.36 for ChatGPT-3, and 4.68 for ChatGPT-4. The paper treats this as evidence that the model can produce high-quality argumentative writing, though it also highlights tradeoffs such as rigidity and formulaic structure.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of argumentative essay quality across topic/completeness, logic/composition, expressiveness/comprehensiveness, language mastery, complexity, vocabulary/text linking, and language constructs
finding.std_deviation: SD ranged roughly 1.01 to 1.37 across rubric dimensions

paper_profiles.title: Automated Feedback in Math Education: A Comparative Analysis of LLMs for Open-Ended Responses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models can support automated scoring and feedback for middle-school mathematics open-response items. The authors compare three approaches: a fine-tuned Mistral-based model called GOAT, the prior SBERT-Canberra similarity-based method, and GPT-4 used in zero-shot mode with a grading rubric. The main questions are whether these models can predict teacher scores accurately and which model produces the most useful feedback for student responses.

The study uses student responses to open-ended math problems drawn from an online learning platform, specifically from a group of about 50 teachers who used open-ended questions in their classrooms. The dataset is filtered to language-based problems only and includes 50 math problems with 100 student responses each. The models are evaluated on held-out test data using AUC, RMSE, and Cohen’s kappa for scoring, and two human evaluators with teaching experience rate feedback for accuracy, relevance, motivation, and preference.

Quantitatively, GOAT performs best on score prediction, outperforming SBERT-Canberra and GPT-4 on all scoring metrics. Qualitatively, however, GPT-4 produces the most accurate, relevant, motivating, and preferred feedback according to the human raters. The authors conclude that fine-tuned open-source LLMs can improve automated scoring, but that GPT-4 currently generates stronger educational feedback. They also note tradeoffs: GOAT inherits weaknesses from imperfect teacher-written feedback in its training data, while GPT-4’s stronger feedback quality comes from its broader pretraining rather than task-specific adaptation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a comparative model-evaluation study with a held-out test split and human ratings, but it is not an experimental study of student learning outcomes. Evidence is useful and reasonably systematic, yet primarily technical/qualitative rather than a rigorous causal educational evaluation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but modest practical impact for teacher-facing automation, especially for scoring and feedback workflow support. However, it does not demonstrate student achievement gains, and the evidence is limited to model performance and human preference judgments rather than classroom impact.

interventions.use_case: automated scoring and feedback generation for middle-school students' open-ended math responses using fine-tuned LLMs and an LLM baseline

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily evaluates whether AI can automate scoring and feedback generation for open-ended middle-school math responses, which would reduce teacher grading workload. GOAT achieved the best scoring performance (AUC=0.697, RMSE=1.119, Kappa=0.422) on 1,000 held-out responses, suggesting improved efficiency for auto-scoring relative to SBERT and GPT-4. Human evaluators also judged GPT-4 and GOAT-generated feedback as usable starting points, indicating potential workflow support for teachers.
finding.measure: Auto-scoring accuracy (AUC, RMSE, Cohen's Kappa) and human-rated feedback usefulness/preference
finding.study_size: n=5000 responses total; n=1000 test responses for scoring; n=100 sampled responses for feedback review

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Auto-Grading and Feedback System for Constructive Geometry Tasks Using Large Language Models on an Online Math Platform
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a large language model (LLM)-based auto-grading and feedback system can support middle school students’ learning in constructive geometry tasks on an online math platform. The authors focus on a gap in mathematics education technology: providing scalable, individualized feedback for open-ended and construction-based geometry work, where answer-only grading is insufficient. Their system uses GPT-4 for grading open-ended explanations and generating adaptive feedback, while deterministic rules grade closed-ended and geometry-construction responses.

The intervention was implemented on Algeomath, a Korean web-based dynamic geometry platform, and centered on a six-stage sequence of circumcenter/circumcircle tasks. Students completed closed-ended items, written explanations, and dynamic geometry construction tasks, with up to three retries per item and feedback that became progressively more explicit across attempts. The field study involved 79 middle-school students in four classes in South Korea. Outcomes included agreement between LLM and teacher judgments, feedback quality ratings by an expert, and student response patterns across attempts.

The study found strong alignment with teacher grading for rule-based items and substantial agreement for open-ended explanations, though the LLM was more reliable at identifying correct answers than incorrect ones. Expert ratings suggested that feedback was generally usable but sometimes suffered from answer leakage, imprecise terminology, or overly generic prompts. Student data showed that many initially incorrect answers were corrected after feedback, especially on simpler items, but evidence for longer-term transfer to later questions was weak and not statistically significant. Overall, the paper concludes that LLMs can support scalable formative assessment in mathematics, but feedback design, terminology handling, and prevention of solution leakage need improvement.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a field study/pilot with 79 middle-school students, combining descriptive analytics, qualitative review, and non-randomized comparisons rather than a controlled experiment. It provides useful implementation evidence, but causal claims about learning impact are limited by the design and by the absence of a direct counterfactual.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful short-term gains in task completion and moderate grading reliability, but the learning impact is modest and not clearly causal. Transfer effects were not statistically significant, so the overall educational impact is promising but still unclear.

interventions.use_case: LLM-assisted auto-grading and personalized formative feedback for constructive geometry tasks on an online math platform, with up to four attempts and adaptive hints based on student response history.
Dynamic geometry platform (Algeomath) delivering interactive constructive geometry tasks, embedded prompts, and automated evaluation during middle-school math practice.

finding.finding_summary: The system supported short-term correction and completion of middle-school geometry tasks, with an overall post-feedback conversion rate of 36.7% (260/708) across initially incorrect responses. In the iterative learning analysis, cumulative success rose from about 0.60 on the first attempt to about 0.73 on the second and about 0.80 by the fourth, suggesting feedback helped procedural performance on constructive geometry items.
finding.measure: Attempt-level correctness on constructive geometry tasks; post-feedback conversion rate; cumulative learning curves by attempt

finding.finding_summary: The paper examined conceptual understanding through open-ended explanation tasks and expert ratings of whether feedback supported correct mathematical reasoning. Grading agreement with teachers was substantial overall for open-ended items (agreement rate 0.866, Cohen’s κ=0.737 across n=878 responses), but concept-level transfer to later questions was not clearly demonstrated (all p>0.05), indicating clear short-term gains but unclear longer-term transfer.
finding.measure: Teacher agreement on open-ended explanation grading; expert rubric ratings of feedback quality; transfer to later target questions

finding.finding_summary: The iterative feedback design was associated with more precise, conceptually grounded revisions in student explanations, such as moving from vague responses to accurate references to equidistance. However, the evidence for broader metacognitive transfer was limited because later-question transfer tests were not statistically significant (e.g., Q10 p=0.547, Q11 p=0.643, Q18 p=0.624).
finding.measure: Iterative answer refinement quality; transfer tests across subsequent questions

finding.finding_summary: The LLM-based grading system achieved substantial agreement with teacher judgments on open-ended responses (overall agreement 0.866, Cohen’s κ=0.737, n=878), and rule-based grading for closed-ended/CGT items reached 100% agreement. This indicates strong potential for scalable formative assessment with reduced teacher grading burden, although some items still required refinement.
finding.measure: Agreement with teacher grading; Cohen’s kappa; item-level grading reliability

paper_profiles.title: Combining Large Language Models with Tutoring System Intelligence: A Case Study in Caregiver Homework Support
paper_profiles.venue: LAK 2025 (Proceedings of the 15th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how large language models (LLMs) can be combined with intelligent tutoring system data to support caregivers who help children with math homework. The authors focus on a practical problem in learning analytics: caregivers often want to help but lack confidence or up-to-date knowledge of school math curricula, and existing support tools do not provide timely, context-sensitive instructional guidance.

The intervention is the Caregiver Conversational Support Tool (CCST), embedded in a middle school equation-solving tutoring system (Lynnette). CCST uses real-time problem-solving context from the tutoring system—such as whether the student used hints, whether the latest attempt was correct, the current equation, prior chat messages, and suggested next steps—to prompt an open-source Llama 3 model to generate three caregiver message recommendations. The researchers iteratively engineered prompts and then evaluated the tool through a prototyping study with ten middle school caregivers, including in-person workshop sessions and remote Zoom interviews. The study used thematic analysis of interview and annotation data to understand caregiver perceptions of the generated conversational support.

Findings suggest that caregivers valued content-level support more than motivational support. They especially liked recommendations that prompted students to explain their thinking, because these helped caregivers understand student metacognition and potential knowledge gaps. Caregivers also appreciated that the system incorporated live contextual information, but they found many generated messages too long and sometimes too slow for real-time use. The authors conclude that LLMs can be made more useful for hybrid tutoring when combined with tutoring-system intelligence and tutoring best-practice examples, but that message length, latency, tone, and personalization remain important design tradeoffs.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative prototyping/case study with a small convenience sample and no controlled comparison of student outcomes. It provides useful design evidence, but credibility for causal claims is limited by the absence of experimental evaluation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful support for hybrid tutoring, but it reports no measurable learning gains and only qualitative perceptions from caregivers. The practical impact is promising yet unclear, with notable tradeoffs in latency and message length.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated conversational recommendations for middle school caregivers supporting a child’s math homework in an ITS, using real-time problem-solving context (accuracy, hint use, next steps) and tutoring-practice examples to generate messages.
Equation-solving tutoring system (Lynnette) providing adaptive step feedback, hinting, and solution-path context that is used to condition caregiver chat recommendations.

finding.finding_summary: Caregivers reported that the generated messages were most valuable when they prompted student self-explanation and metacognition, helping caregivers better understand their child’s reasoning and knowledge gaps. In the qualitative sample of n=10 caregivers, five explicitly preferred prompts that elicited thought processes, and the authors report these metacognitive prompts were seen as especially useful for supporting constructive homework help.
finding.measure: Caregiver interview themes about metacognitive support and self-explanation prompts

finding.finding_summary: The tool was perceived as improving the quality of math support by giving caregivers content-level guidance aligned to the live equation-solving context, rather than generic encouragement. The paper does not report student achievement gains, but in design evaluation with n=10 caregivers, six preferred content-focused recommendations and the authors report that context-based prompting produced mathematically relevant, non-hallucinated advice for equation solving.
finding.measure: Caregiver perceptions of math-content support and contextual relevance of generated messages

finding.finding_summary: Caregivers had mixed views on motivational/praise-oriented messages: some found them encouraging and appropriately gentle, while others judged them artificial, unnecessary, or poorly aligned with how they normally support homework. In the caregiver sample, six preferred content-level support over motivational support, two liked both, and one preferred to handle motivation independently.
finding.measure: Caregiver interview themes about motivational support, praise, tone, and message usability

finding.finding_summary: The system was viewed as feasible but somewhat burdensome in real-time use because message generation could be slow and recommendations were often too long to process quickly during live tutoring. The authors report average latency of about 25 seconds, with 2 of 6 caregivers finding generation slow and 6 of 9 caregivers finding messages too long.
finding.measure: Caregiver judgments of latency, message length, and usability during prototyping interviews

paper_profiles.title: Seeing the Big Picture: Evaluating Multimodal LLMs’ Ability to Interpret and Grade Handwritten Student Work
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can accurately interpret and grade handwritten student mathematics work, and where their capabilities break down. The authors focus on two related tasks: grading routine handwritten arithmetic with objective answers, and evaluating more complex student-drawn mathematical illustrations that require visual interpretation and pedagogical judgment.

The study uses two experiments. Experiment A analyzes 288 scanned handwritten arithmetic responses from middle school students in Ghana completing fractions, percentages, and basic algebra. Experiment B analyzes 150 mathematical illustrations drawn by American elementary students, using the DrawEDU dataset. In the first experiment, four frontier MLLMs are asked to identify students’ answers and judge correctness. In the second, the models first grade images directly and then grade the same items again with human-provided descriptions of the visual content to separate visual perception from judgment.

Results show a sharp divide between task types. On routine arithmetic, the best model, Gemini 2.5 Pro, reached near-human performance, with 95% grading accuracy and substantial agreement with human raters. On mathematical illustrations, however, performance was much weaker: direct image-only grading was poor, and even with human descriptions the models plateaued around moderate agreement levels, similar to initial human inter-rater agreement but not sufficient for autonomous deployment. The authors conclude that current MLLMs may be useful for screening routine handwritten arithmetic, but they still lack the visual and contextual tacit knowledge needed for reliable interpretation of student mathematical thinking in more open-ended, ambiguous work.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical evaluation with two experiments and careful human-adjudicated ground truth, but it is not an RCT or QED about student learning outcomes. It is best classified as a methodological/benchmarking study with strong internal procedures but limited causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows potentially useful operational gains for automating routine math grading, but it does not test effects on student achievement. Its practical impact is therefore indirect and currently constrained by the modest performance on ambiguous mathematical illustrations.

interventions.use_case: evaluating multimodal LLMs for automated grading and feedback-like assessment of handwritten student mathematics work, including arithmetic worksheets and drawn mathematical responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds near-human performance on routine handwritten arithmetic work from Ghanaian middle school students: the best model (Gemini 2.5 Pro) reached 95% grading accuracy and LWK=0.90 on 288 responses. However, performance dropped sharply on 150 student-drawn mathematical illustrations, where direct image-only grading was only about 61-64% accuracy with kappa as low as 0.15-0.38, improving to 72-75% accuracy and kappa 0.43-0.47 when provided human descriptions. This suggests current MLLMs can handle objective procedural math grading reasonably well but remain weak on more conceptually and visually ambiguous mathematical work.
finding.measure: Grading accuracy, Linear Weighted Kappa (LWK)/kappa, precision, recall, F1 on handwritten arithmetic worksheets and mathematical illustration grading

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests a substantial potential productivity gain for educators because MLLMs achieved 95% accuracy on routine handwritten arithmetic grading, implying they could automate a large share of routine scoring work. For more ambiguous illustration-based work, human-in-the-loop support would still be required because direct model performance was only moderate and improved to a ceiling around kappa=0.47 even with human descriptions, indicating limited autonomy for complex grading tasks.
finding.measure: Automated grading performance as a proxy for teacher workload reduction

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Large Language Models Creation of Interactive Learning Lessons
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether large language models can automatically generate high-quality scenario-based lessons for training novice human tutors in middle school mathematics. The authors focus on a practical curriculum-design problem: creating structured tutor training lessons is time-consuming and hard to scale, so they investigate whether an LLM can produce lessons that are pedagogically sound, clear, and useful for instructional design.

The intervention is not a student-facing tutoring treatment but a lesson-generation pipeline built with retrieval-augmented generation and GPT-4o. The system generates English-language tutor training lessons around three middle-school math tutoring topics: encouraging students’ independence, encouraging help-seeking behavior, and turning on cameras. The authors compare several prompting strategies that vary in task decomposition, from generating a whole lesson in one step to splitting it into five segments.

The study evaluates the generated lessons with two experienced human coders using a rubric, and also collects written feedback from two expert lesson designers who compared LLM-generated lessons with human-crafted ones. The context is an online tutor-training platform for novice tutors teaching middle school mathematics. The main finding is that moderate task decomposition worked best: the three-segment approach produced the highest-rated lessons, while one-step generation was weakest and five segments was not better than three. The generated lessons were seen as useful for saving time and producing realistic scenarios, but they also had important weaknesses, especially generic feedback, unclear or overly verbose instructions, and unreliable references. The paper concludes that LLMs can support lesson design as part of a human-AI workflow, but human review remains necessary.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative human-evaluation study of LLM-generated lesson content with coder agreement (Cohen’s κ=0.72), but it is not an experimental study of learner outcomes and does not include a randomized or quasi-experimental comparison on student achievement.
