No original empirical effect sizes are reported because this is a position paper, but the claimed benefit is improved efficiency in producing personalized learning materials and managing adaptive systems.
finding.measure: teacher workload, content-generation efficiency, automated feedback/grading capability

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents a normative argument that combining generative AI with adaptive learning could reshape educational infrastructure, improve personalization at scale, and create new research directions for AI-in-education systems. It also highlights institutional risks and governance needs around fairness, hallucination, accountability, and human oversight, but provides no empirical effect sizes.
finding.measure: governance, fairness, accountability, and broader educational system implications

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that GenAI-supported adaptive learning may support metacognition, self-directed inquiry, and critical thinking if designed carefully, while also warning that overreliance could erode these skills. This is discussed conceptually rather than with measured outcomes, so no empirical effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: critical thinking, metacognition, self-directed inquiry

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI and Its Impact on Personalized Intelligent Tutoring Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how generative artificial intelligence, especially large language models such as GPT-4, can be integrated into intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) to improve personalization, adaptivity, and learner support. The authors frame the work as a synthesis of current research and practical implementation ideas rather than an empirical evaluation. The central question is how generative AI changes the capabilities of ITS for producing educational content, feedback, and dialogue in real time.

The approach discussed includes automated question generation, personalized feedback mechanisms, and interactive dialogue systems. These capabilities are described as ways to tailor instruction to individual learner needs by generating questions of varying difficulty, offering step-by-step explanations of errors, and maintaining conversational tutoring interactions. The paper also discusses broader system design issues such as pedagogical accuracy, bias, engagement, multimodal AI, affective computing, and ethical policy development.

The population and context are general educational settings rather than a specific grade band, subject area, or country. Although examples include mathematics and language learning, the paper does not report a direct study with participants or a target sample. Its main conclusion is that generative AI has strong potential to transform ITS into more responsive and engaging learning environments, but that this promise depends on careful validation, bias mitigation, and thoughtful integration with educational standards and oversight.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/report-style synthesis rather than an empirical study. It does not report a defined design, comparison groups, or original outcome data, so it provides no direct evidence meeting causal or correlational credibility criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No empirical impact is estimated in the paper. The article argues for potential benefits of generative AI in ITS, but it does not report effect sizes or measured student outcomes, so impact remains unquantified.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI/LLMs such as GPT-4 embedded in intelligent tutoring systems to generate personalized questions, real-time feedback, and interactive tutoring dialogues tailored to learner responses.
Personalized tutoring systems that adapt instruction, feedback, and learning pathways to individual learners, with generative AI added to extend traditional rule-based ITS capabilities.

paper_profiles.title: Improving Student Learning with Hybrid Human-AI Tutoring: A Three-Study Quasi-Experimental Investigation
paper_profiles.venue: The 14th Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK ’24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether combining human tutoring with AI-based math software can improve middle school students’ learning engagement and early achievement-related indicators, especially in low-income settings where access to high-quality tutoring is limited. The authors argue that AI can help scale tutoring by handling adaptive instruction while human tutors provide motivation, relationship-building, and targeted support. The key question is whether this hybrid human-AI model improves student learning processes more effectively than software use alone, and whether benefits differ by students’ baseline math ability.

The study reports three quasi-experimental implementations across three urban U.S. middle schools, each using a different math platform and tutoring configuration. Site 1 used IXL in a Pennsylvania middle school with a delayed-treatment design comparing software only, software plus math teacher support, and software plus math teacher plus remote tutoring. Site 2 used i-Ready in a California middle school and compared weeks before tutoring to a brief late-spring tutoring period delivered remotely in a round-robin format. Site 3 used Carnegie Learning’s MATHia in a Pennsylvania charter school and examined changes when tutor availability improved and a real-time dashboard was introduced. Across sites, students were overwhelmingly low-income and in grades 6–8, with mostly Latinx, Black, or Black male student populations depending on the site.

Findings consistently showed that hybrid human-AI tutoring increased student engagement with the software and improved intermediate learning measures such as time spent, questions answered, skills proficient, lessons passed, and workspaces completed. Effects were strongest for students with lower baseline performance, suggesting the model may help close gaps rather than only benefiting higher-achieving students. The paper concludes that rapid quasi-experimental methods can provide useful early evidence for AI-supported tutoring programs and that future work should refine dashboards, tutor-student ratios, and eventually test impacts on external achievement measures.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental multi-site field study, but it lacks random assignment and includes site-specific implementation differences and non-equivalent comparisons. The design provides useful early evidence, yet internal validity is weaker than a well-designed RCT or strong QED with tighter controls.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports positive, practically meaningful gains in engagement and progress, including a tutoring effect of β=0.202 for time spent and 0.36 additional workspaces/hour in one site. However, the outcomes are mostly intermediate process measures rather than external achievement tests, so the overall impact is modest rather than large.

interventions.use_case: math software use within hybrid human-AI tutoring across middle school sites (IXL, i-Ready, and MATHia) with remote tutors and/or math teacher support, including dashboard-guided support in one site

adaptive one-on-one math learning software used as the instructional engine within the tutoring model, especially MATHia; the paper also treats IXL and i-Ready as adaptive math practice platforms in a tutoring context
personalized math practice platforms (i-Ready Personalized Instruction and IXL) that adapt lesson assignment and skill progression based on student performance data
tutor-facing real-time dashboard/learning analytics (MATHia LiveLab) used to surface student engagement and productivity signals such as idle time and workspaces completed to guide tutor attention

finding.finding_summary: Across three quasi-experimental middle school sites, hybrid human-AI tutoring improved math-learning process outcomes relative to software-only or earlier pre-treatment periods. Site 1 showed significant gains in time spent, questions answered, and skills proficient when tutoring was added; for time spent, the mixed-effects model estimated a positive tutoring effect of β=0.202 (95% CI [0.057, 0.347], p=0.006). Site 2 showed more lessons passed during the 3-week tutoring period (β=0.244, 95% CI [0.106, 0.381], p<0.001), and Site 3 showed an additional 0.36 workspaces per hour after tutor-to-student ratios improved from 1:8 to 1:4 (95% CI [0.02, 0.70], p=.03).
finding.measure: math software engagement and progress measures: time spent, questions answered, skills proficient, lessons passed per week, workspaces completed per hour
finding.confidence_interval: Site 1 time spent β=0.202 [0.057, 0.347]; Site 2 lessons passed β=0.244 [0.106, 0.381]; Site 3 workspaces/hour +0.36 [0.02, 0.70]

finding.finding_summary: The intervention increased student engagement with math software, a key behavioral proxy for persistence/engagement. In Site 1, tutoring significantly increased time spent and in Site 2 weekly time on task rose from 24 to 33 minutes during the tutoring period; these gains were strongest for lower-pretest students, suggesting the human component helped sustain participation among students most at risk of disengagement.
finding.measure: time spent on task, weekly engagement minutes, participation in software practice

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues and presents evidence that hybrid human-AI tutoring can improve tutoring efficiency and better target support without raising costs to typical high-dosage tutoring levels. The reported marginal cost averaged below $750 per student annually (range $597-$1170), far below the $3,500-$4,300 per-student annual cost cited for comparable human-only high-dosage tutoring models.
finding.measure: annual marginal cost per student and tutor-to-student ratio / deployment efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Effectiveness and Safety of Selective IL-23 Receptor Antagonists in Moderate to Severe Ulcerative Colitis: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis and Trial Sequential Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether selective IL-23 receptor antagonists are effective and safe for treating moderate to severe ulcerative colitis, and whether the evidence base is sufficiently large and robust to support firm conclusions. The authors note that although individual randomized trials had shown promise, the overall comparative effectiveness, safety profile, and consistency across agents remained unclear.

To address this, they conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials comparing IL-23 receptor antagonists with placebo in moderate to severe ulcerative colitis. The included drugs were ustekinumab, mirikizumab, guselkumab, and risankizumab. Outcomes included clinical remission, clinical response, endoscopic remission/response, histologic and mucosal healing, symptomatic remission, quality-of-life change, and adverse events. They also conducted subgroup analyses, meta-regression, and trial sequential analysis.

The synthesis included nine RCTs representing 3,808 patients in induction and 1,734 patients in maintenance. Across both phases, IL-23 receptor antagonists improved clinical and endoscopic outcomes versus placebo and did not meaningfully worsen overall safety; serious adverse events were lower in induction and comparable in maintenance. Trial sequential analysis suggested the evidence was sufficiently powered for the main clinical outcomes. The authors conclude that IL-23 receptor antagonists are a promising and relatively safe option for moderate to severe ulcerative colitis.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a systematic review/meta-analysis, but it is about IL-23 receptor antagonists for ulcerative colitis, not education or AI/technology intervention in learning. It does not provide relevant evidence for the requested education taxonomy.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no educational intervention or student outcome evaluated, so it has no direct impact on K-12 learning or implementation contexts.

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a review article that examines the emergence of artificial intelligence in education, with a particular focus on chatbots and ChatGPT. The authors ask how AI technologies may transform teaching and learning, what benefits they may offer, and what ethical and practical concerns must be addressed for responsible use. Rather than testing a specific intervention, the paper synthesizes existing literature on AI, intelligent tutoring systems, chatbots, automated assessment, personalized learning, and related educational applications.

The article discusses AI-supported educational use cases across student learning, teacher support, and administrative tasks. It highlights potential gains such as personalized instruction, instant feedback, improved motivation and engagement, reduced teacher workload, and adaptive support for learners with diverse needs. It also emphasizes challenges including bias, privacy, misinformation, over-reliance on technology, academic integrity concerns, and the need for teacher preparation and institutional support.

The review is not tied to one participant population, grade band, or country; instead, it draws on a broad international literature on AIEd. The main conclusion is that AI and ChatGPT have substantial promise for education, but effective adoption requires careful alignment with pedagogy, ethical safeguards, and implementation supports. The authors argue that future research and policy should clarify when and how these tools can be used responsibly to improve learning and teaching.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review/opinion-style article rather than an empirical study. It synthesizes prior literature on AI and ChatGPT in education but does not present original methods, data, or causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that AI and ChatGPT may improve learning, engagement, feedback, and efficiency, but it reports no direct effect sizes from its own study. Its impact claims are plausible but remain general and largely unsupported by new empirical results in this paper.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual overview of ChatGPT and other chatbots as conversational AI for education, including personalized instruction, student Q&A, feedback, and tutoring-like support.
Discussion of classical AI tutoring systems such as ALEKS, Knewton, and AI tutors as examples of adaptive instructional software that can personalize learning paths and feedback.
Overview of AI systems that automatically grade, score, and provide feedback on student work, reducing teacher workload and supporting timely feedback.
Discussion of AI systems that monitor student performance and predict disengagement or dropout risk, including early warning and performance forecasting tools.
Mention of personalized learning platforms that tailor content and pacing to student needs, such as individualized learning paths and adaptive instruction.

paper_profiles.title: Differentiated Instruction in Secondary Education: A Systematic Review of Research Evidence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the limited and fragmented evidence base on whether differentiated instruction improves student achievement in secondary education. The authors ask what empirical studies exist, how differentiated instruction has been operationalized, what overall achievement effects are found, and which contextual or personal factors may shape implementation and outcomes.

Using a systematic best-evidence review of literature published between 2006 and 2016, the authors screened more than 1,000 papers and retained 14 papers representing 12 unique empirical studies. The review focuses on within-class differentiated instruction, defined as planned adaptations in content, process, product, learning environment, or learning time based on student readiness or other relevant characteristics. The included studies span multiple operationalizations, including generic teacher training for adaptive teaching, ability grouping, tiering, individualized instruction, mastery learning, heterogeneous grouping, and remediation in flipped classroom lessons.

The studies were conducted in secondary education contexts in the United States, Europe, Taiwan, and Africa, across subjects such as mathematics, science, reading, and prevention education. Most studies reported small to moderate positive effects on achievement, though the evidence was heterogeneous and some studies were non-significant. The authors conclude that differentiated instruction shows promise for secondary education, but the evidence base remains limited and more rigorous research is needed before strong conclusions can be drawn about which forms work best and under what conditions.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review using a transparent best-evidence synthesis approach with explicit inclusion criteria, dual coding, and effect-size extraction. It is not blue because it synthesizes a small number of heterogeneous studies and includes some studies with quasi-experimental designs and implementation limitations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests modest-to-strong positive impacts in some included secondary math and science studies, but the overall evidence base is uneven and context-sensitive. Because the average evidence is mixed and several effects are small or non-significant, the likely practical impact is modest rather than uniformly large.

finding.finding_summary: This systematic review synthesized 12 unique studies (14 papers) on within-class differentiated instruction in secondary education, including several mathematics interventions. Across the included mathematics studies, effects varied widely: some showed very large positive effects (e.g., Altintas & Özdemir combined d=+4.504, Bal d=+1.085, Bikić et al. overall d=+0.539), while others were small or near-zero (e.g., Bhagat et al. combined d=+0.376, with subgroups ranging from d=+0.176 to d=+0.826). The review’s overall conclusion was that differentiated instruction tends to show small to moderate positive effects on achievement, but the evidence is heterogeneous and methodologically limited.
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement tests, including researcher-made algebra and mathematics tests
finding.study_size: n=varied across included math studies; review included 12 unique studies total
finding.effect_size: review range cited as d=+0.509 to +0.741 across studies (omitting an outlier); individual math study effects included d=+4.504, d=+1.085, d=+0.539, d=+0.376

finding.finding_summary: The review included science-related differentiated instruction studies in secondary education, and the overall pattern favored positive effects on achievement. For example, Mastropieri et al. (2006) reported combined science achievement effects of d=+0.386 (95% CI [0.115, 0.657]) across a sample of n=213, and the adaptive teaching study by Vogt & Rogalla was described as showing a small non-significant effect around d=+0.133. Overall, the review concluded that differentiated instruction can improve science achievement, but results depend on implementation quality and are inconsistent across studies.
finding.measure: Science achievement tests and unit/high-stakes science tests
finding.study_size: n=213 for one highlighted science study; review total n across included studies varied
finding.effect_size: d=+0.386 for one science study; d=+0.133 for adaptive teaching study

finding.finding_summary: The review also included a reading intervention based on individualized differentiated instruction in middle school. Little et al. (2014) found near-zero effects in two sites and small positive effects in others, with site-level combined effects ranging from d=+0.007 to d=+0.266 on reading comprehension and fluency outcomes across a large sample (approximately n=832 control and n=1179 experimental, depending on test). This indicates that literacy gains from differentiated instruction were modest and context-dependent rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension and fluency tests
finding.study_size: n≈2011 total across conditions in one multi-site study; site-level n varied by test
finding.effect_size: site-level combined effects ranged from d=+0.007 to d=+0.266

finding.finding_summary: Some included differentiated instruction approaches were designed to respond to student interests, learning profiles, and motivation, and the review notes these features as part of implementation. However, the paper does not present a substantive pooled analysis of social-emotional outcomes; motivation is mostly discussed as a design element rather than an outcome. Any effects on engagement or motivation are therefore indirect and not quantifiable from the review’s main results.
finding.measure: Motivation/engagement discussed as an implementation factor, not a primary quantitative outcome

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the question of how education should adapt to the rapid spread of AI tools such as ChatGPT, with particular attention to the skills students and educators need in order to use AI responsibly and productively. Rather than testing a specific educational intervention, it offers a conceptual discussion informed by a case study from a Swiss university of applied sciences and a narrative literature review. The author argues that AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking are the three core competencies needed for effective AI use in modern education.

The paper describes how Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich responded to the rise of generative AI by creating internal guidelines for student use. These guidelines allow AI use but require transparency, documentation in appendices, and critical evaluation of outputs. The case emphasizes a middle ground between banning AI and allowing unrestricted use, positioning AI as a sparring partner rather than a tutor or ghostwriter. The discussion is framed primarily around higher education, although the author notes that the ideas may also be useful for children and younger learners.

The paper further reviews the meaning of AI literacy and proposes a set of components for AI literacy education, including understanding basic AI concepts, machine learning, data handling, practical applications, ethics, governance, hands-on experience, and prompt engineering. It also surveys several prompt engineering approaches, such as zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, self-consistency, automatic prompt engineering, generated knowledge prompting, and tree-of-thought prompting. The main conclusion is that schools and universities should build a broader “culture of AI” through workshops, curricula, guidelines, and dedicated support so that AI use becomes transparent, critical, and educationally beneficial rather than passive or deceptive.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual discussion and narrative literature review with an illustrative case study, not a controlled empirical evaluation. It does not report a rigorous methodology, comparison group, or outcome estimates for the claimed effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper proposes plausible implementation and governance ideas for AI use in education, but it does not measure student or institutional impacts. Its likely practical value is moderate and mainly advisory rather than evidentiary.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual guidance for using ChatGPT and other large language models as an 'informed conversational partner' in academic work, classroom experimentation, and prompt-engineering practice; not as a direct tutor but as a sparring partner for idea generation and critique.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking should improve students’ ability to evaluate AI outputs and use them responsibly, but it provides no direct empirical estimate of skill gains. It cites prior work suggesting prompt learning can increase awareness of AI limits, but in this article the claim is conceptual rather than tested (no n, no effect size reported).
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of critical thinking, AI literacy, and prompt-engineering skill development

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on institutional policy responses to ChatGPT, including the creation of AI guidelines, transparency requirements, workshops, budget allocation, and dedicated AI support roles. These are presented as practical recommendations for governance and implementation, but they are not evaluated with outcome data (no n, effect size, or confidence interval reported).
finding.measure: Institutional policy and implementation recommendations for AI governance

finding.finding_summary: The article suggests AI can help with curriculum creation, brainstorming, and classroom preparation, potentially reducing teacher workload and improving efficiency. However, this is descriptive and not supported by measured workload outcomes in the paper (no sample size or effect size reported).
finding.measure: Teacher workload / curriculum development efficiency (conceptual)

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective paper examines the emerging role of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in human learning and education. It asks how GenAI may transform learning support, resource creation, feedback, and assessment, while also identifying major risks such as hallucinations, bias, privacy concerns, and the disruption of conventional assessment practices. Rather than reporting a single empirical study, the paper synthesizes prior literature and current examples to frame a research agenda for educational use of GenAI.

The paper discusses GenAI systems such as large language models, including ChatGPT-like tools and GPT-4-powered educational assistants, as well as generative systems for multimedia and assessment support. It highlights how these tools may provide scalable personalized tutoring, generate instructional materials, automate feedback, and enable more authentic assessments. The discussion is situated broadly across learning contexts, with specific examples from K-12, higher education, and professional learning, but it does not present a direct participant sample or intervention trial.

The authors conclude that GenAI has substantial promise for supporting learning, but its benefits depend on careful human-centered design, AI literacy, evidence-based decision-making, and methodological rigor in future research. They emphasize that educators, researchers, policymakers, and technologists must collaborate to ensure that GenAI augments rather than replaces human learning, while mitigating risks related to overreliance, inequity, and unreliable outputs.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective/theoretical article rather than an empirical study. It synthesizes prior literature and examples but does not present a direct research design, sample, or original causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for potentially substantial educational effects of GenAI, but it reports no original outcome data or effect sizes. Impact is therefore speculative and not empirically established in this paper.

interventions.use_case: Perspective discussion of GenAI/LLM tutors such as ChatGPT and Khanmigo as scalable personalized learning support, including step-by-step math tutoring and guided questioning within learners' zone of proximal development.
GenAI systems that analyze student work and generate immediate, personalized feedback for writing, programming, and dashboard-based learning analytics explanations.
GenAI-created instructional resources and practice materials, including quiz questions, explanations, multimedia learning content, and assessment items.

paper_profiles.title: The application of AI technologies in STEM education: a systematic review from 2011 to 2021
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how artificial intelligence (AI) has been applied in STEM education and what effects these applications have had across the empirical literature from 2011 to 2021. The authors argue that AI-STEM is a complex system and use general system theory to organize evidence across multiple elements, including the AI technique itself, the learning content, instructional medium, educational context, and roles of instructors and learners.

The study is a systematic review of 63 empirical peer-reviewed articles retrieved from major databases and screened under PRISMA-style procedures. The review identifies six broad categories of AI applications: learning prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, student behavior detection, automation, educational robots, and a small set of other applications such as AI textbooks and group formation. The included studies span STEM domains, with most focused on technology/computing and science, and only a small number on mathematics.

Across the reviewed studies, most AI-STEM applications were conducted in higher education, though some work involved elementary, middle, and high school settings. Common contexts included face-to-face classrooms, web-based learning, and laboratory environments, with computer systems as the most common medium. The review concludes that AI applications generally show positive effects on learning performance, motivation, and higher-order thinking, while also helping detect learning behaviors and patterns; however, the evidence base is dominated by higher-education studies and is uneven across STEM subjects, with relatively little mathematics research.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review, but it synthesizes heterogeneous empirical studies without meta-analysis and does not provide pooled effect sizes. The evidence quality is therefore correlational/descriptive rather than a single rigorous causal estimate.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests generally positive effects of AI-STEM interventions, but the reported outcomes are broad, heterogeneous, and mostly not quantified with pooled effects. For middle school math specifically, evidence is indirect and limited, so the likely impact is modest and unclear for this target population.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of AI-enabled tutoring systems in STEM education, including instructional content delivery, personalized learning-path recommendation, and resource recommendation through adaptive tutoring and feedback.
Learning performance prediction and at-risk student prediction using machine learning, educational data mining, and learning analytics to forecast outcomes and identify students needing intervention.
Automated assessment of STEM work, including grading open-ended responses, syntax/structure checking for programming tasks, and automatic argument assessment with immediate feedback.
AI-supported educational robots used as tutors, tutees, or learning companions in STEM lessons, including humanoid and programming robots that deliver science or programming instruction.
Digital game-based learning and simulation-like STEM environments, such as personalized math games and mixed-reality learning systems, used as the instructional setting for AI-driven personalization.
Personalized STEM learning environments that adapt content, sequencing, or recommendations to learner profiles and performance without being framed as full dialogue tutoring.

finding.finding_summary: The review identified mathematics-focused AI-STEM studies, but the evidence base was small (n=3 studies). Across the broader STEM literature, AI applications in math-related contexts generally improved learning performance, though the review does not report a pooled effect size for mathematics specifically.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning performance and course outcomes

finding.finding_summary: Across 22 studies reporting learning performance outcomes, 20 found significantly positive effects of AI-supported STEM interventions on achievement. Examples included improved geoscience learning achievements, stronger problem-solving in programming, and better computational thinking in AR-based instruction; the review does not provide a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Learning performance, achievement tests, problem-solving, computational thinking, final exam scores
finding.study_size: n=63 studies in review; 22 studies reported learning performance outcomes

finding.finding_summary: Seventeen studies reported affective outcomes and generally found positive attitudes, satisfaction, interest, and motivation toward AI-supported STEM learning. The review summarizes these as favorable perceptions, but does not report a pooled effect size or standardized estimate.
finding.measure: Questionnaires, surveys, interviews on attitude, interest, motivation, satisfaction
finding.study_size: n=17 studies reporting affective perception outcomes

finding.finding_summary: Seven studies found improvements in higher-order thinking skills such as problem-solving, computational thinking, self-regulated learning, and argumentation. Reported examples include stronger problem-solving in flowchart-based ITSs and better computational thinking in a deep-learning-supported AR system, but no pooled effect size is provided.
finding.measure: Problem-solving ability, computational thinking, self-regulated learning, argumentation
finding.study_size: n=7 studies reporting higher-order thinking outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that AI techniques often achieved good technological performance, including efficient prediction and accurate automated assessment. Examples include better scoring performance for automated assessment systems and high-accuracy prediction models, but the paper does not synthesize these into a single effect size.
finding.measure: Algorithm accuracy, prediction performance, automated scoring efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Learning design to support student-AI collaboration: perspectives of leading teachers for AI in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of guidance on how to design learning when AI is introduced into K-12 classrooms as a collaborative learning agent. Rather than studying student outcomes directly, the authors investigate what teachers believe is needed for effective student-AI collaboration (SAC), focusing on curriculum design, student-AI interaction, learning environments, and how SAC may evolve over time.

The study uses in-depth semi-structured interviews with 10 Korean leading teachers in AI in Education, drawn from primary and secondary schools that were already involved in software education, AI pilot programs, or AI-convergence initiatives. The paper frames SAC through distributed cognition and proposes that AI should be treated as a learning partner rather than only as a tool. Teachers emphasized learning goals such as higher-order thinking, social and digital capacities, and subject-matter knowledge building; content should include interdisciplinary learning, authentic tasks, and creative projects; assessment should be process-oriented and include collaboration performance.

Teachers also argued that effective implementation requires explicit instruction on AI principles, data literacy, debugging, and AI ethics, along with AI systems that provide scaffolding, intuitive interfaces, and rich digital tools. They stressed the importance of flexible classrooms, strong digital infrastructure, systematic policy support, teacher capacity building, collaborative school culture, and a safe-to-fail environment. Overall, the paper concludes that SAC may evolve in stages from learning about AI, to learning from AI, to learning together with AI, offering design implications for AI-enabled schooling rather than evidence of measured learning effects.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative interview study with 10 teachers and a clear thematic analysis, so it provides credible contextual evidence. However, it does not test an intervention experimentally or estimate causal effects, which limits internal validity for impact claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper offers useful implementation insight for AI-supported learning in K-12, including design principles relevant to mathematics and middle school contexts. Because it reports perceptions rather than measured outcomes, the direct impact on achievement is unclear and best treated as moderate, contextual evidence.

interventions.use_case: Qualitative study of student-AI collaboration design for K-12 classrooms, including AI used as a collaborative learning agent, tutor-like scaffolder, and learning mate across subject learning tasks.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed student-AI collaboration could support durable skills such as critical thinking, creativity, problem-solving, collaboration, communication, leadership, and computational thinking, but the paper reports perceptions rather than measured learning gains. The study references prior quantitative work suggesting positive impacts on creativity, logical thinking, and problem-solving, but does not itself estimate an effect size.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on perceived student capacities and collaboration skills

finding.finding_summary: Teachers viewed student-AI collaboration as supporting subject-matter knowledge building by helping students organize new information, connect it to prior knowledge, and apply knowledge to tangible products and solutions. The paper does not report student achievement scores, so this is a qualitative positive inference rather than a quantified effect.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on subject-matter knowledge building

finding.finding_summary: Teachers expected AI-supported learning to improve motivation, persistence, self-confidence, willingness to try again, and tolerance for failure through gamification, affect-aware interaction, and a safe-to-fail classroom culture. No direct student outcomes were measured, so the evidence is interpretive and based on teacher perceptions.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on engagement, motivation, persistence, and emotional responses to failure

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described AI as potentially reducing workload by automating repetitive tasks, supporting personalized instruction, and streamlining data collection and analysis through integrated platforms. These are implementation-oriented expectations rather than measured efficiency outcomes, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of workflow, automation, and instructional support needs

finding.finding_summary: The study strongly emphasizes the need for systemic supports such as national AIED policy, governance, teacher professional learning, flexible scheduling, digital infrastructure, and collaborative school culture to make student-AI collaboration feasible. No numeric effect size is reported because this is a qualitative policy and implementation study, but the paper presents robust consensus among the 10 interviewed teachers.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on policy, governance, infrastructure, and school culture

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in intelligent tutoring systems toward sustainable education: a systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how artificial intelligence (AI) and information technology can support sustainable education through intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs), with a particular focus on challenges, implementation patterns, outcomes, and future directions. The authors frame sustainable education as a long-term, equitable, student-centered approach and argue that AI-enabled ITSs may help by personalizing learning, improving access, and supporting teachers with data-driven insights.

The study is a systematic review of 29 papers on AI in ITSs, selected from Scopus and Web of Science, published between 2014 and 2023. The reviewed studies span multiple educational settings and levels, though most are in higher education; the review also includes a smaller set of studies at the K-12, high school, and elementary levels. The paper categorizes AI uses in ITSs by purpose (e.g., performance prediction, behavior analysis, dropout prevention, personalization, instructor support), technologies used (e.g., supervised and unsupervised machine learning, NLP, XAI), scenarios of deployment, observed outcomes, limitations, and future research directions.

The main conclusions are that AI-enabled ITSs can improve prediction accuracy, identify learner behaviors, support early intervention, increase engagement, and enable personalization, but the field still faces major implementation barriers. These include data limitations, portability issues, fairness and bias concerns, weak interpretability, and limited grounding in educational theory. The authors conclude that future work should emphasize larger and better-quality datasets, stronger theory validation, more explainable and human-centered AI, and broader attention to equity, trust, and teacher support.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review with a clear search/screening approach (PRISMA-informed) and coded synthesis, but it does not present a new causal evaluation or pooled meta-analytic estimate. The evidence is therefore descriptive and synthesis-based rather than high-credibility experimental evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests meaningful benefits for learning support, engagement, and teacher decision-making, but it provides no pooled effect sizes and most included studies are higher-education focused rather than middle school. That makes the likely impact relevant but still uncertain for middle school math ChatGPT-adjacent use cases.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of AI-embedded intelligent tutoring systems for sustainable education, including performance prediction, learning behavior analysis, dropout prevention, personalization, and explainable decision support.

finding.finding_summary: This is a systematic review, so it does not report a single pooled effect size. Across 29 included studies, the paper concludes that AI-embedded ITSs generally support better learning performance through personalized learning paths, adaptive feedback, and early intervention, with several studies reporting improved performance after intervention or personalized diagnostic feedback.
finding.measure: Learning performance, performance prediction accuracy, and knowledge gain as reported across reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: The review finds consistent support for engagement- and dropout-related benefits, with studies reporting improved participation rates after early dropout notification, higher engagement, and detection of emotional states to prompt teacher support. These outcomes were synthesized qualitatively across the reviewed studies rather than estimated with a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Engagement, dropout risk/participation, emotional detection, and satisfaction measures

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI-enabled ITSs can reduce teacher workload by automating performance prediction, learning-behavior analysis, and early warnings that help instructors target intervention more efficiently. It also notes that only a small subset of studies used explainable AI, suggesting operational gains are tempered by the need for more transparent decision support.
finding.measure: Teacher support, monitoring, intervention targeting, and explanation/provision of actionable analytics

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames AI in ITSs as beneficial for sustainable education at the system level by improving access, flexibility, and equity, while also highlighting implementation constraints such as privacy, fairness, interpretability, infrastructure, and policy/regulation needs. No single quantitative effect is reported; the conclusion is based on the review of challenges, outcomes, and future directions across the included literature.
finding.measure: Access, equity, privacy/security, fairness, interpretability, infrastructure readiness, and policy implications

paper_profiles.title: AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how artificial intelligence (AI) literacy is being integrated into K-12 education worldwide. The authors conduct a systematic literature review to map the field, identify major approaches, and highlight gaps in current research and implementation. They review 179 documents retrieved from Scopus using a search strategy centered on AI literacy/education and school levels, while excluding papers focused only on computer-based learning or intelligent tutoring systems.

The review organizes the literature into two broad categories: learning experiences and theoretical perspectives. Learning experiences include activities aimed at helping K-12 students recognize AI in artifacts, understand how AI works, use AI-related tools, and reflect on the societal and ethical implications of AI. Theoretical perspectives include curriculum design, AI as a subject, student perspectives, teacher training, support resources, and gender diversity. The paper notes that many learning experiences emphasize technical or applied skills but rarely assess student learning outcomes rigorously.

The authors conclude that AI literacy in K-12 should be interdisciplinary, competency-based, and integrated into existing subjects rather than added as a standalone course. They argue that curricula should be modular, contextualized, and co-designed with teachers, and that teacher preparation is essential for successful implementation. The review also emphasizes the importance of ethics, social implications, and critical engagement with AI, while noting that current work is still limited and uneven across countries.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic literature review, but it synthesizes heterogeneous K-12 AI literacy papers rather than reporting a causal evaluation of a single intervention. The methodology is transparent and structured, yet the evidence base is largely descriptive and the paper does not provide pooled effect estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review identifies important implementation directions for K-12 AI literacy, including curriculum design, teacher co-design, and interdisciplinary integration, but it does not demonstrate measured student outcome impacts. Its practical value is moderate and mainly strategic rather than evidentiary for achievement effects.

paper_profiles.title: AutoTutor and Family: A Review of 17 Years of Natural Language Tutoring
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews 17 years of research on AutoTutor and related natural-language tutoring systems. The central question is which design features of dialog-based intelligent tutoring systems help students learn, and how those features compare with human tutoring and other tutoring technologies. Rather than reporting one new experiment, the paper synthesizes findings from many prior studies on AutoTutor, WHY2/AutoTutor, DeepTutor, Guru, iSTART, MetaTutor, and related systems.

The intervention approach is natural-language tutoring: animated agents that use question-answer dialogue, hints, prompts, feedback, and sometimes affect detection, collaborative lecturing, or learning-progressions-based adaptivity. The reviewed systems were used across several domains, including computer literacy, physics, biology, critical thinking, reading comprehension, and self-regulated learning. The paper describes how these systems model human tutoring moves, use semantic analysis to interpret student responses, and extend tutoring with pedagogical agents and complementary media.

Across the reviewed studies, the authors conclude that dialog-based tutoring can produce substantial learning gains, often outperforming static materials and in some cases approaching human tutoring. The review emphasizes that deep reasoning questions, explanatory dialogue, and adaptive scaffolding are particularly effective, while affect-sensitive support can help low-knowledge learners under some conditions. It also concludes that different domains require different tutoring strategies, and that future systems should balance content coverage, adaptivity, engagement, and metacognitive support rather than relying on a single tutoring style.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review synthesizing prior studies rather than a new controlled evaluation. It is peer reviewed and reports many experimental findings, but the paper itself does not meet RCT/QED credibility criteria as a primary empirical study.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review summarizes several medium-to-large learning gains for ITS and related dialog systems, including effects around 0.5σ to 1.22σ in some domains. For middle-school-relevant adjacent evidence, the impact is promising but indirect rather than direct to ChatGPT math use, so green is appropriate.

interventions.use_case: Review of AutoTutor-family natural-language intelligent tutoring systems that provide deep-reasoning dialog, hints/prompts, and adaptive scaffolding across domains including physics, biology, and literacy-related skills.
Review includes game-like and simulation-adjacent tutors in the AutoTutor family, such as Operation ARIES/ARA serious game training for scientific inquiry and 3D simulation extensions.
Animated talking-head pedagogical agents used to deliver tutoring dialog and convey feedback through facial expression, intonation, and gesture.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that AutoTutor-family systems were extended to mathematics-adjacent instruction, including a corpus of high school students tutoring seventh-grade students on algebra concepts. However, the paper does not present a standalone math trial in this review; it uses these algebra dialogs as design evidence for natural-language tutoring strategies rather than as a separate evaluated math intervention.
finding.measure: Algebra tutoring dialogs / instructional design evidence

finding.finding_summary: Across physics and biology tutoring studies, the paper reports substantial learning gains for AutoTutor-family systems. Reported effects include about 0.5σ over textbook controls for AutoTutor 1.1/2.0 in computer literacy, 0.61σ over a control and 1.22σ over reading a textbook in physics, 0.72σ in Guru biology versus classroom instruction only, and 0.79σ in a small DeepTutor evaluation (n=30) with macro-adaptivity.
finding.measure: Pretest-posttest learning gains; physics concept tests; biology concept posttests
finding.study_size: multiple studies; e.g., n=30 for DeepTutor small-scale evaluation

finding.finding_summary: The review describes positive effects for reading-comprehension and writing-related descendants of AutoTutor. iSTART improved reading comprehension for middle-schoolers and college students, with benefits varying by reader skill, and Writing-Pal supported writing skills through automated essay assessment and feedback, though this paper does not report a single pooled effect size for these literacy tools.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension questions; writing-skill performance / automated essay assessment

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes evidence that dialog-based tutoring can improve higher-order reasoning, especially when students explain, justify, and elaborate answers. It reports positive findings for critical thinking and scientific inquiry tools: Operation ARA showed 1.4σ learning gains on a scientific research skills test versus no instruction, while SEEK did not significantly improve information-finding skills after only 1 hour of training.
finding.measure: Critical thinking / scientific inquiry skill tests; information-finding performance
finding.study_size: multiple studies; specific ARA/SEEK sample sizes not fully reported here

finding.finding_summary: Affect-sensitive tutoring showed that adapting to frustration and low-knowledge learners can improve outcomes, but mainly for students who actually need support. Supportive AutoTutor produced a 0.71σ gain for low-knowledge students on a second session, whereas high-knowledge students did not benefit and sometimes learned less; GazeTutor increased attention and yielded 0.26σ overall gains (p<.178) and 0.45σ on deep learning (p<.035).
finding.measure: Posttest scores; attention to tutor; affective state/engagement measures
finding.study_size: multiple studies; exact ns not fully reported in this review

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that metacognitive and self-regulated learning supports can help, but effects are uneven across contexts. MetaTutor showed higher learning efficiency when prompts and feedback were counted during page interaction (0.84σ), but overall efficiency was approximately equal once total time was considered; the paper notes that other SRL-help-seeking interventions have not consistently changed domain learning gains.
finding.measure: Learning efficiency; self-regulated learning outcomes
finding.study_size: multiple studies; n not fully reported
finding.effect_size: 0.84σ for in-system efficiency; overall effect approximately nil

paper_profiles.title: Animated pedagogical agents effects on enhancing student motivation and learning in a science inquiry learning environment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an animated pedagogical agent (APA) can improve students’ motivation and learning in a science inquiry learning environment. The authors focus on two motivational constructs from expectancy-value and ARCS frameworks: task relevance and self-efficacy. They also consider whether the agent’s gendered design matters, given prior evidence that girls often report lower science motivation than boys.

The intervention was an inquiry-based computer learning environment for kinematics called Motion, implemented in SimQuest. Students were assigned to one of three conditions: control (no agent image or voice), voice-only (audio messages from the agent without image), or embodied agent (image plus voice). The APA, Emma, was designed as a young, cool, female peer model and delivered motivational messages intended to support relevance and confidence. Participants were 61 third-year secondary school students in the Netherlands, approximately 14.7 years old, working individually on computers in a classroom setting.

Results showed that self-efficacy increased over time for all students, but task relevance did not change meaningfully. Girls rated the agent as a better model than boys, and there was a time-by-condition-by-gender interaction for self-efficacy during training: girls’ self-efficacy rose in the experimental conditions and fell in the control condition, while boys showed the opposite pattern. However, the APA did not produce significantly higher learning gains than the control condition; all groups improved on the knowledge test. The authors conclude that motivational scaffolding via pedagogical agents is promising but that effects are modest and depend heavily on agent design and the motivational needs of learners.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed randomized experiment with a control group, multiple conditions, and repeated measures, which supports causal inference. However, it is a single small study (n=61) in one school, with some missing data and no independent replication in the paper.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows clear learning gains in the base inquiry environment and modest motivational effects for self-efficacy, but the agent did not improve learning outcomes over control. The impact is therefore informative but overall unclear/modest for educational implementation, especially for middle school math analog evidence.

interventions.use_case: computer-based inquiry learning environment in kinematics with embedded motivational animated pedagogical agent messages and feedback

finding.finding_summary: Students in all three conditions made significant knowledge gains from pretest to posttest on a 27-item kinematics test, with no differences by condition or gender. The overall gain was large (total d=1.10, n=61), indicating the inquiry environment supported learning of the science content, but the animated pedagogical agent did not add measurable learning benefit over the control or voice-only versions.
finding.measure: 27-item kinematics knowledge pretest/posttest

finding.finding_summary: Self-efficacy increased significantly over time for the full sample, with a large within-person gain from before to after training (d=0.51, n=61). However, condition effects were mixed: a significant time × condition × gender interaction emerged during training, with girls increasing self-efficacy in the agent and voice conditions while decreasing in control, but no main effect of condition on task relevance or overall self-efficacy.
finding.measure: Task relevance and self-efficacy ratings on a 10-point TRSE questionnaire

finding.finding_summary: Girls rated the animated pedagogical agent as a significantly better model than boys did. The difference was moderate-to-large (d=0.95, n=21 in the agent condition), suggesting the female embodied agent was more persuasive or relatable for girls than for boys.
finding.measure: Agent model appraisal questionnaire (11 items, 10-point Likert scale)

paper_profiles.title: Trends and research foci of robotics-based STEM education: a systematic review from diverse angles based on the technology-based learning model
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what the existing research on robotics-based STEM (R-STEM) education shows across three dimensions: research characteristics, participant-robot interaction, and how robotics is used in STEM instruction. The authors argue that prior reviews had not fully captured the role of robotics in STEM learning, especially in terms of disciplinary integration, educational goals, and the kinds of learners and teachers involved.

To address this gap, the paper systematically reviews 39 SSCI journal articles published from 2012 to 2021 and indexed in Web of Science. The reviewed studies covered K-12 and some higher education settings, with many conducted in the United States and a large share involving elementary students. Across the studies, robots were most often used as learning tools, most commonly LEGO MINDSTORMS, and the dominant STEM focus was technology, especially programming. The most frequent instructional approach was project-based learning.

The review concludes that R-STEM research has largely emphasized learner and teacher perceptions, learning performance, and motivational outcomes rather than rigorous evidence on long-term achievement. It also finds that science and mathematics are less represented than technology and engineering, and that most studies use robots to support content integration rather than as intelligent tutors. The authors recommend more research on low-cost robotics, stronger pedagogical design, broader disciplinary balance, and greater attention to teachers and higher education contexts.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review with transparent search and coding procedures, but it is not a meta-analysis and does not estimate pooled causal effects. The evidence base summarized is largely descriptive and heterogeneous, so credibility for effect estimation is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests generally positive but mixed impacts of robotics on learning, motivation, and durable skills, yet no pooled effect sizes are reported. Because the paper is syntheses-of-syntheses and the underlying evidence is mixed, the practical impact is promising but unclear in magnitude.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of robotics-based STEM education, focusing on physical educational robots (especially LEGO MINDSTORMS and Arduino-based kits) used as learning tools, tutees, or occasional tutors in K-12 STEM instruction.

finding.finding_summary: This review synthesized 39 studies of robotics-based STEM education rather than estimating a single pooled effect. Across the literature, robotics was most often linked to learning performance and conceptual understanding in programming/technology and STEM problem-solving, but the evidence was mixed: for learning performance, 6 studies reported positive effects, 2 found no significant difference, and 5 found mixed or conditional results.
finding.measure: Learning performance; conceptual understanding in STEM/programming tasks
finding.study_size: n=39 studies (with learning performance measured in 15 studies)

finding.finding_summary: The review found that affective outcomes were a major focus: 23 of 39 studies examined perceptions, attitudes, motivation, self-efficacy, interest, or satisfaction. Of these, 14 studies reported positive perceptions of robotics in STEM, while 9 reported mixed results, suggesting generally favorable but not uniform motivational/attitudinal effects.
finding.measure: Technology acceptance, attitude and motivation, self-efficacy, satisfaction/interest, learning perceptions

finding.finding_summary: Robotics-based STEM was frequently used to support durable skills such as problem-solving, collaboration/teamwork, communication, creativity, and higher-order thinking. The review reports that problem-solving (6 studies), communication (8), collaboration/teamwork (4), and creativity (4) were commonly targeted, with several studies reporting positive results and few negative findings.
finding.measure: Problem-solving, collaboration/teamwork, communication, creativity, critical thinking, higher-order thinking

finding.finding_summary: A smaller subset of studies examined operational or psychomotor skills such as construction, building, and modeling robots. The review states that 3 of 5 studies found positive results, indicating that robotics activities can improve hands-on technical execution and build-related task performance.
finding.measure: Psychomotor/operational skills (construction, building, modeling robots)

paper_profiles.title: Authoring Tools for Designing Intelligent Tutoring Systems: a Systematic Review of the Literature
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the question of how authoring tools support the design of intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) for non-programmer authors. The authors note that although ITS research has produced evidence that well-designed intelligent tutors can be effective, ITS development remains costly and authoring tools may reduce the burden of building tutors and broaden who can participate in design. Their review is intended to synthesize recent literature and identify what parts of ITS can be authored, what types of ITS are being created, which features help the authoring process, what technologies are used, when authoring occurs across the learning lifecycle, and whether there is evidence that these tools improve design outcomes.

To answer these questions, the paper conducts a systematic literature review of studies published from January 2009 to June 2016. The search covered seven digital libraries and yielded 4,622 records, which were narrowed to 33 primary studies after duplicate removal and multi-stage screening. The review focused on authoring tools for non-programmer authors in ITS contexts; it excluded secondary studies and several specialized domains such as simulation, augmented reality, serious games, storytelling, and disability-focused systems. The included studies were mostly academic, with a mix of conference and journal publications.

The review finds that authoring tools most often support pedagogical models and domain models, while student and interface models are less frequently targeted. The most common ITS types were model-tracing/cognitive tutors and example-tracing tutors, followed by content/problem-based and dialog-based systems; about a quarter of the studies were too general to fit a specific ITS type. Frequently reported authoring features included defining/giving feedback, defining problem solutions, authoring by demonstration, generating domain models, viewing learner statistics, and reusing tutor designs. Overall, the paper concludes that authoring tools show empirical and practical promise for making ITS development more accessible, but many important areas remain underexplored, especially broader support across all ITS components and more systematic empirical evaluation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic literature review with a clearly described search, screening, and quality-assessment protocol. However, it synthesizes heterogeneous primary studies rather than directly testing an intervention, so it does not meet RCT/QED evidence standards for a higher tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper indicates positive effects of ITS authoring tools on efficiency and quality of tutor development, but it reports no pooled effect sizes and no direct student-achievement outcomes. The impact is therefore real but indirect and unclear in magnitude for K-12 learners.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of authoring tools for designing intelligent tutoring systems for non-programmer authors, including tools for authoring domain, pedagogical, student, and interface models across model-tracing, example-tracing, constraint-based, dialog-based, and other ITS types.

finding.finding_summary: The review found empirical evidence that ITS authoring tools improve the efficiency of ITS design for non-programmer authors, along with effectiveness, quality of authored artifacts, and usability. Across 33 included studies, the paper synthesizes prior evaluations rather than reporting a single pooled effect size; the evidence is described as positive and mainly supported by controlled experiments and case studies (e.g., 15 empirical studies total).
finding.measure: Reported efficiency of ITS authoring/design, usability, and quality/effectiveness of authored artifacts across included studies
finding.study_size: n=33 studies included in the review

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests ITS authoring tools can reduce production effort and expand who can participate in ITS development, potentially broadening the availability of ITSs in educational settings. This is a synthesis claim from the included literature, not a direct causal estimate, and no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Reported benefits for ITS development workflow, reuse, and broader participation in tutor creation
finding.study_size: n=33 studies included in the review

paper_profiles.title: Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a theoretical problem in educational technology research: how to explain why digital tools sometimes improve learning, rather than treating technology use as the cause by itself. The authors argue that learning effects are mediated by cognitive processes and propose the CoDiL framework (Cognitive process framework on the Learning mechanisms of Digital tools in educational settings) to connect digital-tool features, student learning activities, and knowledge acquisition.

The framework synthesizes three prior perspectives: the knowledge-learning-instruction (KLI) framework, the selection-organization-integration (SOI) model, and utilization-of-learning-opportunity (ULO) frameworks. It distinguishes between digitally enriched instructional features (e.g., adaptive feedback, prompts, contrasting cases, opportunities to try and fail) and the learning activities these features may stimulate, such as exploration, refinement, revision, self-explanation, abstraction, and conducting experiments. The paper also emphasizes that process data from student-tool interactions can be used to operationalize these activities empirically.

The paper is not an intervention study with participants; instead, it is a conceptual and design-oriented article intended to guide future research and tool development across content areas, including mathematics. The authors illustrate how the framework could inform the design of an online math tutor for fraction arithmetic by aligning features like adaptive feedback and adaptive task difficulty with content-specific learning mechanisms. Their main conclusion is that effective digital learning research should specify the content to be learned, the relevant learning activities, the instructional features meant to support them, and the process data needed to test the proposed mechanisms.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual review/framework paper rather than an empirical study. It synthesizes prior literature and proposes the CoDiL framework, but does not report new primary data, effect estimates, or a rigorous evaluation design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct measured impact on student outcomes; its contribution is theoretical and methodological. It may inform future interventions, but it does not provide evidence of effect size or realized educational impact.

paper_profiles.title: Intelligent tutoring systems for word problem solving in COVID-19 days: could they have been (part of) the solution?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses two related questions about technology in mathematics education during COVID-19 remote schooling. First, it asks whether mainstream mathematics education research had already produced enough evidence on autonomous, teacher-independent technology use to be useful in emergency remote teaching. Second, it examines whether intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs) could serve as a practical, cost-effective alternative to human one-to-one support for arithmetic and word-problem solving.

The authors begin with a systematic review of empirical studies published in mathematics education journals indexed in Web of Science. The review classifies studies by whether technology use was teacher-mediated or standalone. The review found that almost all studies involved teacher mediation; only a very small number supported autonomous student use, and only one reviewed study used an ITS. Most studies focused on teachers, higher education, or non-compulsory settings, suggesting that research relevant to independent home learning was scarce.

The paper then presents an empirical example using HINTS, a step-based intelligent tutoring system for arithmetic word problems. The intervention involved 133 fifth- and sixth-grade students from one public primary school in Castilla-La Mancha, Spain, during COVID-19 emergency remote teaching. Students completed four weekly online sessions over four weeks, with 28 word problems in total, and all participants had access to devices and internet. The system provided automated validation and short reports, while on-demand hints were disabled to prevent students from relying only on system guidance. Results showed that low-income students were less likely to attend the online lessons, even when technology access was provided, but among participating students there was no statistically significant income gap in performance on the HINTS tasks. The authors conclude that ITSs may help provide individualized mathematics practice in remote settings, but that participation barriers linked to socioeconomic conditions remain a serious challenge.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed article combining a systematic review with an exploratory observational case study, but it is not a randomized trial and the intervention evidence is limited to one school context. The methods provide useful descriptive evidence, yet causal confidence is limited by design and by the small, context-specific ITS sample.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests a modest positive potential for ITSs in middle/elementary mathematics problem solving, especially for maintaining performance across income groups, but the observed effects are small and not clearly causal. The strongest benefit is in implementation relevance rather than demonstrated large learning gains.

interventions.use_case: step-based tutoring for arithmetic and algebraic word problem solving with automated validation of solution steps and configurable on-demand hints; studied here in remote standalone homework-like use during COVID-19 ERT

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that a standalone ITS (HINTS) used for arithmetic word problems showed no significant income gap in performance during remote use: low-income and non-low-income students did not differ significantly in problems addressed (t(87)=1.04, p=0.8502, d=0.30) or correctness ratio (t(87)=0.74, p=0.4609, d=0.21). However, prior math grades before school closure were significantly lower for low-income students than non-low-income students (M=6.11 vs 7.25, t(127)=2.57, p=0.0113, d=0.55), indicating baseline inequity even though ITS performance during the intervention was similar.
finding.measure: Mathematics grades prior to closure; number of problems addressed in HINTS; ratio of problems solved correctly in HINTS
finding.study_size: n=133 overall; HINTS performance comparisons n=89 (15 low-income, 74 non-low-income)
finding.effect_size: d=0.55 (pre-closure math grades); d=0.30 (problems addressed); d=0.21 (correctness ratio)
finding.std_deviation: SD=2.08 (pre-closure math grades); SD=8.73/8.81 (problems addressed); SD=0.23/0.24 (problem score ratio)

finding.finding_summary: Participation/attendance in the remote standalone ITS sessions was significantly lower for low-income students, suggesting an engagement barrier rather than a learning-performance gap. The paper reports significant associations between income level and attendance at the first lesson (χ2(1)=6.06, p=0.0138; odds of non-attendance 2.82 times higher for low-income students) and at any lesson (χ2(1)=3.87, p=0.0492; odds 2.29 times higher).
finding.measure: Attendance at the first virtual lesson and attendance at any virtual lesson
finding.effect_size: odds ratio 2.82 (first lesson non-attendance); odds ratio 2.29 (any lesson non-attendance)

finding.finding_summary: The paper combines a systematic review and an empirical COVID-era case study to argue that standalone technology use in mathematics education is rare and underrepresented, especially in compulsory schooling. The review found 174 eligible studies out of 817 records, but only 10 involved standalone use of technology and none used an ITS in standalone mode; this is used to support the claim that mathematics education research has been overly teacher-mediated and not well aligned with remote-learning needs.
finding.measure: Systematic review counts of studies by instructional mode and technology type
finding.study_size: 817 records screened; 174 included studies; 10 standalone-use studies

paper_profiles.title: Virtual reality and augmented reality-supported K-12 STEM learning: trends, advantages and challenges
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the growing use of virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) in K-12 STEM education and the need for a broad synthesis of how these technologies are being used, for whom, and with what reported benefits and challenges. The authors note that prior reviews tended to focus on earlier studies, on a single discipline, or on narrower technology subsets, leaving an updated and wider view of VR/AR-supported K-12 STEM learning incomplete.

To answer this gap, the study systematically reviewed 117 empirical articles published from 2010 to 2022, using PRISMA procedures and a technology-based learning model. The review coded learning subject, device type, participant age group, research method, sample size, and learning strategy, with an emphasis on K-12 STEM contexts. The included studies covered elementary, middle, and high school students, with the largest share in elementary school; mathematics was the second most common subject after science, and there were far fewer studies in technology or engineering.

The review found that VR/AR was most often associated with positive effects on academic achievement, motivation, self-efficacy, attitudes, attention, and some higher-order cognitive skills. It also supported learning processes such as engagement, visualization, inquiry, collaborative learning, and interaction. At the same time, the paper identified recurring implementation challenges, including distraction, operational difficulties, teacher classroom-management and design burdens, and school-level constraints such as cost, infrastructure, and privacy concerns. Overall, the paper concludes that VR/AR is promising for K-12 STEM learning but needs better-designed implementations, more attention to immersive tools, and more research in underexplored areas such as technology, engineering, and senior high school settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review using PRISMA and explicit coding procedures, but it is not a primary causal study and does not estimate pooled effects. The evidence is therefore syntheses-level and descriptive, with moderate credibility for mapping trends but limited for causal inference.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review reports several positive educational associations, including a large attention effect in one included study (d=1.28) and recurring improvements in achievement, motivation, and engagement. At the same time, it emphasizes mixed implementation realities and substantial school/teacher constraints, so the overall impact is promising but not uniformly strong.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of VR/AR-supported K-12 STEM learning, including immersive and non-immersive simulations, virtual labs, and game-based learning activities used to teach science and mathematics concepts.

finding.finding_summary: The review includes mathematics among the STEM domains studied (22 of 117 articles) and reports that VR/AR was often associated with improved understanding and achievement in STEM learning, but the mathematics-specific evidence base was comparatively smaller than science. The paper synthesizes prior empirical studies rather than estimating a single pooled effect, so no overall meta-analytic effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning outcomes across included empirical studies (e.g., achievement tests, understanding, learning gains)
finding.study_size: n=117 studies reviewed; 22 studies in mathematics
