finding.measure: Self-reported creative cognition scale (5-item Creative Cognition subscale)

finding.finding_summary: Generative AI use was associated with higher self-efficacy and lower anxiety in design tasks, which served as significant mediators of creative cognition. The indirect effect through self-efficacy was β=0.256 (95% CI [0.140, 0.418]) and through anxiety was β=0.093 (95% CI [0.018, 0.195]); the serial mediation via self-efficacy then anxiety was β=0.053 (95% CI [0.012, 0.114]).
finding.measure: Self-efficacy and anxiety reduction subscales (5-point Likert survey measures)

paper_profiles.title: A Systematic Review of the Effectiveness of Algebraic Teaching Interventions: A Meta-Analysis and Meta-Synthesis
paper_profiles.venue: Nordic Journal of Systematic Reviews in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a protocol for a systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-synthesis focused on algebraic teaching interventions in K-12 education. The authors ask which interventions improve algebra learning, for whom they work best, and under what conditions, with a particular emphasis on identifying moderators that explain variation in effects. The paper is motivated by longstanding student difficulties with algebra and by the need to understand how changes in mathematics standards and instruction over the last four decades have shaped outcomes.

The approach combines quantitative and qualitative synthesis of empirical studies conducted in the United States from 1980 onward. Eligible studies include randomized controlled trials, quasi-experimental studies with baseline equivalence, and empirical qualitative or mixed-methods studies. The review will examine interventions delivered by teachers, researchers, or technology, and will consider moderators such as grade level, gender, race/ethnicity, socioeconomic status, intervention length, delivery mode, teacher training, publication year, and algebra content category.

The target population is students in elementary and secondary grades (K-12), with the review explicitly covering early algebra, pre-algebra, and algebra contexts. The authors do not report study findings because this is a protocol rather than a completed review. Instead, they conclude that the planned meta-analysis and meta-synthesis should produce a more nuanced account of effective algebra instruction and help inform research, policy, and classroom practice.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review/meta-analysis protocol, not a completed effect study. It has a clear methodology and planned quantitative synthesis, but it does not yet report primary-study results or completed risk-of-bias findings.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No empirical impact is reported in this protocol; it only specifies planned analyses of algebraic teaching interventions. As a result, there is no demonstrated effect on student outcomes to score for impact.

paper_profiles.title: Integrating Chat-GPT in the Classroom: A Study on Linear Algebra Learning in Higher Education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Information and Education Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether and how Chat-GPT can support linear algebra learning in higher education. The authors ask two questions: whether students’ mathematical performance differs across instruction conditions using Chat-GPT versus conventional teaching, and how students perceive Chat-GPT as a learning tool. The study is motivated by the challenge of learning abstract linear algebra concepts and by the growing interest in AI tools for education.

The intervention was evaluated using a mixed-methods design. Quantitatively, the study compared three groups of mathematics education students aged 20–23 from three Indonesian universities: a group taught only with Chat-GPT, a group taught with Chat-GPT plus an expert mathematics educator, and a conventional instruction control group. A post-test and one-way ANOVA were used, and the paper also included a meta-analysis of 19 prior studies on technology and algebra achievement. Qualitatively, five students who experienced the Chat-GPT-supported classes were interviewed using hermeneutic phenomenology to explore their perceptions.

The results showed that the Chat-GPT-plus-instructor condition produced the highest achievement, outperforming both Chat-GPT alone and conventional teaching. Chat-GPT alone did not outperform traditional instruction, suggesting that the tool is most effective when guided by an educator. The meta-analysis found a moderate overall positive effect of technology on algebra achievement, with Chat-GPT-like multimedia showing the strongest moderator effect. Students generally reported that Chat-GPT helped them understand concepts, receive step-by-step explanations, and learn more flexibly, but they also noted that it sometimes made errors and needed human verification. The authors conclude that Chat-GPT should complement rather than replace teachers, especially for more abstract mathematical ideas.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods paper with a small quasi-experimental component, a meta-analysis of prior studies, and qualitative interviews. Because the focal evidence presented here is not a standalone well-controlled RCT and the design includes substantial heterogeneity and interpretive components, the overall evidence quality is best rated yellow despite the included meta-analytic element.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The meta-analysis reports a moderate pooled effect size (g=0.56, 95% CI [0.40, 0.72]) for technology interventions on algebra achievement, and the Chat-GPT+instructor condition shows a large practical advantage over the comparison groups. This meets the threshold for a medium-or-larger impact on the studied population, even though the Chat-GPT-specific evidence is context-dependent.

interventions.use_case: Chat-GPT 3.5 used as a conversational math tutor for linear algebra problem solving, step-by-step explanations, immediate feedback, and concept support; in one condition it was used alone and in another alongside an expert mathematics educator.

finding.finding_summary: A quasi-experimental ANOVA found significant differences in post-test linear algebra performance across groups (n=30; F=9.745, p=0.001). The Chat-GPT + instructor group scored highest (M=87.58, SD=7.84), Chat-GPT alone scored lowest (M=53.25, SD=22.97), and conventional instruction was intermediate (M=68.40, SD=20.39); Tukey tests showed Chat-GPT + instructor outperformed both other groups, while Chat-GPT alone did not differ significantly from conventional instruction.
finding.measure: Linear algebra post-test scores; one-way ANOVA and Tukey HSD comparisons
finding.std_deviation: Chat-GPT alone SD=22.97; Chat-GPT+instructor SD=7.84; control SD=20.39

finding.finding_summary: Student perceptions were strongly favorable: 36.84% agreed and 57.89% strongly agreed that Chat-GPT helped them understand mathematical concepts better, while 26.32% agreed and 73.68% strongly agreed that it increased interest in learning. The qualitative interviews also suggested reduced anxiety and a more comfortable, non-judgmental learning environment when students could ask repeated questions freely.
finding.measure: Perception questionnaire and semi-structured interview themes on interest, engagement, and comfort

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that Chat-GPT supported step-by-step reasoning, error detection, and conceptual explanation, which students said helped them understand why procedures worked. However, the study also notes a risk of reduced independent thinking if students rely on Chat-GPT for quick answers, making the overall durable-skills effect conditional rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Interview themes on conceptual understanding, reasoning, and independent problem solving

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that Chat-GPT can provide quick responses, immediate feedback, and 24/7 access to explanations, which may reduce the time students spend waiting for help and support self-paced learning. This is presented as a practical efficiency benefit rather than a separately quantified outcome, with no direct effect size reported.
finding.measure: Interview and questionnaire perceptions of accessibility, immediacy, and ease of use

paper_profiles.title: Exploring automatic scoring of mathematical descriptive assessment using prompt engineering with the GPT-4 model: Focused on permutations and combinations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether GPT-4-based ChatGPT can automatically score mathematical descriptive assessment items in a way that aligns with human teachers. The authors focus on the challenge that scoring constructed-response mathematics items is time-consuming for teachers and can be difficult to make consistent, especially when problems allow multiple solution strategies.

The study uses prompt engineering to improve GPT-4’s scoring performance. The researchers designed structured prompts using techniques such as Few-Shot-CoT, Self-Consistency, and iterative prompt refinement. For one item with multiple solution strategies, they also added a classification step so GPT-4 first identified the solution type and then applied a type-specific scoring prompt. Teacher scoring was used as the comparison benchmark.

The participants were 204 first-year high school students in one high school in Suwon, South Korea, who completed three permutation-and-combination descriptive items. Two experienced teachers scored the responses and their scores were compared with GPT-4’s scores. The paper concludes that GPT-4’s scores were strongly correlated with teacher scores, and that self-consistency improved reliability. It also found that classification by solution strategy substantially improved GPT-4 performance on the item with multiple valid approaches, suggesting that prompt engineering can help GPT-4 function as a scoring aid for teachers.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical correlational study comparing GPT-4 scoring with two teachers on real student responses, but it is not an RCT and does not isolate causal effects on learning. The evidence is useful but limited to a single school, a small set of items, and grading agreement outcomes rather than student achievement gains.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests a modest practical benefit for grading efficiency and scoring consistency, especially for constructed-response math items. However, it does not test student learning outcomes or show large-scale operational impact, so the observed impact is promising but still unclear/modest.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4-based automatic scoring of middle/high school students' descriptive mathematics answers in permutations and combinations, using prompt engineering, few-shot CoT, self-consistency, and structured prompts to emulate teacher grading.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that GPT-4 can support teacher scoring of mathematical constructed-response items with strong teacher-model correlations, suggesting potential workload reduction in grading descriptive assessments. For items 1 and 2, teacher vs. GPT-4 scoring correlations were high (roughly r=0.80-0.91 across individual runs; mode correlations 0.872-0.905), and for item 3 correlations improved further after answer-type classification (mode correlations 0.928-0.931), indicating a practical grading-aid use case.
finding.measure: Correlation between teacher scoring and GPT-4 scoring; consistency of GPT-4 scoring across repeated runs
finding.study_size: n=197 (items 1 and 2), n=174 (item 3); correlations reported on subsets after excluding non-mode cases

finding.finding_summary: The system demonstrated strong agreement with teacher grading on permutation and combination constructed-response items, indicating that GPT-4 can accurately evaluate mathematical reasoning and symbolic expression in this content area. Correlations between teacher and GPT-4 scores were about 0.8 overall, with stronger performance on items 1 and 2 and improved alignment on item 3 when responses were first classified by solution strategy.
finding.measure: Teacher-grade vs GPT-4-grade correlation on mathematics descriptive assessment items
finding.study_size: n=197 for items 1-2; n=174 for item 3

paper_profiles.title: Towards Responsible Development of Generative AI for Education: An Evaluation-Driven Approach
paper_profiles.extended_summary: This paper addresses the problem of how to responsibly develop and evaluate generative AI systems for education, especially conversational tutors. The authors argue that current AI systems are often optimized for general helpfulness rather than pedagogy, and that the field lacks shared evaluation practices and clear pedagogical benchmarks.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a technical report/framework paper with participatory design and benchmark development, not a causal evaluation study. It is peer-reviewed/archival-style scholarly work with systematic methods, but it does not provide an experimental estimate of learning impact on students.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports promising pedagogical preference and evaluation results for the LearnLM-Tutor model, but these are primarily model- and human-rating outcomes rather than demonstrated student learning gains. As such, the practical educational impact is plausible but still unclear for general K-12 outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Developing and evaluating LearnLM-Tutor, a text-based generative AI tutor for 1:1 conversational tutoring, including grounded multi-turn educational dialogues, feedback, hints, and pedagogical prompting/fine-tuning for learners and teachers.

paper_profiles.title: MathVC: An LLM-Simulated Multi-Persona Virtual Classroom for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of supporting collaborative problem-solving (CPS) in middle school mathematics, where real classrooms often lack enough suitable peers, time, and orchestration capacity to sustain productive group work. The authors ask whether large language models can simulate multiple student peers well enough to create a believable and pedagogically useful collaborative environment for mathematics learning.

To study this, they designed MathVC, a multi-persona virtual classroom platform in which one student works with two LLM-simulated classmates. MathVC uses a meta-planning controller to manage CPS stages (shared understanding, team organization, planning, execution, and validation) and a persona-simulation layer that gives each virtual peer a mathematical skill profile, including common mistakes injected into one persona to mimic a weaker peer. The system was implemented as a web application and powered by GPT-4o.

The evaluation involved 14 U.S. middle school students in grades 6–8, who used MathVC to solve grade-appropriate mathematics problems and then completed interviews and exit surveys. The study found that students generally perceived the virtual peers as authentic and engaging, especially because they made realistic mistakes, offered corrections, and supported collaborative dialogue. Participants reported that MathVC increased their engagement, motivation, and confidence, while also reducing cognitive burden through diverse perspectives and immediate scaffolding. Some students noted that the agents sometimes sounded too formal or adult-like, suggesting room for improvement in conversational style.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative human-subjects evaluation with 14 participants, interviews, logs, and descriptive survey data. It is informative but lacks experimental comparison, randomization, or pre/post causal estimates, so it does not meet stronger causal evidence criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are positive but modest and primarily perception-based, with no achievement effect sizes or controlled outcome evidence. The study suggests potential impact for middle school math collaboration, but the evidence is currently exploratory and limited in scale.

interventions.use_case: LLM-simulated multi-persona virtual classroom for middle school collaborative mathematical problem solving, where GPT-4o-generated virtual peers discuss, question, critique, and scaffold a student's work through staged conversation and persona simulation.

finding.finding_summary: In a qualitative evaluation with 14 U.S. middle school students (40 dialogue sessions; 695 total messages), participants reported that MathVC helped them reach shared solutions and work effectively on math problems. The paper does not report pre/post achievement gains or effect sizes, but students’ exit survey responses were high on understanding the math problem and solving it collaboratively (e.g., means around 4.2-4.4 on a 5-point scale).
finding.measure: Exit survey items on understanding the math problem, contributing to task completion, planning steps, and reaching a shared solution; qualitative interview reports about collaborative math problem solving

finding.finding_summary: Students reported increased engagement, motivation, confidence, and persistence while working with the virtual peers. The study is qualitative/descriptive, but survey results were high for constructive interaction (Mean=4.36) and the collaborative environment being easy to work in (Mean=4.21) on a 5-point scale.
finding.measure: Exit survey responses; semi-structured interview themes on engagement, motivation, confidence, and persistence

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed to scaffold collaborative problem solving, and students reported constructive interaction, shared understanding, planning, and collaboration with the virtual peers. Survey means were high for interacting constructively (Mean=4.36) and planning steps/understanding contributions (Mean=4.36), suggesting perceived benefits for collaboration and metacognitive coordination.
finding.measure: Exit survey items on constructive interaction, planning, and shared understanding; dialogue logs and interview themes

paper_profiles.title: The Role of Value on Mathematics Between Self-Efficacy and Like Mathematics: A Moderated Mediation Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how students’ mathematics self-efficacy relates to their enjoyment of learning mathematics, and whether this relationship operates through students’ valuing of mathematics. It also tests whether parents’ belief that mathematics is important changes the strength of this indirect pathway. The authors frame the work in relation to self-efficacy and expectancy-value theory and aim to understand these relationships in a Turkish context where TIMSS results have lagged behind many other countries.

The analysis uses TIMSS 2019 student questionnaire data from 3,600 eighth-grade students in Türkiye. The study is not an intervention study; instead, it applies mediation and moderated mediation models to survey measures of students’ liking for learning mathematics, mathematics self-efficacy, students’ value of mathematics, and parents’ valuing of mathematics. The paper also reports factor-analytic checks and reliability analyses for the TIMSS attitude scales used in the model.

Results show that higher mathematics self-efficacy is associated with greater liking of mathematics, and that students’ value of mathematics partially mediates this relationship. Parents’ valuing of mathematics significantly moderates the mediation: the indirect effect of self-efficacy through students’ value of mathematics is stronger when parents do not strongly endorse the importance of mathematics. The authors conclude that students’ and parents’ mathematics attitudes jointly shape students’ enjoyment of mathematics, and they suggest that schools and families should help students see mathematics as useful and worthwhile.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational/secondary-data study using TIMSS 2019 with moderated mediation analysis, not an experiment or quasi-experiment. It provides statistical modeling evidence but limited causal credibility because the design is cross-sectional.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports statistically significant associations and indirect effects, but the practical effect sizes are small to moderate for the moderated pathway (e.g., interaction ΔR²=0.001; index of moderated mediation CI near zero). Because this is an attitude/motivation study rather than a direct instructional intervention, the impact on student outcomes is modest and unclear for general practice.

finding.finding_summary: Among 8th-grade students in Türkiye (initial n=4,077; analyses reduced to n=3,600 after listwise deletion, plus smaller analysis samples after outlier removal), mathematics self-efficacy positively predicted students' liking learning mathematics. The total effect in the mediation model was β=0.75 (t=59.44, p<0.01), indicating a strong positive association between self-beliefs and enjoyment/liking of math.
finding.measure: Students Like Learning Mathematics (SLM) scale from TIMSS 2019

finding.finding_summary: Students' valuing of mathematics partially mediated the relationship between mathematics self-efficacy and liking learning mathematics. The indirect effect was 0.15 with 95% bootstrap CI [0.13, 0.16], accounting for 19.41% of the total effect, suggesting that higher self-efficacy increases math liking partly by increasing perceived value of mathematics.
finding.measure: TIMSS 2019 Students Value Mathematics (SVM) mediator and Students Like Learning Mathematics (SLM) outcome

finding.finding_summary: Parents' valuing of mathematics moderated the mediation pathway, with a significant interaction predicting students' valuing of mathematics (β=0.05, p<0.05; ΔR²=0.001). The conditional indirect effect of self-efficacy on liking mathematics through value was smaller when parents strongly valued mathematics (0.12, 95% bootstrap CI [0.10, 0.13]) than when they did not strongly value mathematics (0.15, 95% bootstrap CI [0.12, 0.19]).
finding.measure: Moderated mediation using TIMSS 2019 student-reported parents' valuing of mathematics, SVM, and SLM
finding.effect_size: conditional indirect effects: 0.12 vs 0.15; interaction β=0.05
finding.confidence_interval: conditional indirect effects 95% CIs [0.10, 0.13] and [0.12, 0.19]; index of moderated mediation 95% CI [0.00, 0.07]

paper_profiles.title: Applications of artificial intelligence in education: Implications for pedagogy, learning outcomes, and policy development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter surveys the role of artificial intelligence in education and argues that AI can improve pedagogy, learning outcomes, personalization, and institutional efficiency. The paper focuses on how AI systems can support smart education through tools such as intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, predictive analytics, chatbots, and automated feedback and assessment.

Rather than reporting a single empirical study, the chapter synthesizes existing literature and presents a proposed “Smart Education” model. It discusses how AI could tailor content to individual learners, identify learning gaps, support teachers with dashboards and automated tasks, and improve student engagement and performance. The chapter also outlines concerns about ethics, bias, privacy, equity, and the changing role of educators.

The context is broad education systems across levels, from schooling through higher education, and it includes students, teachers, administrators, parents, and institutions as stakeholders. The main conclusion is that AI has strong potential to transform education when implemented thoughtfully, but its adoption must be accompanied by safeguards, teacher professional development, and attention to fairness, transparency, and data protection.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative chapter/review with no original empirical design, no comparison group, and no reported quantitative analysis of ChatGPT effects or moderators. It is useful background, but it does not meet research-design criteria for causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The chapter claims broad positive educational impacts of AI, but these are unsupported by new effect estimates and are not specific to middle school mathematics or subgroup moderation. Impact is therefore unclear and best treated as general, descriptive background rather than evidence of measurable impact.

interventions.use_case: GenAI/ChatGPT-style chatbots and virtual assistants used for personalized student support, question answering, and real-time instructional assistance within a smart education system.
Personalized learning platform that adapts content, pace, and learning paths to individual students based on ongoing comprehension and knowledge-level assessment.
AI-driven tutoring system that mimics one-on-one tutoring by giving customized explanations, hints, and feedback aligned to each student’s pace and style.
Student-performance analytics that identify at-risk learners, predict poor performance or dropout risk, and trigger proactive interventions.
Real-time AI feedback on assignments and assessments, including instant error correction and formative feedback to support learning.
AI-supported instructional delivery and content generation used to create customized educational materials, assignments, and learning resources.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that AI-driven adaptive learning and GenAI tools increase student engagement, motivation, and enthusiasm by providing interactive and personalized content. No primary study data are reported in the chapter itself, so this is a narrative synthesis rather than an empirical estimate.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, and enthusiasm as described in the narrative review

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that AI-enabled personalized instruction and real-time feedback improve academic outcomes and retention of concepts across subjects. It cites prior work and examples but does not report a study-specific effect size, sample size, or controlled comparison in this chapter.
finding.measure: Academic performance / learning outcomes / concept retention

finding.finding_summary: The chapter emphasizes that virtual assistants, predictive analytics, and AI tutoring reduce teacher administrative burden and improve classroom management. The evidence is descriptive and policy-oriented, with no original quantitative estimate reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / administrative burden / classroom management efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI adoption can promote inclusive and equitable education, improve institutional decision-making, and support policy development around smart education. These claims are framed at the institutional level and are not supported by a new empirical evaluation in the chapter.
finding.measure: Institutional inclusivity, equity, and policy/implementation considerations

paper_profiles.title: Pragmatic AI in education and its role in mathematics learning and teaching
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This commentary argues that the post-ChatGPT discourse on AI in education has been too focused on producing student artifacts (for example, essays or lesson plans) and not enough on the learning processes that those artifacts are meant to support. The authors frame mathematics anxiety as a particularly important problem, especially in middle school and other K-12 settings, and suggest that AI should be designed to support socio-emotional learning (SEL), perceptions of competence, control, and value, and emotion regulation rather than simply automate content delivery.

The paper does not report an empirical intervention; instead, it proposes a conceptual model and a research agenda for pragmatic AI in mathematics education. The authors outline six possible AI roles: individualizing task difficulty and learning pathways, supporting agency and collaboration, tailoring achievement goals and expectations, improving value induction by connecting mathematics to personally relevant contexts, moderating feedback to preserve students’ sense of control, and fostering emotion regulation through emotion-aware tools such as chatbots or dashboards. The discussion emphasizes keeping teachers in the loop while using AI to provide fine-grained monitoring and personalization that a single teacher cannot easily achieve in a large classroom.

The intended context is mathematics learning and teaching, with explicit attention to persistent math anxiety that often appears in middle school students. The authors conclude that AI has promise if it is implemented as a means to transform learning processes and emotional experiences, but they also stress ethical concerns around privacy, data collection, teacher autonomy, and the need for careful governance before implementation. Overall, the paper is a position piece calling for multi-method, longitudinal, and context-sensitive research rather than reporting study results.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed commentary/call-to-action paper with no original empirical design, no comparison group, and no outcome data. It is useful for theory and research agenda setting, but it does not meet criteria for experimental or correlational evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not provide measured impacts, so the practical effect is unclear. It nonetheless addresses a priority K-12 issue—math anxiety and mathematics learning—using plausible AI design ideas, but impact remains speculative.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual proposal for using chatbots based on large language models to provide supportive, closed-environment conversational feedback, reframing of mistakes, and emotional support for mathematics learning and maths-anxiety reduction.
AI-supported adaptive learning platforms that dynamically adjust task difficulty, pacing, and achievement goals based on students' learning patterns and mastery data.

Predictive models and learning analytics to recommend next steps, identify student readiness, monitor progress over time, and flag moments when students need more structured guidance or are ready for more autonomous tasks.

AI-powered feedback mechanisms that analyze student work and emotional cues, then provide constructive, personalized feedback to preserve students' sense of control and support positive appraisals of effort and progress.

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual/commentary paper rather than an empirical study, but it argues that AI could positively affect students' socio-emotional learning, especially competence, control, value, and emotional regulation in mathematics. The paper proposes that adaptive task design, personalized goals, feedback, and chatbot support may reduce mathematics anxiety and improve self-regulation, but it does not report original data, sample sizes, or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Proposed changes in maths anxiety, perceived control/competence/value, self-regulation, and emotional responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI could improve mathematics learning by matching task difficulty and supporting productive struggle, but also warns that poorly designed AI could miscalibrate challenge levels and confuse or frustrate students. No empirical results are reported; the paper is a research agenda and conceptual model rather than an outcomes study.
finding.measure: Proposed mathematics learning progress, task success, and alignment of task difficulty with student proficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes that AI may strengthen metacognition, self-regulated learning, and collaborative problem-solving through individualized goals, dashboards, and cooperative AI tools. These claims are theoretical and programmatic, with no reported experimental evidence, sample size, or effect size.
finding.measure: Proposed metacognitive reflection, self-regulated learning, and cooperation in mathematics tasks

finding.finding_summary: The commentary suggests AI could help teachers scale individualized support in large classes by monitoring multiple student data streams in parallel and reducing the burden of manual differentiation. This is framed as a potential efficiency gain rather than a measured one, and the paper provides no empirical estimates.
finding.measure: Proposed teacher support, monitoring efficiency, and personalization at scale

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that AI implementation may have broad institutional consequences for ethics, privacy, governance, teacher autonomy, and data collection requirements. It highlights both potential benefits and risks, but does not report empirical institutional outcomes or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Proposed governance, privacy, data-security, and teacher-autonomy implications

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing students’ authentic mathematical problem-solving skills and confidence through error analysis of GPT-4 solutions
paper_profiles.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether an error-analysis learning activity built around GPT-4-generated solutions can improve students’ authentic mathematical problem-solving skills and their mathematical confidence. The study is motivated by the challenge that authentic word problems are often text-heavy and difficult for elementary students to understand, especially lower-achieving learners, and by the possibility that AI-generated solutions can be used not only as worked examples but also as objects for critical analysis.

The intervention combined GPT-4 problem solving, error analysis, peer explanation, and class staging. Students first asked GPT-4 to solve authentic mathematics problems, then examined the solution step by step, identified and corrected errors, discussed their reasoning in small groups, and presented findings to the class. The comparison condition was traditional instruction using the same materials, teacher, and instructional time. The study lasted ten weeks and involved 59 fifth-grade students from one primary school in northern Taiwan.

Quantitative results showed that students in the experimental group improved significantly from pre- to post-test in authentic mathematical problem solving and mathematical confidence. Compared with the control group, the experimental group showed a significant advantage for low-achieving students in problem-solving performance, and significant advantages for both high- and low-achieving students in mathematical confidence. Interview data suggested that GPT-4 explanations supported understanding, peer discussion promoted collaborative problem-solving and critical thinking, and the activity increased patience and reduced anxiety. The authors conclude that GPT-4, when combined with structured error analysis, can support mathematics learning, though it does not replace the teacher and is especially helpful when paired with peer and teacher guidance.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental study with a control group, but it is not randomized and uses purposive sampling from one school. The paper includes quantitative pre/post and between-group tests plus qualitative interviews, supporting internal inference but with moderate design limitations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention shows clear positive effects on a priority population, especially low-achieving students, but the reported effects are mostly statistical significance without standardized effect sizes. This makes the impact promising but still somewhat unclear in magnitude for broad generalization.

interventions.use_case: error analysis learning activity using GPT-4 solutions for fifth-grade authentic mathematical word problems, where students query GPT-4, inspect its step-by-step reasoning, and discuss/correct AI-generated errors

finding.finding_summary: The quasi-experimental study with 59 fifth-grade students found that the experimental group improved significantly on authentic mathematical problem-solving after the GPT-4 error-analysis intervention (Wilcoxon signed-rank z=-4.318, p<.001). In between-group post-test comparisons, the experimental group outperformed the control group overall but not significantly (U=316, p=.069), while low-achieving students in the experimental group significantly outperformed low-achieving controls (U=48, p=.01).
finding.measure: Authentic Mathematical Problem-Solving Test (AMPS) pre/post scores; Mann-Whitney U and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests

finding.finding_summary: Mathematical confidence increased significantly in the experimental group after the intervention (Wilcoxon signed-rank z=-3.881, p<.001). Post-test confidence was also significantly higher than the control group overall (U=215, p=.001), and this held for both high-achieving students (U=64, p=.045) and low-achieving students (U=43, p=.007).
finding.measure: TIMSS 2019 Mathematical Confidence Scale pre/post scores

finding.finding_summary: Interview data indicated perceived gains in understanding, collaborative problem-solving, critical thinking, mathematical creativity, and metacognitive knowledge. The paper reports that 93% of experimental-group students felt GPT-4 explanations improved understanding, 79% endorsed collaborative problem-solving, 43% reported gains in critical thinking, 43% in creative problem-solving diversity, and 86% in metacognitive knowledge.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interviews coded by expert raters (Fleiss' kappa=0.934)

paper_profiles.title: Digital learning and student outcomes: a mathematical synthesis from the last decade
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IJERE)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the overall effectiveness of digital learning interventions on students’ cognitive learning outcomes and asks whether the effects vary by intervention characteristics. The motivation is that prior research on e-learning has produced conflicting findings, and the authors argue that clearer evidence is needed before educators and policymakers expand digital investments or move toward newer AI-driven tools.

The study is a meta-analysis of 17 randomized pretest-posttest controlled studies published between 2013 and 2023, comprising 1,896 participants. The included interventions covered a range of digital learning formats, such as online quizzes, web-based platforms, virtual reality, augmented reality, mobile learning apps, and online/blended courses. The sample spans primary, middle school, secondary, undergraduate, and graduate/tertiary contexts, with outcomes focused on objective cognitive measures such as academic achievement, subject knowledge, and interpretation skills.

The meta-analysis found a positive overall effect of digital learning compared with traditional instruction, with a small-to-moderate adjusted effect size. Subgroup analyses suggested somewhat larger gains for active cognitive engagement, school settings, shorter interventions, smaller samples, and controlled implementation contexts, but none of these moderators produced statistically significant differences in pooled effects. The authors conclude that digital learning can improve cognitive outcomes, but the evidence base is still heterogeneous and methodologically limited, so stronger controlled studies are needed, including future work that may combine established digital tools with AI-supported solutions.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed meta-analysis of 17 randomized pretest-posttest controlled studies with explicit inclusion criteria and quantitative synthesis. It uses random-effects modeling and reports publication-bias adjustment, though heterogeneity is high (I2=83%).
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled effect on cognitive outcomes is medium in size (g=.62; adjusted g=.49), indicating a meaningful positive impact of digital learning on student achievement overall. However, moderator effects were not statistically significant, so subgroup-specific impact remains uncertain.

interventions.use_case: Meta-analysis of digital learning interventions such as online quizzes, web-based e-learning, learning platforms, virtual reality apps, augmented reality activities, mobile learning apps, and online courses used to support cognitive learning outcomes versus traditional instruction.

finding.finding_summary: Across 17 randomized controlled studies (n=1,896), digital learning interventions produced a positive moderate gain in cognitive learning outcomes compared with traditional instruction. The pooled effect was Hedge’s g=.62 (95% CI [.38, .86], p<.01), and the publication-bias-adjusted estimate remained positive at g=.49 (95% CI [.40, .59]).
finding.measure: Objective cognitive learning outcomes / academic achievement scores across included studies

paper_profiles.title: A meta-analysis of AI-enabled personalized STEM education in schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how effective AI-enabled personalized STEM education is in K-12 schools and which study characteristics moderate its effects. The authors note that prior research on AI in STEM education has been fragmented, with many review studies focusing on qualitative synthesis rather than pooled quantitative evidence. To address this gap, they conducted a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trial studies published between 2012 and 2024.

The intervention of interest is AI-enabled personalized learning in STEM contexts, including intelligent tutoring systems, personalized educational games, augmented/virtual reality tools, and other AI-based applications. The review examines how these technologies support personalization through automated feedback, adaptive content, and classroom or student-centered learning models. The authors also code whether the systems used generative AI and analyze multiple moderators, including school level, AI application type, personalized learning model type, observed outcome type, and subject area.

The meta-analysis includes 32 journal articles yielding 99 independent effect sizes from K-12 settings. The results show a statistically significant overall positive effect of AI-enabled personalized STEM education over non-AI instruction. Moderator analyses indicate stronger effects in secondary school than in kindergarten or elementary settings, the largest effects for AR/VR tools, stronger impacts when AI is embedded in more collaborative or classroom-based personalized learning models, and larger effects in comprehensive courses. Generative AI usage did not significantly moderate outcomes. Overall, the study concludes that AI can support personalized STEM learning in schools, but effectiveness depends strongly on educational level, subject, and implementation design.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-analysis of 32 randomized controlled trials with 99 effect sizes, which is the highest evidence tier in the framework. The study reports subgroup analyses, heterogeneity statistics, and publication-bias checks, supporting strong methodological credibility.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The overall effect is statistically significant and above the blue-tier threshold (g=0.455), indicating a medium practical impact on K-12 STEM learning. Several moderators also show meaningful gains, especially AR/VR and comprehensive courses, reinforcing substantive educational impact.

interventions.use_case: AI-enabled personalized STEM learning systems classified as ITSs, including computerized tutoring environments that adapt instruction and feedback to K-12 students' needs.
AI-enabled personalized educational games used for STEM learning with adaptive tutoring and feedback.
AI-enabled AR/VR learning environments for STEM, including immersive/embodied simulations sometimes incorporating AI-powered virtual agents.

finding.finding_summary: Across 99 effect sizes from 32 randomized controlled trials, AI-enabled personalized STEM education produced a significant overall gain in learning outcomes (Hedges' g=0.455, 95% CI [0.327, 0.583]). For mathematics specifically, the subgroup analysis found a small positive effect (g=0.398, p<0.001; k=45).
finding.measure: STEM learning outcomes, including mathematics achievement and knowledge/skills outcomes
finding.study_size: n=99 effect sizes from 32 RCT studies

finding.finding_summary: The meta-analysis found a significant overall positive effect of AI-enabled personalized STEM education on learning outcomes (g=0.455, 95% CI [0.327, 0.583], k=99 effect sizes). Outcomes were strongest for knowledge/skills (g=0.603, 95% CI [0.364, 0.842]) and for comprehensive courses (g=2.161, p=0.004), indicating gains in STEM conceptual understanding and problem solving across studies.
finding.measure: Knowledge/skills, comprehensive ability, and course-level STEM learning outcomes
finding.study_size: n=99 effect sizes from 32 RCT studies

finding.finding_summary: AI-enabled personalized STEM education showed small positive effects on perceptions/attitudes and engagement, suggesting benefits beyond achievement. Perceptions/attitudes had g=0.264 (p<0.001; k=24) and engagement had g=0.386 (p<0.001; k=25), both statistically significant.
finding.measure: Perceptions/attitudes and engagement surveys or related study measures
finding.study_size: n=24 to n=25 effect sizes by subgroup

finding.finding_summary: The review included a small set of studies assessing broader capabilities such as comprehensive ability, which encompasses critical thinking and problem solving. The comprehensive ability subgroup was positive but not statistically significant (g=0.381, 95% CI [-0.065, 0.826], k=1), so evidence for durable-skill gains is limited.
finding.measure: Comprehensive ability (e.g., critical thinking, problem solving)

paper_profiles.title: A Systematic Review of the Effectiveness of Algebraic Teaching Interventions: A Meta-Analysis and Meta-Synthesis
paper_profiles.venue: Nordic Journal of Systematic Reviews in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a protocol for a systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-synthesis of algebraic teaching interventions for K-12 students. The authors ask which algebra interventions are effective, for whom, and under what conditions, motivated by the persistent difficulty students have with algebra and the importance of algebra for later mathematics and STEM success.

The planned review will synthesize empirical studies conducted in the United States from 1980 to the present, covering early algebra, pre-algebra, and algebra instruction across elementary, middle, and high school grades. The intervention category is broad: any classroom-based algebraic teaching intervention delivered by a teacher, researcher, or technology compared with business-as-usual instruction. The meta-analysis will estimate standardized mean differences and examine moderators such as grade level, algebraic big ideas, demographic variables, intervention type, delivery mode, training, publication type, and assessment type.

The meta-synthesis will qualitatively examine the characteristics of effective interventions, their learning goals, and the nature of students’ mathematical thinking. The authors argue that combining quantitative and qualitative synthesis will provide a more complete picture of algebra instruction than prior reviews and help identify best practices across grade levels and student groups. Because this is a protocol paper, it reports planned methods rather than completed results.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a protocol for a systematic review/meta-analysis rather than a completed empirical study. It describes planned methods, not analyzed evidence or results, so it does not meet the criteria for a completed meta-analysis or trial.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No intervention effects are reported, so there is no demonstrated educational impact to classify. The paper is important as a research protocol, but it provides no measurable student or institutional outcome effect.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is a systematic review/meta-analysis protocol, not a completed intervention study, so it reports no empirical effect estimate yet. It proposes to synthesize the effectiveness of algebraic teaching interventions on mathematics learning, thinking, and knowledge across Grades K-12, but provides no results, effect sizes, or sample sizes in the text provided.
finding.measure: Planned measures of mathematics learning, thinking, or knowledge; standardized mean differences (Hedges' g) from included studies

finding.finding_summary: The article’s substantive contribution is methodological and agenda-setting: it lays out a protocol for a mixed-methods evidence synthesis intended to inform policy, practice, and future research in school algebra. No empirical impact is reported because the review has not yet been conducted and no effect estimates are available.
finding.measure: Planned synthesis of intervention effects, moderators, and thematic recommendations for policy/practice

paper_profiles.title: Can GenAI improve students’ mathematics learning outcomes effectively? — A meta-analysis of empirical research 2023-2025
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), including tools such as ChatGPT and other large language models, improves students’ mathematics learning outcomes. It is presented as a systematic review and meta-analysis of empirical studies published from 2023 to 2025, motivated by mixed findings in the emerging literature and the need to move beyond isolated studies.

The review synthesizes 22 empirical studies (46 independent effect sizes; N=5,132) comparing GenAI-supported mathematics learning with traditional instruction or other non-GenAI approaches. The included studies cover students from primary school through university, and the analysis separates outcomes into cognitive skills (including higher-order and lower-order thinking) and non-cognitive skills such as motivation, anxiety, self-efficacy, and attitudes. It also examines moderators such as educational level, intervention duration, learning content, sample size, and the degree of GenAI integration using the PIC-RAT model.

The meta-analysis finds a moderate positive overall effect of GenAI on mathematics learning outcomes (Hedges’ g = 0.539), with stronger effects on cognitive outcomes than non-cognitive outcomes. Within cognitive skills, the impact is larger for higher-order thinking than for lower-order thinking. Moderator analysis suggests that effects are strongest for elementary students, for interventions classified as “Creative Transformation,” and in smaller studies; intervention duration and learning content are not significant moderators. Overall, the paper concludes that GenAI can be beneficial in mathematics education, especially when integrated in more transformative ways rather than as a simple instructional replacement.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review and meta-analysis with a defined search strategy, explicit inclusion criteria, quality appraisal (MERSQI), and quantitative synthesis across 22 studies. The evidence base is strong for an educational synthesis, though it is a protocol/reporting text rather than a completed journal meta-analysis article in the excerpt provided.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled effect on mathematics learning outcomes is moderate and clearly positive (g=0.539), exceeding the threshold for medium impact. The finding is relevant to a priority K-12 population, with especially strong effects reported for elementary and middle school learners and for higher-order mathematical thinking.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI/ChatGPT-style large language model support for mathematics learning, including conversational problem-solving, step-by-step guidance, personalized explanations, and generated practice/content in school and university math contexts.

finding.finding_summary: This meta-analysis of 22 empirical studies (46 independent effect sizes, N=5,132) found a moderate positive overall effect of GenAI on mathematics learning outcomes (Hedges' g=0.539, p<0.005; 95% CI [0.374, 0.704]). Effects were stronger for cognitive outcomes (g=0.596) than non-cognitive outcomes (g=0.320), with the largest gains for higher-order thinking (g=0.740) and lower-order thinking also positive (g=0.562).
finding.measure: Mathematics learning outcomes, pooled standardized mean differences (Hedges' g) across achievement and cognitive outcome measures

finding.finding_summary: Across non-cognitive outcomes, GenAI showed a smaller but still positive effect (g=0.320) on variables such as motivation, self-efficacy, mathematics anxiety, attitudes, and engagement. The manuscript reports that these affective and motivational outcomes improved overall, though less strongly than cognitive outcomes.
finding.measure: Non-cognitive mathematics-related outcomes including motivation, self-efficacy, anxiety, attitudes, and engagement

finding.finding_summary: GenAI had a stronger impact on higher-order cognitive skills than lower-order ones, with higher-order thinking showing a sizable positive effect (g=0.740). This suggests benefits for analysis, evaluation, creation, and complex problem-solving in mathematics, especially when GenAI was integrated as 'Creative Transformation' (g=1.075).
finding.measure: Higher-order cognitive skill outcomes (analysis, evaluation, creation, complex problem-solving)

paper_profiles.title: AI-Powered Chatbots in Science Education: Meta-Analysis of Pedagogical Integration and Student Achievement
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Chemistry Education Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether AI-powered chatbots improve student achievement in science education and which contextual, pedagogical, and learner factors moderate their effectiveness. The authors note that prior research has often focused on technical features or user satisfaction rather than instructional design and learning context, leaving uncertainty about when and for whom chatbot-supported learning works best.

To address this, the study conducted a PRISMA-guided meta-analysis of 26 empirical studies published from 2020 to 2024. The included studies examined chatbot use in science-related and STEM contexts across primary, secondary, and especially higher education settings. The intervention varied widely, including scaffolded learning, personalized learning, inquiry-based learning, gamified learning, flipped classrooms, autonomous learning, collaborative learning, and micro-learning, with chatbots used either as supplementary tools or primary instructional agents.

The meta-analysis found a statistically significant moderate positive overall effect on learning outcomes, with stronger effects in lower-middle-income countries, in computer science and natural sciences, and when chatbots were embedded in scaffolded or personalized pedagogies. Effects were stronger for higher-order thinking and mixed assessments than for lower-order measures, and noncognitive benefits such as engagement, satisfaction, and perceived equity were also reported. However, the results were highly heterogeneous, showing that chatbot effectiveness depends heavily on context, design, learner experience, and intervention duration rather than being uniformly beneficial.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-analysis following PRISMA with 26 empirical studies and random-effects modeling, which meets the highest credibility standard in the requested framework. It also includes moderator and bias analyses, though heterogeneity is very high (I²=96.58%), which should temper precision.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled effect on learning outcomes is moderate and practically meaningful (g=0.610), exceeding the threshold for blue impact. The intervention shows positive effects across a large synthesized sample and in several priority contexts, especially lower-middle-income settings and scaffolded/personalized instruction.

interventions.use_case: Meta-analysis of AI-powered chatbots and conversational assistants (including ChatGPT and similar tools) used for instructional support, scaffolding, and personalized science learning.

finding.finding_summary: Across 26 studies (n=3,287), AI-powered chatbots produced a statistically significant moderate improvement in science learning outcomes overall (Hedges’ g=0.610, 95% CI [0.550, 0.670], p<0.001). The synthesis focused on achievement in science education, with strongest effects in computer science and natural sciences and weaker effects in health sciences.
finding.measure: Student achievement / learning outcomes in science education (study-specific tests and performance measures aggregated in meta-analysis)

finding.finding_summary: The review reports common gains in engagement and satisfaction, with subgroup evidence showing positive effects for engagement/motivation (e.g. overall noncognitive outcomes and several included studies). For noncognitive outcomes, the pooled pattern was positive overall, though some specific affective measures such as self-efficacy were mixed.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, satisfaction, perceived equity, and self-efficacy measures

finding.finding_summary: The meta-analysis indicates stronger effects when outcomes were assessed with higher-order thinking skills (HOTS) or mixed HOTS/LOTS measures, with moderator estimates of g=0.974 for HOTS and g=1.778 for mixed assessments. The paper also notes gains in critical thinking, problem-solving, metacognition, and conceptual understanding in several included studies.
finding.measure: Higher-order thinking skills, critical thinking, problem-solving, metacognition, conceptual understanding

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests chatbots can improve learning efficiency and reduce the need for direct teacher support in some contexts, especially as supplementary tools and in lower-resource settings. However, this is discussed mainly as an implementation implication rather than a directly measured pooled outcome, so the evidence is indirect.
finding.measure: Teacher support / instructional efficiency implied in discussion of supplementary use and compensatory support

paper_profiles.title: Transforming Learning or Empty Promise? A Meta-Analysis of Generative AI in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative AI tools such as ChatGPT improve student learning and, importantly, under what conditions they are most effective. The authors conducted a meta-analysis of experimental and quasi-experimental studies published from late 2022 through 2025, focusing on academic achievement outcomes such as test scores, grades, and GPA. Their goal was not just to estimate an overall effect, but also to identify moderators that explain why some implementations work better than others.

The synthesis included studies using GenAI as part of instruction across K–12 and higher education settings, in both STEM and non-STEM subjects. The authors coded study characteristics including educational level, sample size, learning domain, subject area, intervention duration, and the instructional role of GenAI (for example, tutoring, assessment/feedback, or personalized support). The included interventions varied widely, but all compared GenAI-supported learning against traditional instruction without GenAI.

Overall, the meta-analysis found a large positive effect of GenAI on academic achievement. The strongest and most consistent benefits appeared when GenAI was used for assessment and feedback or tutoring, and effects also differed substantially by subject area, with language education showing the largest gains. Educational level, sample size, duration, and STEM versus non-STEM domain did not significantly moderate effects, though descriptive patterns suggested stronger impacts in higher education and in longer interventions. The authors conclude that GenAI can improve learning when it is aligned with formative instructional purposes and the subject matter, but they also caution that publication bias and high between-study heterogeneity limit overgeneralization.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-analysis synthesizing 52 experimental and quasi-experimental studies, which is the strongest evidence tier in the requested framework. It reports pooled effects, heterogeneity, moderator analyses, and publication-bias checks, though the very high I² and evidence of bias warrant some caution.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled effect on academic achievement is large (g = 1.193), clearly exceeding the threshold for blue impact. Despite variability across contexts, the average effect indicates substantial positive impact on general learning outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Meta-analysis of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT used to support learning through tutoring, feedback, assessment, and personalized guidance across educational settings.

finding.finding_summary: Across 52 experimental and quasi-experimental comparisons (two outlier studies excluded from pooling), GenAI-based instruction produced a large positive effect on academic achievement relative to conventional instruction. The pooled effect was Hedges' g = 1.193 (SE = 0.243, 95% CI [0.716, 1.669], p < 0.001), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 98.0%, τ² = 2.98).
finding.measure: Academic achievement outcomes such as test scores, grades, and GPA

paper_profiles.title: Fraction magnitude student explanations: A latent class analysis
paper_profiles.venue: International Electronic Journal of Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how upper-elementary students explain their reasoning on fraction magnitude comparison problems and whether those explanations cluster into distinct latent profiles. The central question is not about an intervention, but about the kinds of explanations students produce, how those explanations relate to accuracy, and whether they align with conceptual or procedural knowledge of fractions.

The study analyzed responses from students who answered four fraction comparison items and then explained how they figured out their answers. Explanations were coded into five categories: absent, faulty, conceptual-partially developed, algorithmic, and conceptual-fully developed. The sample was drawn from two prior studies and included 428 fifth-grade students, with additional data from a smaller set of lower elementary and middle-grade students used in the broader source studies. Students were assessed individually on the Math Reasoning Inventory and also completed the WRAT-4 mathematics computation subtest. The setting was schools in Oregon and Texas, with students from public and private schools and a range of achievement levels.

Latent class analysis supported a five-class solution: conceptual-partially developed, conceptual-fully developed, faulty, absent, and algorithmic. The algorithmic class was the largest and was associated with the highest accuracy on the fraction comparison items and the highest WRAT-4 scores. The findings suggest that students’ explanations are meaningfully differentiated, but that conceptual and procedural knowledge did not combine into a single mixed class in this sample. The authors conclude that asking students to explain their fraction reasoning can help teachers better understand students’ knowledge profiles and may inform more targeted instruction, while also noting that item difficulty, prompting style, and instructional context may shape the kinds of explanations students give.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed observational latent class analysis, not an intervention study. It provides descriptive evidence about student explanation profiles and their association with accuracy, but it does not meet experimental or quasi-experimental credibility criteria for causal effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct intervention impact because it does not test a technology or instructional treatment. Its contribution is conceptually useful for understanding fraction reasoning patterns, but reported effects are descriptive associations rather than impacts of an educational intervention.

finding.finding_summary: This study did not evaluate an AI or instructional intervention; it used latent class analysis of 428 fifth-grade students' explanations on four fraction magnitude comparison items. Five explanation profiles emerged, and the algorithmic class had the highest fraction-comparison accuracy (M=3.80/4), followed by conceptual-fully developed (M=3.47), conceptual-partially developed (M=3.14), absent (M=2.18), and faulty (M=1.81). Pairwise differences were statistically significant, with Cohen's w ranging from 0.10 to 0.72.
finding.measure: Accuracy on four fraction magnitude comparison items (MRI) and associated explanation-type profiles

paper_profiles.title: School guidance support and growth in mathematics discourse feedback skills: a three-wave longitudinal mediation study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether school guidance support is associated with growth in students’ mathematics discourse feedback skills, and whether that association operates through two mechanisms: major decision-making self-efficacy and feedback literacy behavior. The authors frame mathematics discourse feedback skills as the ability to interpret feedback, justify reasoning, monitor progress, diagnose errors, and revise work in classroom dialogue.

The study used a three-wave longitudinal survey design with Chinese senior high school students. School guidance support was measured at Time 1, major decision-making self-efficacy at Time 2, feedback literacy behavior at Time 3, and mathematics discourse feedback skills were measured at all three waves. The analysis used structural equation modeling with autoregressive controls, demographic covariates, and bootstrapped indirect effects. The sample came from three senior high schools in Hebei, China, with data collected about three months apart across the school year.

Results showed that stronger perceived school guidance support predicted later mathematics discourse feedback skills both directly and indirectly. The relationship was partially mediated by decision-making self-efficacy and by feedback literacy behavior, and the sequential pathway from guidance support to self-efficacy to feedback literacy behavior to later mathematics discourse feedback skills was also supported. The authors conclude that school-level guidance can foster disciplinary feedback skills by strengthening students’ confidence in making academic decisions and their routine use of feedback-seeking and feedback-using behaviors.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed three-wave longitudinal correlational study with structural equation modeling and measurement invariance testing, but it is not an experimental or randomized design. It provides moderate credibility for directional associations and mediation, though causality remains limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are statistically significant and often moderate in size, but they concern a school guidance/context intervention rather than a direct instructional technology intervention, and the paper does not test an implementable AI or software treatment. The practical impact is therefore plausible but indirect and context-specific.

finding.finding_summary: School guidance support at T1 positively predicted later major decision-making self-efficacy at T2 in a sample of Chinese senior high school students (n=2,120 at baseline; n=1,938 at T3). In the longitudinal SEM, guidance support showed a strong standardized effect on T2 self-efficacy (β=0.476, 95% CI [0.434, 0.512], p<0.001), indicating that higher perceived school guidance was associated with stronger decision-making confidence over time.
finding.measure: Major Decision-Making Self-Efficacy Scale at T2

finding.finding_summary: School guidance support was positively associated with growth in mathematics discourse feedback skills across the three waves. In the single-mediator model, the direct effect of T1 guidance support on T3 skills remained significant (β=0.159, 95% CI [0.120, 0.200]) after controlling for prior skills, and in the sequential model the total effect was β=0.371, 95% CI [0.308, 0.430].
finding.measure: High School Students’ Mathematics Discourse Feedback Skills Scale (MDFSS) across T1–T3

finding.finding_summary: Major decision-making self-efficacy mediated the association between school guidance support and later mathematics discourse feedback skills. The indirect effect through T2 self-efficacy was significant in the single-mediator model (β=0.126, SE=0.009, 95% CI [0.107, 0.142]) and remained significant in the sequential model (β=0.070, SE=0.020, 95% CI [0.033, 0.109]).
finding.measure: Longitudinal indirect effect via Major Decision-Making Self-Efficacy Scale

finding.finding_summary: Feedback literacy behavior was positively associated with mathematics discourse feedback skills, and it significantly mediated the effect of school guidance support. In the sequential model, the indirect path via feedback literacy behavior was β=0.059, SE=0.014, 95% CI [0.034, 0.088], and feedback literacy behavior predicted T3 mathematics discourse feedback skills (β=0.276, SE=0.033, p<0.001).
finding.measure: Feedback Literacy Behavior Scale at T3 and MDFSS at T3

paper_profiles.title: Local Experiences, Global Perspectives: Preparing Future Teachers for Diverse Societies through Community Engagement
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how community engagement can be systematically integrated into teacher education to prepare future teachers for increasingly diverse and socially complex educational settings. The authors frame the issue around the need for teacher candidates to develop not only disciplinary knowledge but also responsiveness to diversity, reflective practice, and social responsibility. They ask how community engagement experiences shape students’ professional identity and their understanding of teaching as a relational, context-sensitive profession.

The study focuses on 19 teacher education students enrolled in a university course on community engagement at Ludwigsburg University of Education in Germany. The course combined theoretical input, student-designed community projects, and reflective discussion. Students participated in local, digital, and international forms of engagement, including work with schools, youth-oriented projects, online collaboration, and some transnational experiences. Data came from semi-structured interviews, project abstracts, participant observation, and recorded discussions, and were analyzed using qualitative thematic content analysis.

The findings suggest that community engagement helped students develop leadership, teamwork, adaptability, empathy, and a stronger awareness of diversity and inequality. Participants reported that engagement made abstract ideas about inclusion and social responsibility concrete, and many said it influenced how they viewed their future roles as teachers. The paper concludes that community engagement, when embedded thoughtfully and supported institutionally, can strengthen professional learning in teacher education. It argues for flexible, sustainable, and ethically grounded partnerships that connect local, digital, and international engagement opportunities.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative study using interviews, project documents, and observations with thematic content analysis. It provides credible exploratory evidence, but it is not experimental and does not support causal claims or effect-size estimation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful but unquantified benefits for teacher candidates' professional development, diversity responsiveness, and institutional engagement structures. Because findings are qualitative and effect sizes are not reported, the magnitude of impact remains unclear.

finding.finding_summary: This qualitative study of 19 teacher education students found that community engagement was perceived to strengthen the institutional case for embedding engagement more systematically into teacher education curricula. Students reported that clearer frameworks, better visibility of opportunities, stronger partnership structures, and sustained recognition within academic programs would improve engagement outcomes.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interviews, project abstracts, participant observation, and recorded class discussions analyzed via qualitative thematic content analysis

finding.finding_summary: Students consistently reported gains in collaboration, leadership, communication, adaptability, and reflective practice through community engagement projects. The paper does not provide quantitative effect sizes, but the thematic analysis indicates that engagement experiences supported professional identity development and critical reflection across multiple project contexts.
finding.measure: Self-reported reflections on teamwork, leadership, communication, adaptability, and reflective practice

finding.finding_summary: Participants described increased confidence, resilience, empathy, and motivation to pursue teaching after engaging with diverse community settings. Students also reported stronger awareness of diversity and more positive orientations toward inclusive educational practice, but the evidence is qualitative and not quantified with an effect size.
finding.measure: Interview themes on confidence, resilience, empathy, motivation, and diversity responsiveness

paper_profiles.title: The use of ChatGPT in teaching and learning: a systematic review through SWOT analysis approach
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapidly growing interest in ChatGPT in education and asks what strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats have been reported in prior studies. The authors specifically organize the evidence using Biggs’s Presage-Process-Product (3P) model to understand how ChatGPT may affect the teaching and learning environment, learning activities, and learning outcomes.

The intervention or approach studied is not a single classroom implementation but a systematic review of empirical studies on ChatGPT and related chatbots in education. The review searched Scopus, ERIC, and Google Scholar for studies from 2022–2023, ultimately including 51 articles. The included studies covered both higher education and general education contexts, with most work in higher education and a smaller set in general education. The studies were conducted across multiple countries, including the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Germany, China, Hong Kong, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Türkiye, Jordan, Peru, Uruguay, Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa.

The review concludes that ChatGPT offers several educational strengths, including positive perceptions among teachers and students, support for course material development, personalized learning, immediate feedback, help with idea generation and writing, and some gains in learning outcomes. However, the paper also identifies important weaknesses and risks, such as generic outputs, limited response length, bias, inaccurate information, fabricated citations, reduced critical thinking, and academic dishonesty. The authors argue that ChatGPT should be treated as a support tool rather than a replacement for teachers, and that successful use requires human mediation, critical verification, and new skills for both educators and students.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review using PRISMA, but the included studies are largely qualitative, descriptive, and heterogeneous, with no meta-analysis or single high-credibility causal design. The evidence base is useful for mapping themes but does not meet strong causal evidence criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests potentially meaningful benefits for learning support and teacher efficiency, but the paper does not provide pooled effect sizes and much of the evidence is qualitative or task-specific. The overall impact on general K-12 populations remains plausible but unclear.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of ChatGPT use in teaching and learning, including its role as a conversational tutor, content provider, teaching assistant, evaluator, and writing/learning support tool across presage, process, and product stages.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that ChatGPT can support writing tasks, idea generation, and feedback on writing, with studies noting automated assistance for composition and evaluation of writing tasks. Evidence is qualitative and comparative rather than causal, but the paper synthesizes multiple reports that ChatGPT can improve writing-related learning processes and outcomes in English and other contexts.
finding.measure: Writing task support, composition quality, feedback provision, and related learning outcomes reported across included studies

finding.finding_summary: The review includes a mathematics education study indicating ChatGPT can provide basic understanding of mathematical concepts, but also notes inaccuracy issues for more complex math problems and dependence on equation complexity and prompts. Overall, the synthesis suggests some support for math learning, but with important reliability limits.
finding.measure: Mathematics concept understanding and solution accuracy in math tasks

finding.finding_summary: Across science and physics examples, the review finds ChatGPT can generate course materials, explain solutions, and assist with unit design, but its outputs may be generic or inaccurate depending on the task. The paper therefore characterizes scientific support as useful but constrained by accuracy and context sensitivity.
finding.measure: Science/physics task generation, explanation quality, and instructional material creation

finding.finding_summary: The synthesis reports that ChatGPT can improve learning outcomes across several non-literacy domains, including programming, construction hazard identification, health education, and general assessment tasks. Examples cited include improved computational thinking, self-programming ability, and hazard recognition rates exceeding 25% in one construction study, though the overall review is not a pooled effect estimate.
finding.measure: Domain-specific learning outcomes such as computational thinking, programming ability, hazard recognition, and exam/task performance

finding.finding_summary: The review highlights that ChatGPT can provide personalized, interactive, and engaging learning experiences that may support motivation and learner autonomy. However, it also notes that AI tools alone may not improve motivation for challenging tasks, so the overall pattern is beneficial but not uniformly strong.
