finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, and learner autonomy reported in included studies

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes evidence that ChatGPT can support idea generation, explanations, critical thinking, and metacognitive engagement, but it may also decrease critical thinking if relied on too heavily. In one cited programming study, ChatGPT improved computational thinking and problem-solving, yet the paper also flags risks of overdependence and reduced critical evaluation.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, computational thinking, problem-solving, metacognition, and collaboration-related outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review consistently reports that ChatGPT can reduce teacher workload by providing immediate responses, basic explanations, and automated assistance for writing and course material creation. This is a prominent process-level benefit across the synthesis, although no pooled quantitative effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, efficiency of course material generation, and responsiveness to student questions

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes threats and governance issues such as plagiarism, copyright concerns, academic dishonesty, and the need for new skills and assessment models. It frames ChatGPT as an intervention that may require institutional changes in pedagogy, assessment design, and AI literacy rather than reporting direct outcome gains.
finding.measure: Academic integrity concerns, assessment design challenges, and skill requirements for students/teachers

paper_profiles.title: Scaling up successfully: Lessons from Kenya’s Tusome national literacy program
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how Kenya’s Tusome national early-grade literacy program was implemented at scale and whether the education system’s capacity supported successful large-scale instructional reform. The authors use the Crouch and DeStefano core-functions framework to ask whether Tusome reinforced system capacity to set expectations, monitor progress and accountability, and provide differentiated support for schools and teachers.

Tusome is a government-run literacy program funded by USAID and built on evidence from earlier pilot studies in Kenya, especially PRIMR. It supplied teachers’ guides and student books, delivered teacher training and coaching through government officers, and used tablet-based tools and dashboards to record classroom observations, student reading assessments, and school-visit data. The context was Kenya’s public primary schools and low-cost private APBET schools, with implementation spanning Classes 1–3 in the early primary grades.

The authors conclude that Tusome did many things needed for scale-up well: it clearly communicated benchmarks, distributed inputs consistently, increased classroom observation and feedback, and produced large gains in reading outcomes. However, they also find weaknesses in using monitoring data to target differentiated support to the schools and officers most in need. Overall, the paper argues that Tusome shows how coherent system design, structured pedagogy, and accountability mechanisms can help a piloted literacy intervention succeed nationally, while also showing that data use for targeted support remained incomplete.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed case study/system analysis using program documents, administrative monitoring data, and an external evaluation report, but it is not a randomized or quasi-experimental design for the main claims about system change. The learning-outcome evidence is based on a pre/post comparison without a counterfactual.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports large learning gains well above the 0.20 threshold, with average effect sizes ranging from 0.63 to 1.04 SD in early grade reading. It also documents substantial system-level strengthening in implementation, monitoring, and instructional support at national scale.

interventions.use_case: national-scale early grade literacy reform implemented through government systems, including structured lesson sequences, teacher guides, coaching by curriculum support officers, and tablet-based classroom observation/dashboard monitoring

finding.finding_summary: Tusome was associated with large gains in early grade literacy outcomes in a nationally representative pre/post evaluation. In Kiswahili, average effect sizes were 0.63 SD for Class 1 and 0.76 SD for Class 2 across six subtasks; in English, average effect sizes were 0.67 SD for Class 1 and 1.04 SD for Class 2 across eight subtasks, with statistically significant improvements on nearly all subtasks.
finding.measure: Early Grade Reading Assessment subtasks: letter sound knowledge, syllable fluency, invented/nonword decoding, oral reading fluency, reading comprehension, listening comprehension; English also included phoneme segmentation and vocabulary
finding.effect_size: 0.63 SD (Kiswahili Class 1 avg); 0.76 SD (Kiswahili Class 2 avg); 0.67 SD (English Class 1 avg); 1.04 SD (English Class 2 avg)

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that Tusome strengthened Kenya’s education system in setting expectations, monitoring implementation, and providing instructional support at scale. Evidence includes widespread dissemination of benchmarks, more than 113,604 classroom observations uploaded in 2016, over 90 visits per CSO on average, and use of dashboard data for accountability and support, though differentiated support based on observation data remained incomplete.
finding.measure: Program implementation indicators: benchmark dissemination, classroom observation frequency, dashboard use, GPS-verified visits, school support structures, provision of materials/training/coaching

paper_profiles.title: The Role of Analogy in Teaching Middle-School Mathematics
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how analogy is used in ordinary middle-school mathematics teaching and asks whether the structure and purpose of analogies in classrooms resemble patterns predicted by cognitive science research on analogical reasoning. The authors focus on a practical instructional issue: how teachers use analogies to support understanding of abstract mathematical ideas and procedures, and whether classroom analogies are organized in ways that may help or hinder student reasoning and transfer.

The study analyzes 25 videotaped U.S. eighth-grade mathematics lessons drawn from the TIMSS classroom video sample. The researchers identified 103 explicit analogy units and coded each one for its participant structure (teacher/student roles in producing source, target, mapping, inference, and problem solving), source and target structure, surface similarity, and mathematical function (teaching concepts, procedures, both, or supporting students as math learners). No intervention was assigned; instead, the paper is a discourse-analytic observation of naturally occurring classroom practice.

Findings show that analogies are common in middle-school math lessons and follow regular patterns. Teachers typically initiate analogies and provide most of the source, target, and mapping structure, while students more often contribute inferences, adaptations, and final computations. Analogies used to teach concepts tended to rely on more distant or schema-based comparisons, whereas analogies used to teach procedures tended to use higher surface similarity. The authors conclude that teachers appear to use analogies in systematic ways, but that heavy teacher structuring may limit opportunities for students to engage in higher-order analogical reasoning themselves.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed observational/discourse-analytic study of classroom video, which provides credible descriptive evidence but no experimental manipulation or causal estimate. It is best classified as yellow because the methodology is systematic yet correlational/qualitative rather than an RCT or QED.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has educational relevance for how analogies are structured in middle-school mathematics, but it does not evaluate a technology or report outcome gains attributable to an intervention. Its impact on student learning is therefore suggestive and unclear rather than demonstrably positive.

finding.finding_summary: This is a descriptive classroom discourse study of 25 videotaped eighth-grade mathematics lessons (103 analogies identified), not an intervention trial. It finds that analogy use is common and structured to support conceptual understanding, inferential adaptation, and problem solving, but teacher-led structure may limit the extent to which students independently perform higher-order comparative reasoning.
finding.measure: Classroom discourse coding of analogy frequency, structure, participant roles, and mathematical function

paper_profiles.title: Unlocking potential in underachieving learners: self-regulation development through AI-supported e-mentoring among socioeconomically disadvantaged students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether an AI-supported e-mentoring intervention can improve self-regulated learning (SRL) and related academic outcomes among socioeconomically disadvantaged students who are underachieving in school. The authors argue that these students often struggle not only with content knowledge, but also with goal setting, planning, monitoring, and reflection, and that traditional human mentoring is difficult to scale.

The intervention was a three-tiered AI-supported mentoring system delivered through a conversational AI mentor using GPT-4o. It combined structured SRL training with goal clarification, micro-strategy prompting, reflective coaching, adaptive challenge modules, reminders, and safety guardrails. The platform used fixed prompts, limited response length, no browsing or external tools, and a human-supervised governance system that included teacher or supervisor oversight for risk alerts. The study ran for 8 weeks of intervention with a 4-week follow-up, for a total of 12 weeks.

The trial involved 168 students in grades 10 and 11 from socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds in school settings in China, randomized at the class level to intervention or control conditions. The intervention group showed stronger gains than controls in self-reported SRL, behavioral SRL markers, academic performance, learning engagement, and persistence, with effects largely maintained at follow-up though somewhat attenuated. The results suggest that AI-supported e-mentoring, when structured and supervised, can help disadvantaged adolescents develop stronger self-regulation and improve learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a cluster randomized controlled trial with baseline equivalence, follow-up, mixed-effects modeling, and intention-to-treat analysis, which supports strong causal inference. Some concerns remain because the paper reports many outcomes and the excerpt does not provide all model details/effect sizes, so it is not assigned blue.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports large, statistically significant improvements in SRL-related behavioral outcomes and clear gains in core SRL scales for a priority population of socioeconomically disadvantaged underachieving students. Several reported effects are well above the 0.20 threshold, indicating medium to large practical impact.

interventions.use_case: AI-supported e-mentoring via GPT-4o conversational prompts for middle/high school students, delivering goal clarification, micro-strategy prompting, reflective coaching, task decomposition, reminder scheduling, and safety-guardrailed learning support for self-regulated learning.

finding.finding_summary: In a cluster randomized controlled trial with 168 students (n=84 intervention, n=84 control), the AI-supported e-mentoring condition produced significant gains in self-regulated learning (SRL). Adjusted between-group differences favored the intervention at post-test and follow-up for SRL total and all subdimensions; for SRL total, β=0.41 at T1 and β=0.36 at T2, both p<0.001. The paper also reports improvements in academic self-efficacy, school belonging, learning engagement, and persistence as related psychosocial outcomes.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning scale total and subdimensions; platform-based SRL behaviors; academic self-efficacy; engagement/persistence indicators
finding.effect_size: beta=0.41 at T1; beta=0.36 at T2

finding.finding_summary: The intervention substantially improved behavioral markers of self-regulation, including weekly structured check-ins, on-time plan submission, weekly goal attainment, micro-task completion, and review submission. Adjusted group differences at T1 were large across all co-primary behavioral SRL outcomes, such as weekly check-ins (5.84), on-time plan submission (50.92 percentage points), and micro-tasks completed (15.76), all p<0.001.
finding.measure: Behavioral SRL markers from platform logs and school proxies (check-ins, plan submission, goal attainment, micro-task completion, review continuity)
finding.confidence_interval: Multiple 95% CIs reported, e.g. weekly check-ins [5.34, 6.34]; plan submission [45.11, 56.73]

finding.finding_summary: Secondary analyses found that the AI-supported mentoring group showed larger improvements in academic performance than controls. The paper reports significant gains in composite grade average and in both mathematics and language arts scores at post-intervention, though the excerpt does not provide the exact effect sizes for these academic outcomes. The direction of effects remained favorable and aligned with improved SRL and engagement.
finding.measure: Composite grade average; mathematics scores; language arts scores

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved learning engagement and persistence in addition to SRL. The paper reports significantly higher homework submission rates, teacher-rated engagement, attendance, persistence scores, and consistent engagement across the 8-week period for the intervention group relative to controls, with effects maintained but slightly attenuated at follow-up.
finding.measure: Homework submission rate; teacher-rated engagement; attendance; persistence; consistent engagement

paper_profiles.title: Examining Pre-service Mathematics Teachers' Purposes of Using ChatGPT in Lesson Plan Development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines why pre-service middle school mathematics teachers used ChatGPT when developing lesson plans. The study asks what purposes ChatGPT served in lesson-planning work, especially in relation to creating lesson content and helping teachers deepen their own knowledge while filling gaps in understanding.

The intervention or approach studied was the use of ChatGPT as a support tool during lesson plan preparation. Participants first selected mathematics learning outcomes, prepared a lesson plan using ChatGPT, and then responded to an open-ended questionnaire about how they used the tool. The study used a phenomenological qualitative design with content analysis. Data were collected from 56 third-year pre-service middle school mathematics teachers at a state university in Turkey; all had taken an information technology course, and they also attended a conference on AI in education.

The findings show that participants mainly used ChatGPT to create lesson content, including generating learning activities, problems and examples, evaluation tools, lesson flow, creative ideas, explanations of math concepts, conceptual relationships, lesson scope, and revisions to improve plans. A second major use was deepening individual knowledge, especially about pedagogical approaches such as learning strategies, models, materials, classroom management, and mathematical concepts. The author concludes that ChatGPT can be a useful supplementary support for lesson planning, but it should not replace teachers' own knowledge and expertise. The paper also cautions that AI-generated information may be inaccurate and must be checked against the curriculum and professional judgment.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative phenomenological study using open-ended questionnaire data from a convenience sample, so it provides descriptive evidence but not causal or quantitative estimates. The methodology is peer-reviewed and reasonably transparent, but it does not meet stronger credibility criteria for experimental or quasi-experimental evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports perceived benefits for lesson planning, creativity, and conceptual support, but it does not measure student learning outcomes or quantify impact. Its practical relevance is moderate, yet the evidence is indirect and based on self-report rather than demonstrated educational gains.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used by pre-service middle school mathematics teachers to support lesson plan development, including generating activities, problems, evaluation tools, lesson flow, concept explanations, and pedagogical ideas.

finding.finding_summary: This qualitative phenomenology study (n=56 pre-service middle school mathematics teachers) found that ChatGPT was perceived as helpful for supporting mathematics lesson plan development. Participants used it to simplify and explain math concepts, generate problems/examples, and connect concepts to prior knowledge and real-world contexts, but no quantitative achievement test was reported.
finding.measure: Participant-reported uses of ChatGPT for math concept explanation, problem generation, and lesson-plan development

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT supported pre-service teachers' creativity, idea generation, and pedagogical thinking during lesson planning. Participants described it as helping them think differently, identify relationships among concepts, and deepen their knowledge of learning strategies and models; no effect size was reported because the study was qualitative.
finding.measure: Participant-reported creativity, pedagogical reasoning, and knowledge deepening during lesson-plan preparation

finding.finding_summary: The study strongly indicates that ChatGPT improved lesson-planning efficiency for pre-service teachers by helping them create lesson flow, activities, problems, assessment tools, and revised drafts more quickly. The evidence is based on interview/questionnaire themes from n=56 participants rather than quantified time-savings, so no effect size is available.
finding.measure: Participant-reported support for lesson planning, drafting, revision, and task completion efficiency

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: A revolutionary tool for teaching and learning mathematics
paper_profiles.venue: EURASIA Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines early perceptions and user experiences of ChatGPT for teaching and learning mathematics, with attention to both benefits and risks. The authors ask whether ChatGPT can support mathematics instruction, what kinds of errors or limitations appear in practice, and whether it can be used responsibly in educational settings. The work is motivated by the rapid public adoption of ChatGPT and the need to understand its implications for education before widespread classroom use.

The study uses a qualitative instrumental case study design with two stages. First, the authors conducted content analysis of interviews drawn from 30 people who had publicly discussed their use of ChatGPT in mathematics, including educators and students. Second, three experienced educators tested ChatGPT across a week using several math-teaching scenarios and problem-solving prompts, including linear equations, cubic equations, limits, derivatives, and geometry/Pythagorean theorem tasks. The paper focuses on how ChatGPT performs as a math helper and potential tutor, rather than on a formal classroom intervention.

The findings are mixed. Participants saw ChatGPT as potentially useful for instant feedback, basic problem solving, and explaining geometry in accessible language. At the same time, the user tests showed clear weaknesses: ChatGPT made arithmetic and algebraic errors, mishandled some limit and derivative tasks, and demonstrated shallow or incorrect understanding of geometry and misconceptions. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can be a helpful educational tool but should be used cautiously, with human verification and guidelines for safe, responsible use. They argue that further research is needed before ChatGPT can be relied on for mathematics teaching.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative case study with content analysis and user-experience testing rather than a controlled quantitative evaluation. It provides useful descriptive evidence, but there is no randomized design or effect-size estimation, and the sample is small.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests possible benefits for speed and explanatory support, but the evidence is exploratory and mixed, with clear correctness problems in several math tasks. Because the study does not quantify learning gains and includes substantial errors, the practical impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a mathematics teaching and problem-solving chatbot for middle school and broader math education, including answering equations, limits, derivatives, and geometry questions with natural-language explanations and examples.

finding.finding_summary: This qualitative case study and user-experience investigation found both helpful and harmful mathematical performance from ChatGPT. It solved some geometry and algebra prompts well, but also made clear errors on linear equations, cubic equations, limits, derivatives, and Pythagorean theorem problems; no effect size was reported (n=30 interviewees; 3 educators used ChatGPT in scenario testing).
finding.measure: Accuracy of ChatGPT responses to mathematics prompts; qualitative judgments of correctness in equations, limits, derivatives, and geometry tasks
finding.study_size: n=30 interviewees; 3 educators in user experience testing

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT can provide very fast, step-by-step answers to math questions and generate explanations in less time than manual typing, suggesting potential efficiency gains for teachers and learners. However, these efficiency benefits were qualified by the need to double-check outputs because the model sometimes produced incorrect calculations or misleading explanations; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived speed, convenience, and ease of producing math explanations and solutions
finding.study_size: n=30 interviewees; 3 educators in user experience testing

paper_profiles.title: The Effect of the AI-Powered ChatGPT Application on Middle School Students' Mathematics Learning Experiences: A Qualitative Inquiry
paper_profiles.venue: The Eurasia Proceedings of Educational and Social Sciences (EPESS)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how ChatGPT shapes middle school students’ mathematics learning experiences, with a focus on both perceived benefits and harms. The authors were interested in students’ lived experiences with the tool, including how they interpret its usefulness, its limitations, and its influence on learning, motivation, trust, and classroom alignment.

The study used a phenomenological qualitative design and thematic analysis. Data came from semi-structured interviews with two 7th-grade boys attending a public school in Istanbul, Türkiye. Both students had prior experience with ChatGPT and used it in daily life. The interviews explored cognitive experiences, affective responses, and comparisons with traditional classroom learning.

Findings suggested that ChatGPT could support conceptual understanding when it provided step-by-step explanations, but it also created problems. Some answers were too long or too advanced for the students’ cognitive level, leading to superficial learning, confusion, and reduced critical thinking. Students also reported boredom over time, feelings of inadequacy, difficulty formulating prompts, distrust when ChatGPT made mistakes, and confusion when AI-generated solutions differed from the teacher’s methods. The paper concludes that ChatGPT may be helpful in mathematics only when used with pedagogical guidance, age-appropriate support, digital literacy, and attention to equity of access.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative phenomenological study, which provides useful exploratory evidence but lacks experimental control, comparison groups, and generalizability. The sample is extremely small (n=2), so credibility is limited to descriptive insight rather than causal inference.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests both potential benefits and harms of ChatGPT for middle school mathematics, but the evidence is based on two interviews with no effect sizes. The likely impact is therefore modest and unclear at the population level, though it is highly relevant to a priority K-12 group.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used by 7th-grade middle school students to ask mathematics questions, receive explanations, and generate step-by-step solutions during informal learning.

finding.finding_summary: In this qualitative study with 2 seventh-grade students (n=2), ChatGPT sometimes supported mathematical understanding by providing step-by-step explanations and helping with concept clarification. However, students also reported superficial learning, direct-answer copying, and incorrect or overly complex explanations that produced confusion and limited their ability to solve similar problems independently.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes about mathematics learning experiences; perceived understanding, solution process, and ability to solve similar problems

finding.finding_summary: Students reported an initial increase in curiosity and motivation when using ChatGPT, followed by boredom and reduced interest over time as responses felt repetitive. One student also described feelings of inadequacy and decreased self-confidence when the system’s explanations were difficult to follow.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on motivation, boredom, trust, and self-efficacy

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT sometimes encouraged passive copying and reduced opportunities for critical thinking, questioning, and active problem solving. Students also struggled with prompt formulation and evaluating whether AI output was correct, indicating weaknesses in metacognitive and critical digital literacy processes.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on critical thinking, question-asking, and evaluation of AI responses

finding.finding_summary: Students experienced conflicts between ChatGPT explanations and classroom/teacher solutions, creating confusion about which method was correct. The study also identified access inequities such as unreliable Wi-Fi and limited device availability at home, highlighting infrastructure barriers to equitable AI use.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on teacher-tool conflict and access limitations

paper_profiles.title: The new reality of education in the face of advances in generative artificial intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: RIED-Revista Iberoamericana de Educación a Distancia
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the rapid emergence of generative artificial intelligence, especially ChatGPT, and its implications for education. The authors aim to move beyond extreme enthusiasm or rejection by systematically reviewing early scientific literature and mapping the main tools, opportunities, risks, and challenges associated with generative AI in teaching and learning. A major concern is that these systems are probabilistic language models that can produce plausible but incorrect outputs, so their use in education requires careful verification and critical judgment.

The paper does not study a single intervention with participants; instead, it reviews generative-AI tools with potential educational use and synthesizes early research published in the first months after ChatGPT appeared. The review focuses on literature indexed in Web of Science and Scopus and classifies findings across educational contexts such as pre-university education, university teaching, medicine, writing, engineering, and other disciplines. It also organizes tools by function, including text generation, image generation, video generation, audio generation, code generation, and AI-text detection.

The main conclusions are that generative AI offers substantial benefits, such as personalized support, content generation, productivity gains, and new possibilities for learning and assessment. At the same time, it raises important risks, including superficial learning, reduced critical thinking, hallucinations, plagiarism, privacy concerns, bias, inequity, and unreliable AI-text detection. The authors argue that education should not prohibit these tools outright, but should instead prioritize teacher and student training, ethical guidelines, curriculum revision, and assessment redesign to support responsible use.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a rapid review and conceptual synthesis rather than a primary intervention study, RCT, or meta-analysis. It is peer reviewed, but the evidence base is largely early, heterogeneous, and mostly qualitative/reflexive, so causal credibility is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that generative AI is already reshaping teaching, assessment, and policy, but it does not provide quantified outcome effects for K-12 learners. Its impact is therefore important and broad in scope, but the specific measured educational impact remains unclear from this paper alone.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI chatbots and large language models such as ChatGPT used for educational dialogue, question answering, explanation, summarization, and support for teaching/learning across subjects.
AI systems used to provide feedback on student writing and other academic work, including automated evaluation and support for assessment practices.
Generative writing and language-support tools such as paraphrasing, translation, grammar help, text summarization, and writing assistance for students and teachers.
Non-tutoring educational uses of generative AI for content delivery, activity generation, and instructional support materials in classroom and pre-university settings.
Generative AI used to create instructional simulations and synthetic examples, including GAN/deepfake and synthetic-case activities to teach AI concepts and ethics.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that generative AI can support durable skills such as critical thinking and creativity by giving feedback, prompting reflection, and helping students focus on higher-order work. However, it also warns that rapid, superficial use may impede independent thinking and creativity, and that some studies cited in the review report these as substantive risks rather than benefits.
finding.measure: Thematic synthesis of reviewed studies and identified benefits/risks related to critical thinking, creativity, and reflection
finding.study_size: 31 studies in the rapid review corpus

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that generative AI can improve productivity for teachers by reducing time spent answering repeated questions, drafting materials, and grading written work. It also notes benefits for automated assessment and other evaluation innovations, but reports no quantitative effect sizes because the paper is a synthesis of early literature rather than a primary impact study.
finding.measure: Thematic synthesis of reported teacher workload and productivity benefits
finding.study_size: 31 studies in the rapid review corpus

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that AI writing and language tools can help students with writing difficulties, provide more control over writing competencies, and support translation and language learning. At the same time, it highlights serious harms such as hallucinated content, incomplete information, plagiarism risk, and weak source attribution, so the overall literacy-related impact is mixed rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Thematic synthesis of writing support, translation, plagiarism, and hallucination-related findings
finding.study_size: 31 studies in the rapid review corpus

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests generative AI may increase engagement and collaboration, especially through asynchronous communication and motivational interaction with virtual instructors. However, it also warns of negative effects on interpersonal interaction with teachers and peers if students rely too heavily on the tools.
finding.measure: Thematic synthesis of engagement, motivation, and interaction-related claims
finding.study_size: 31 studies in the rapid review corpus

finding.finding_summary: The review emphasizes substantial institutional implications: the need for policies on responsible use, academic integrity, assessment redesign, teacher training, and ethical guidelines. It also warns that unreliable AI-detection tools can create false positives with reputational harm, so the institutional impact is both enabling and risky.
finding.measure: Rapid review synthesis of policy, governance, assessment, and institutional-response themes
finding.study_size: 31 studies in the rapid review corpus

paper_profiles.title: C-EVAL: A Multi-Level Multi-Discipline Chinese Evaluation Suite for Foundation Models
paper_profiles.venue: NeurIPS 2023 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces C-EVAL, a Chinese evaluation suite for foundation models and large language models. The central problem addressed is that existing benchmarks are mostly English-centric and do not adequately measure advanced knowledge and reasoning in Chinese-language contexts, especially for Chinese users and Chinese educational or professional content.

C-EVAL is built from 13,948 multiple-choice questions spanning 52 subjects across four difficulty levels: middle school, high school, college, and professional. The benchmark is designed to reduce data contamination by sourcing many questions from mock exams and publicly available documents rather than official national exam papers, and it includes a validation/test split plus a small development set with explanations for few-shot chain-of-thought prompting. The paper also introduces C-EVAL HARD, a subset of eight especially difficult subjects focused on advanced mathematics, physics, and chemistry.

The paper evaluates 11 accessible LLMs, including GPT-4, ChatGPT, Claude, GLM-130B, ChatGLM-6B, LLaMA-65B, Chinese-LLaMA, Chinese-Alpaca, Bloomz-mt, and MOSS. Results show GPT-4 performs best overall, but even it leaves substantial room for improvement; many Chinese-oriented models perform relatively better on Chinese social science and humanities subjects than on STEM. The authors conclude that C-EVAL and C-EVAL HARD fill an important gap for Chinese benchmark evaluation and reveal that advanced reasoning remains difficult for current models.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark paper for evaluating foundation models, not an intervention study in education. It does not test an educational technology with learners, so there is no causal or correlational evidence about educational outcomes to rate for efficacy.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper’s contribution is infrastructural: a Chinese LLM benchmark (C-EVAL) for model evaluation. It has no direct demonstrated impact on K-12 learners, classrooms, or educational outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Students’ perceptions of using ChatGPT in a physics class as a virtual tutor
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how undergraduate students perceive ChatGPT when it is used as a virtual tutor in a college physics course. The paper focuses on three questions: how accurate ChatGPT is at answering physics problems, whether students’ trust depends on the accuracy of the answers, and how trust influences their perceptions of ChatGPT’s usefulness, ease of use, and future use intentions.

The intervention was implemented in an introductory physics class at a public university in the southern United States. Forty students first completed a regular in-person exam, then used ChatGPT over about a week and a half to work through a makeup exam assignment based on questions they had answered incorrectly. Students interacted with ChatGPT using a structured prompt flow but could also ask follow-up questions. Quantitative data came from accuracy checks, trust classification, and a post-study Likert survey; qualitative data came from students’ drawings of how they تصور ChatGPT.

Results showed that ChatGPT answered physics questions with 85% accuracy overall, but many students still trusted its answers even when they were wrong. Trust level was associated with students’ perceptions: those who trusted ChatGPT more also rated it as easier to use and were somewhat more likely to intend to use it in the future. Drawing analysis suggested many students anthropomorphized ChatGPT or viewed it as a robot/machine, and some held misconceptions that it was infallible, magical, or super-intelligent. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can be error-prone in science contexts and that AI literacy, critical thinking, and prompt engineering are needed to reduce blind trust and misconceptions.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational/mixed-methods study with survey, dialogue-log, and drawing analyses, but it is not an experimental causal design and has a small, single-class sample. The evidence is useful for describing perceptions and risks, but it does not meet higher causal credibility thresholds.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows a moderate accuracy problem (85% correct, with some answer instability) and substantial overtrust, but the study is limited to one undergraduate physics class and reports no direct learning outcome gains or harms for achievement. The practical impact is therefore important but still unclear and not yet generalizable.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a virtual tutor/assistant to answer undergraduate physics exam questions and support students in revising incorrect answers through dialogue

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT answered 85% of 362 physics questions correctly (307 correct, 55 incorrect) in an introductory college physics class (n=40). However, it sometimes changed answers after follow-up questioning, including 34 cases where a correct answer became incorrect and 7 cases where an incorrect answer became correct, indicating unstable scientific correctness despite generally high accuracy.
finding.measure: Accuracy of ChatGPT responses to physics questions; correctness of answers in an exam-makeup dialogue task

finding.finding_summary: Students showed strong trust in ChatGPT even when it was inaccurate: the Trust group agreed with ChatGPT 100% of the time, and nearly half of students accepted all answers regardless of correctness. Trust level was significantly related to answer accuracy, F(2,37)=6.383, p=0.004, η2=0.257, and also to perceptions of usefulness/ease of use/intention to use, indicating notable effects on critical evaluation and AI literacy-related judgment.
finding.measure: Trust/agreement with ChatGPT answers; perceptions of usefulness, ease of use, and intention to use; drawing-based misconceptions about AI

finding.finding_summary: Students generally reported favorable perceptions of ChatGPT as a learning aid, and the Trust group rated it higher on ease of use (M=4.34) than the Partial Trust group (M=3.65), with a significant group difference in overall perception, F(6,70)=2.478, p=0.031, η2=0.175. This suggests the tool was viewed as easy and potentially useful, although these perceptions were intertwined with overtrust and misconceptions.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and intention to use in the future

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities, risks, and open challenges of using large language models such as ChatGPT in education. Rather than evaluating a specific intervention with outcome data, it synthesizes emerging applications and argues for responsible integration of LLMs into teaching and learning. The paper is especially concerned with both benefits and harms, including bias, overreliance, privacy, copyright, verification problems, and difficulties distinguishing model-generated from student-generated work.

The authors discuss how LLMs could support learners across educational levels, including elementary, middle school, high school, university, and professional training, and how they could assist teachers with lesson planning, feedback, assessment, and content generation. They also review early research examples in areas such as quiz generation, curiosity prompting, code explanation, adaptive feedback, and math word problem generation. These examples are framed as emerging educational uses rather than a single empirical study.

The paper concludes that LLMs have substantial promise for personalized learning, teaching support, and innovative educational technologies, but their adoption must be guided by human oversight, critical thinking, transparency, privacy protections, fairness measures, and sustainable deployment. The authors emphasize that LLMs should complement rather than replace teachers or authoritative sources, and they propose mitigation strategies for major risks such as misuse, bias, and academic integrity concerns.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper and literature-informed conceptual review, not an empirical study. It does not present original data, a comparison design, or evaluated outcomes with causal identification.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has potentially high relevance for education policy and practice because it synthesizes benefits and harms of ChatGPT/LLMs in schooling. However, because it provides no direct empirical evidence, the measurable impact remains unclear and should be treated as conceptual guidance rather than demonstrated effect.

interventions.use_case: Position paper on ChatGPT/large language models as educational tools for student tutoring, question answering, step-by-step explanations, practice generation, and educational dialogue across subjects including middle school mathematics.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that large language models could support middle and high school mathematics learning by generating practice problems, quizzes, explanations, and step-by-step solutions, which may help students understand reasoning and build problem-solving skills. However, it also warns that model brittleness, incorrect outputs, and overreliance could undermine mathematical reasoning and verification, with no empirical effect size reported because this is a position paper.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of math learning support, practice generation, and problem-solving; no empirical outcome measure reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes possible gains in critical thinking, problem-solving, curiosity, and fact-checking when LLMs are used to generate hypotheses, explanations, and prompts rather than direct answers. It also warns that easy access to generated answers may weaken independent thinking and encourage reliance on the model; no empirical effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of critical thinking, problem-solving, curiosity, and verification skills; no empirical outcome measure reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims LLMs can reduce teacher workload through semi-automated grading, feedback generation, lesson planning, quiz creation, and content drafting. It cites prior work suggesting grading effort could be reduced by up to 85% in large courses, but this paper itself does not report a new empirical estimate.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, and content generation efficiency; cited prior finding of grading effort reduction up to 85%

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses heavily on risks and governance issues such as bias, copyright, privacy/security, integrity, fairness, and access, arguing these could harm educational systems if unmanaged. At the same time, it frames responsible deployment as a way to expand access and improve educational quality; this is conceptual rather than empirical and reports no effect size.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, privacy, fairness, and institutional adoption considerations; no empirical outcome measure reported

paper_profiles.title: SciPy 1.0: fundamental algorithms for scientific computing in Python
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a perspective article introducing SciPy 1.0, an open-source scientific computing library for Python. It does not examine an educational intervention or learner outcomes; instead, it documents the project’s history, design philosophy, technical architecture, testing practices, governance, and ecosystem impact.

The article describes how SciPy evolved from a small set of student-developed numerical tools into a mature foundation for scientific Python. It outlines the library’s major subpackages, the use of wrapped compiled code, API and ABI stability practices, and improvements in sparse matrices, spatial algorithms, optimization, statistics, and interpolation. The paper also discusses community processes such as continuous integration, documentation development, governance, and code of conduct.

Because the paper is about software infrastructure rather than an empirical study, there is no study population, no intervention context in schools, and no measured educational effect. The main conclusion is that SciPy has become a widely used, community-driven, stable core library for scientific computing, with continued emphasis on maintainability, testing, documentation, and long-term ecosystem support.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective/article about the SciPy software project, not an empirical study of an educational or AI intervention. There is no study design, sample, or outcome evaluation relevant to the requested topic.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational intervention outcomes are reported, so there is no measurable impact on middle school mathematics or any other learning outcome.

paper_profiles.title: Metacognitive Knowledge and Metacognitive Regulation in Self-Regulatory Learning Style, and in Its Effects on Performance Expectation and Subsequent Performance across Diverse School Subjects
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary students’ metacognitive knowledge and metacognitive regulation relate to their self-regulatory learning styles, performance expectations, and actual school performance. The authors focus on whether different components of metacognition—declarative, procedural, conditional knowledge, and planning, monitoring, information management, and evaluation—are associated with students’ motivation and achievement across three school subjects: language, mathematics, and physical education.

The study sampled 243 fifth- and sixth-grade students from 20 state primary schools in Greece, along with 25 teachers who rated student performance. Students completed self-report questionnaires in the middle of the school year, including the Junior Metacognitive Awareness Inventory and the Academic Self-Regulation Questionnaire, plus subject-specific performance expectation scales. Teachers provided term grades and ratings of student performance. The analyses were correlational/regression-based and did not test an intervention.

The findings suggest that students reported moderate metacognitive knowledge and regulation, with declarative knowledge and planning used most often and evaluation least often. Students showed a mixed self-regulatory profile, with identified regulation most prominent. Greater metacognition, especially metacognitive regulation, was associated with more adaptive regulatory styles and better performance expectations, but effects varied by subject. External regulation consistently predicted poorer performance, while performance expectations were the strongest positive predictor of achievement; metacognition contributed both directly and indirectly, especially in mathematics and language.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational study with self-report measures and teacher-rated outcomes, not an experimental evaluation. It provides useful associative evidence but does not meet stronger causal-inference criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports modest-to-moderate associations in general elementary-school populations, with several statistically significant predictors and some meaningful variance explained. However, because the study is correlational and not an intervention test, the practical impact is unclear and should be considered modest.

finding.finding_summary: In a correlational study of 243 Greek 5th- and 6th-grade students, metacognition and self-regulatory style were associated with motivational beliefs and achievement. Higher metacognition, especially metacognitive regulation, predicted more self-determined regulation styles, and external regulation negatively predicted performance across subjects. Performance expectations were positively related to later performance, with the strongest models in mathematics (R2=0.29) and language (R2=0.22), but weaker in physical education (R2=0.095).
finding.measure: Self-regulation questionnaire, performance expectations, and teacher/school-record performance ratings across language, mathematics, and physical education
finding.effect_size: R2=0.22; R2=0.29; R2=0.095; beta values reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily examines metacognition and self-regulated learning. Students reported moderate metacognitive knowledge (declarative M=4.27, procedural M=3.20, conditional M=4.09) and metacognitive regulation (planning M=4.06, monitoring M=3.82, information management M=3.72, evaluation M=3.51), with planning the most used component and evaluation the least used. Metacognitive regulation significantly predicted identified regulation (R2=0.22) and intrinsic motivation (R2=0.13), while monitoring negatively predicted external regulation (beta=-0.23).
finding.measure: Junior Metacognitive Awareness Inventory and Academic Self-Regulation Questionnaire
finding.std_deviation: SD=0.67 years; SDs for scale means reported in text

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics outcomes showed positive associations with metacognition, self-regulation, and performance expectations, but with important null/negative components. In the performance model, the combined predictors explained 29% of variance (R2=0.29), with performance expectations the strongest positive predictor (beta=0.40) and external regulation a negative predictor (beta=-0.25); procedural knowledge also contributed positively (beta=0.14).
finding.measure: Term grades and teacher ratings in mathematics; performance expectations in mathematics

finding.finding_summary: In physical education, the combined predictors explained only a small share of performance variance (R2=0.095), and metacognition/self-regulation had mostly indirect or non-significant effects. Performance expectations positively predicted performance (b=0.18), while external regulation was a negative contributor (b=-15), and identified regulation was the only positive predictor of expectations (beta=0.25).
finding.measure: Term grades and teacher ratings in physical education; performance expectations in physical education

finding.finding_summary: Language outcomes were positively associated with metacognition, self-regulation, and performance expectations, but external regulation showed a negative association with school performance. The predictors explained 22% of variance in language performance (R2=0.22); performance expectations was the strongest positive predictor (beta=0.29), followed by introjected regulation (beta=0.24) and declarative knowledge (beta=0.13), whereas external regulation was negative (beta=-0.24).
finding.measure: Term grades and teacher ratings in language; performance expectations in language

paper_profiles.title: Large Language Models: A Survey
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad survey of large language models (LLMs), their architectures, training methods, capabilities, applications, and evaluation benchmarks. It is not an empirical study of an educational intervention or of student use of ChatGPT in mathematics. Instead, it synthesizes the development of LLMs from early neural language models through GPT, LLaMA, PaLM, and related systems, and explains how these models are built and aligned.

The paper reviews model families, data cleaning, tokenization, pre-training objectives, instruction tuning, RLHF, retrieval augmentation, tool use, and agentic workflows. It also summarizes representative datasets and benchmark results, including examples of performance on reasoning, coding, multilingual, and medical tasks. The discussion is technical and model-centric rather than participant- or classroom-centric.

Because the paper is a survey, it does not report a study population, intervention implementation, or outcome measures for middle school mathematics learners. Its main conclusion is that LLM capabilities have expanded rapidly and that future work should address efficiency, multimodality, safety, and responsible use. For the requested research topic, it does not provide direct evidence about ChatGPT in middle school math classrooms.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a broad survey/review article on large language models, not an empirical study of an educational intervention. It contains no original study design, no K-12 sample, and no causal or correlational evaluation of student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct measured impact on educational outcomes or implementation in middle school mathematics. It only discusses LLM capabilities and related benchmark results in general technical contexts.

paper_profiles.title: C-EVAL: A Multi-Level Multi-Discipline Chinese Evaluation Suite for Foundation Models
paper_profiles.venue: NeurIPS 2023 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces C-EVAL, a benchmark suite designed to evaluate the advanced knowledge and reasoning abilities of foundation models in Chinese. The core problem addressed is the lack of comprehensive Chinese-language evaluation resources for large language models, especially for assessing domain knowledge and reasoning beyond casual conversation. C-EVAL contains 13,948 multiple-choice questions spanning 52 subjects across four difficulty levels: middle school, high school, college, and professional.

The paper describes the construction process in detail, including collecting questions from mock exams, local exams, and a smaller number of authorized university-related questions. The authors also carefully process the data into a standardized format, convert mathematical notation to LaTeX, deduplicate and clean the questions, and create development, validation, and test splits. For the development split, they additionally generate explanation data to support few-shot chain-of-thought prompting.

The paper evaluates 11 accessible large language models, including GPT-4, ChatGPT, Claude, GLM-130B, ChatGLM-6B, LLaMA-65B, and others, using zero-shot and five-shot answer-only settings and five-shot chain-of-thought prompting. Results show GPT-4 as the top performer, but also reveal large performance gaps for most models, especially on harder reasoning-focused subjects in the C-EVAL HARD subset. The authors conclude that C-EVAL provides a broader and more Chinese-contextual benchmark than prior resources and can help diagnose model strengths and weaknesses across multiple dimensions.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark/dataset paper for evaluating foundation models, not an education intervention study. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically clear, but it does not test an instructional treatment or produce causal evidence in an educational setting.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct K-12 learning impact; it reports model benchmark accuracy on Chinese exam questions and does not evaluate student outcomes, teacher outcomes, or classroom implementation.

paper_profiles.title: Investigating OpenAI’s ChatGPT Potentials in Generating Chatbot's Dialogue for English as a Foreign Language Learning
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Advanced Computer Science and Applications
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can generate suitable reference dialogues for an English as a Foreign Language (EFL) chatbot system. The central question is not whether ChatGPT improves learning outcomes in a live classroom trial, but whether its generated dialogue content is readable and appropriate for learners at different proficiency levels. The authors argue that dialogue quality matters for chatbot-based language learning because students need materials that are understandable, varied, and not overly complex.

The study uses ChatGPT to generate dialogue pairs for a mobile voice-enabled chatbot intended to support EFL speaking practice. The prompt specifies a conversation between an undergraduate student at Tokyo Denki University and an exchange student from Italy, and the model is also asked to produce alternative lines for each dialogue turn. In total, 450 dialogue combinations are analyzed. The evaluation relies on three readability measures: Flesch Reading Ease, Dale-Chall, and McAlpine EFLAW, which together are used to judge text difficulty from different angles.

The paper concludes that most ChatGPT-generated dialogues fall in a range suitable for CEFR A2 learners, with some materials also providing challenge for B1 learners. The dialogues are generally easy to understand and contain few mini-words or other features likely to confuse EFL readers. The authors suggest that ChatGPT has promise as a low-cost content-generation tool for chatbot dialogue creation, especially for mobile EFL applications, though higher-level learners may find the materials too simple.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical paper, but it is primarily a descriptive readability analysis rather than a controlled experiment or quasi-experiment. It provides systematic measurement of generated text, yet it does not evaluate learner outcomes or compare interventions under a rigorous causal design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical usefulness for EFL dialogue generation, but the impact is indirect and unmeasured with students. Because no effect size on learning or engagement is reported, the demonstrated impact on learners is modest and unclear.

interventions.use_case: Using ChatGPT to generate reference dialogue lines and alternative replies for an EFL chatbot mobile application; the dialogues are intended to support speaking, listening, and reading practice for learners.

A mobile voice-enabled chatbot app that loads ChatGPT-generated reference dialogues, plays the first line via text-to-speech, and supports read-aloud practice with speech recognition-based pronunciation checking.

finding.finding_summary: Across 450 ChatGPT-generated dialogue samples, the text was judged suitable for EFL speaking practice, especially for CEFR A2 learners. Most dialogues scored in the Flesch Reading Ease 80-90 range and were interpreted as easily comprehensible for sixth-grade elementary students, with some content also stretching B1 learners. No experimental learning gain was measured; the paper’s claim is about readability-based suitability rather than student performance.
finding.measure: Readability metrics applied to generated dialogue text (Flesch Reading Ease, Dale-Chall, McAlpine EFLAW)

finding.finding_summary: The study evaluated whether ChatGPT-generated dialogues were linguistically appropriate as instructional reading material for EFL learners. Based on Dale-Chall and McAlpine EFLAW, the dialogue set was generally easy to understand and avoided many mini-words/wordy expressions that can confuse international readers, suggesting favorable literacy-level accessibility for A2-B1 learners.
finding.measure: Readability metrics of written dialogue content

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT could reduce the time and effort needed for teachers or developers to create reference dialogues for a chatbot, since the model can generate multiple topics and alternative lines automatically. This is a conceptual efficiency claim supported by the successful generation of 450 dialogue combinations, not a measured workload comparison.
finding.measure: Dialogue generation feasibility / author-described reduction in content creation effort

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in Higher Education: The ChatGPT Effect
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book-length work addresses the rapid emergence of ChatGPT and generative AI in higher education and the need for educators, administrators, and policymakers to understand both its opportunities and risks. It is not an empirical middle school mathematics study; rather, it is a broad conceptual and practical guide focused on higher education. The text surveys core concepts such as AI, big data, and the mechanics of generative AI, then discusses how ChatGPT may affect curriculum design, assessment, policy, and future institutional practice.

The book presents several frameworks and design-oriented tools, including AI literacy ideas, the Six Assessment Redesign Pivotal Strategies (SARPS), an AI Assessment Integration Framework, and an AI Ecological Education Policy Framework. It also includes illustrative examples, case scenarios, and discussion of prompt engineering, but these are presented as guidance and illustration rather than as a controlled intervention study. One chapter reports research findings on perceptions of students, teachers, and staff regarding AI policy in Hong Kong, but the text provided does not describe a middle school mathematics intervention or quantitative comparator study.

Overall, the book argues that generative AI should be integrated thoughtfully, ethically, and with human oversight. It emphasizes that ChatGPT can support teaching, learning, and assessment redesign, but that institutions need clear policies, AI literacy, and authentic assessment practices to avoid overreliance and integrity problems. The main contribution is conceptual and practical rather than experimental.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a trade book / scholarly monograph chapter text focused on background, frameworks, and commentary about generative AI in higher education, not an empirical middle-school mathematics study. No direct comparator, sample, or causal design is reported in the provided text.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No measurable intervention impact is reported here for middle school mathematics or ChatGPT use. The text is descriptive and conceptual, so it does not provide evidence of academic, behavioral, or institutional effects.

paper_profiles.title: A Meta-Analysis of ChatGPT’s Influence on Learning Achievement
paper_profiles.venue: International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT improves learning achievement and whether its effects vary by learner age, learning outcome type, instructional approach, and research design. Rather than studying a single classroom intervention, the authors conducted a meta-analysis of empirical studies published from November 2022 to December 2024 that reported quantitative outcomes on ChatGPT use in education.

The review included 22 publications comprising 86 independent effect sizes. The synthesized studies covered multiple learner groups, including elementary students, middle and high school students, undergraduates, adult learners, and clinical teachers. Most evidence came from undergraduate settings, but the authors explicitly compared school levels, learning domains, instructional formats, and study designs. ChatGPT was used in a range of instructional contexts such as lectures, self-regulated learning, problem-based learning, flipped learning, game-based learning, project-based learning, and case-based learning.

The meta-analysis found a moderate overall positive effect on learning achievement (g = 0.573). Effects were larger for middle and high school students than for undergraduates, though the difference was not statistically significant. ChatGPT showed similar benefits across cognitive, affective, and metacognitive outcomes, but the strongest effects appeared in self-regulated learning and case-based learning, while game-based learning showed the weakest and non-significant effect. Quasi-experimental studies were the most common design, and the paper concludes that ChatGPT is promising for education, especially in learner-centered and self-regulated contexts, but more research is needed in middle and high school settings and across underrepresented learning domains.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-analysis synthesizing 86 independent studies from 22 publications, with explicit inclusion criteria, random-effects modeling, heterogeneity testing, and publication-bias checks. It meets the highest evidence tier for synthesis studies despite some heterogeneity and early-stage ChatGPT literature constraints.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled overall effect on learning achievement is moderate and statistically robust (g=0.573), which exceeds the threshold for blue impact. Effects are also positive across school levels and outcome domains, indicating meaningful potential impact for education.

interventions.use_case: Meta-analysis of ChatGPT use in educational settings, including classroom, self-regulated learning, problem-based learning, case-based learning, flipped learning, game-based learning, and project-based learning; synthesized studies where ChatGPT functioned as a conversational learning assistant/scaffold for students.

finding.finding_summary: Across 86 independent studies (N=6,992), ChatGPT showed a moderate positive overall effect on learning achievement (g=0.573, 95% CI [0.451, 0.696]). The meta-analysis found substantial heterogeneity (I²=83.37), but the pooled effect remained statistically significant (Z=9.170, p<.001).
finding.measure: Learning achievement / learning outcomes across included empirical studies

finding.finding_summary: For affective outcomes, ChatGPT had a positive but somewhat smaller effect than cognitive or metacognitive outcomes (g=0.481, 95% CI [0.262, 0.700], k=27, n=1,808). The affective domain included motivation, engagement, satisfaction, frustration, and anxiety-related outcomes, and all were statistically significant overall (Z=4.303, p<.001).
finding.measure: Affective learning outcomes (motivation, engagement, satisfaction, frustration, anxiety, attitudes)

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT also showed positive effects on cognitive outcomes (g=0.612, 95% CI [0.446, 0.779], k=46, n=3,757) and metacognitive outcomes (g=0.619, 95% CI [0.319, 0.919], k=13, n=1,427). The paper reports no significant difference among affective, cognitive, and metacognitive domains (QB(2)=0.983, p=.612), suggesting broadly positive effects on higher-order and self-regulatory learning-related skills.
finding.measure: Cognitive outcomes and metacognitive outcomes (e.g., understanding, application, problem solving, higher-order thinking, critical thinking, self-regulation)
finding.study_size: n=5,184 combined across cognitive and metacognitive domains

paper_profiles.title: Can GenAI improve students’ mathematics learning outcomes effectively?—A meta-analysis of empirical research 2023-2025
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), including tools such as ChatGPT, improves students’ mathematics learning outcomes. It focuses on empirical studies published from 2023 to 2025 and uses a systematic review and meta-analysis to quantify the overall effect of GenAI in mathematics education.

The review compares GenAI-based mathematics instruction with traditional teaching or other non-GenAI approaches. It includes experimental and quasi-experimental studies involving students from elementary school through university. Outcomes are organized into cognitive skills and non-cognitive skills, with cognitive outcomes further divided into higher-order and lower-order thinking. The analysis uses Hedges’ g and moderator analyses to examine whether effects differ by grade level, sample size, intervention duration, learning content, and GenAI integration level (using the PIC-RAT model).

Across 22 empirical studies and 46 effect sizes, the meta-analysis found a moderate positive overall effect of GenAI on mathematics learning. The effect was stronger for cognitive than non-cognitive outcomes, and strongest for higher-order cognitive skills. Subgroup analyses suggested that elementary students benefited most, and that “Creative Transformation” implementations outperformed “Interactive/Passive Enhancement” implementations. Sample size was also a significant moderator, with smaller studies showing larger effects. Intervention duration and learning content were not significant moderators.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-analysis synthesizing 22 empirical studies with explicit inclusion criteria, quantitative effect sizes, and risk-of-bias checks. The review also reports quality appraisal (MERSQI) and sensitivity/publication-bias analyses, supporting high evidence credibility.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled effect on mathematics outcomes is moderate and positive (g = 0.539), which meets the threshold for medium impact. The findings are also relevant to priority K-12 populations, especially elementary and middle school learners, where effects were largest.

interventions.use_case: GenAI/ChatGPT used in mathematics instruction as a conversational tutor to provide personalized tutoring, step-by-step problem-solving guidance, immediate feedback, conceptual explanations, and generated practice materials for students from primary school through university.

finding.finding_summary: This meta-analysis of 22 empirical studies (46 effect sizes, N=5,132) found a moderate positive overall effect of GenAI on mathematics learning outcomes, with Hedges' g = 0.539 (p < 0.005, 95% CI [0.374, 0.704]). The primary outcome was mathematics achievement/learning results aggregated across experimental and quasi-experimental studies comparing GenAI-supported instruction with traditional teaching.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning outcomes / achievement (standardized mean difference, Hedges' g)

finding.finding_summary: GenAI also showed a smaller but positive effect on non-cognitive mathematics outcomes, with g = 0.320. The non-cognitive measures included constructs such as motivation, self-efficacy, mathematics anxiety, attitudes, and engagement, indicating benefits beyond achievement alone.
finding.measure: Non-cognitive outcomes in mathematics (e.g., motivation, self-efficacy, anxiety, attitudes, engagement)

finding.finding_summary: Within cognitive outcomes, GenAI had a stronger effect on higher-order thinking than lower-order thinking. The meta-analysis reported g = 0.740 for higher-order skills such as analysis, evaluation, and creation, compared with g = 0.562 for lower-order skills such as remembering, understanding, and applying.
finding.measure: Higher-order and lower-order cognitive skills in mathematics (Bloom’s taxonomy)

paper_profiles.title: Intelligent learning systems in primary and secondary education: a systematic review (2014–2024)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the fragmented state of evidence on intelligent learning systems (ILS) in K-12 education, asking what types of systems are being used, how effective they are, and what implementation factors shape their impact. The authors conducted a systematic review of peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2014 and 2024, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines and synthesizing studies indexed in Scopus and Web of Science.

The review defines ILS broadly as AI-enhanced educational technologies that adapt content, feedback, pacing, or instructional decisions based on learner data. It includes intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, learning analytics tools, AI-enhanced educational applications, automated assessment systems, and personalized learning management systems. The underlying studies covered primary and secondary education, with many focused on mathematics and other STEM domains, and with implementation contexts spanning classroom use, homework support, and blended instructional arrangements.

Across 72 included studies, 65 reported outcome data and most showed positive effects. The review reports 89.2% positive findings among studies with outcomes, with a median reported effect size of d = 0.58 among studies that provided effect sizes. Mathematics was the most common subject area and also one of the strongest in effectiveness, while the review also found substantial regional variation in implementation styles and a large dominance of intelligent tutoring systems. The authors conclude that ILS can improve learning when pedagogically aligned and well supported, but they emphasize gaps in longitudinal evidence, implementation fidelity reporting, equity considerations, and explicit computational thinking assessment in STEM studies.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review following PRISMA 2020 with explicit search, screening, extraction, and quality appraisal procedures, which gives it relatively strong methodological credibility. However, it is not a meta-analysis and relies on heterogeneous primary studies, so some concerns remain about precision and comparability.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review reports large-scope positive findings across 72 studies, with 89.2% positive effects among studies with outcomes and a median effect size of d=0.58 where reported. That places the overall evidence in a medium-to-large impact range for K-12 populations, especially in mathematics and STEM.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of K-12 intelligent tutoring systems and related intelligent learning systems, including classic step-by-step tutoring with adaptive guidance, personalized feedback, and domain/student models in school subjects such as mathematics and science.
Review of adaptive learning systems that personalize content, pacing, sequencing, and difficulty based on student performance data in primary and secondary education.
Review includes learning analytics tools that analyze student data to generate instructional insights and support adaptive intervention in K-12 settings.
Review includes automated assessment systems that provide immediate feedback and evaluation of student performance, especially in school-based learning tasks.

Review includes AI-enhanced educational applications and personalized LMS-like systems that deliver instructional support with varying degrees of adaptation, often functioning as computer-assisted instruction in K-12 classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: Across 65 studies with outcome data, mathematics was the dominant subject and showed strong positive effects: 23 of 25 mathematics studies were positive (92%), with the review reporting overall effects ranging from small to very large across the corpus (d=0.21 to d=1.84; median d=0.58). The paper does not provide a mathematics-only pooled effect size, but characterizes mathematics as the highest-evidence domain and notes alignment between structured content and algorithmic tutoring.
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement / learning outcomes reported across included studies

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that many studies measured engagement, motivation, and related affective outcomes, with the overall corpus showing 89.2% positive effects among studies with outcome data. These benefits were typically attributed to immediate feedback, personalization, and gamification, but no single pooled effect size is reported for engagement or motivation specifically.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, attitudes, and related affective/self-report outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies some positive effects on computational thinking, problem-solving, and critical-thinking-related outcomes, but notes major gaps in explicit measurement. Among 35 STEM-focused studies, only 8 explicitly stated computational thinking objectives and only 3 actually measured CT outcomes with validated assessments, so evidence is positive but sparse and underassessed.
finding.measure: Computational thinking, problem-solving, critical thinking, and related cognitive skill outcomes

finding.finding_summary: Science-related ILS implementations were largely favorable: 7 of 8 science studies showed positive effects (88%), and the broader STEM-oriented set was described as benefiting from adaptive tutoring and data-driven support. The review does not report a pooled science-only effect size, but the evidence is consistently positive across physics, chemistry, and biology studies.
finding.measure: Science achievement / learning outcomes in physics, chemistry, and biology

finding.finding_summary: Language and reading-comprehension applications were mostly positive: the review reports 8 positive and 1 mixed study for language/reading comprehension (89%), and language learning studies were 4/4 positive. The synthesis does not provide a pooled literacy effect size, but indicates consistent gains in reading/writing-related outcomes where reported.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension, language learning, and related literacy outcomes
finding.study_size: n=9 studies for language/reading comprehension; n=4 studies for language learning

finding.finding_summary: For transversal or cross-cutting competencies, the review reports 9 positive studies out of 11 (82%), indicating generally favorable outcomes beyond core STEM and literacy areas. Because the paper does not break these down into a single standardized metric, the finding is best interpreted as broad positive but heterogeneous evidence.
finding.measure: Transversal/cross-cutting competency outcomes

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emerging role of artificial intelligence in education, with a particular focus on chatbots and ChatGPT.
