Rather than testing a specific intervention, the authors review existing literature to explain what AI is, how chatbots work, how ChatGPT differs from earlier tools, and where AI systems may be used across educational settings. The paper asks what benefits AI may offer for teaching and learning, while also considering ethical and practical risks.

The paper is a narrative review and conceptual discussion, not an empirical study. It synthesizes prior work on AI-supported learning systems such as intelligent tutoring systems, automated grading, learning analytics, and chatbots used for feedback, language learning, student support, and administrative tasks. The discussion spans multiple educational levels and roles, including students, teachers, and administrators, but does not report a specific sample, intervention duration, or location of participants.

The authors conclude that AI and ChatGPT have clear potential to improve personalization, engagement, feedback, and efficiency in education. At the same time, they emphasize concerns about bias, privacy, misinformation, over-reliance on technology, and academic integrity. They argue that successful adoption requires teacher preparation, responsible implementation, and continued research on how these tools can be aligned with educational goals and ethics.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review/opinion article, not an empirical evaluation of an intervention with a comparator or measured outcomes. It synthesizes prior literature and discusses ethical/practical issues rather than presenting primary evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct outcome data are reported, so there is no measurable impact on middle school mathematics achievement, transfer, or any other educational outcome in this paper.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual review of ChatGPT as a conversational AI for education, including answering student questions, providing feedback, supporting personalized learning, and assisting with learning tasks.

paper_profiles.title: The effect of ChatGPT on students’ learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking: insights from a meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT improves student learning outcomes and under what conditions its effects are strongest. The authors note that prior studies and reviews produced mixed conclusions, with some reporting benefits and others finding null or negative effects. To resolve these inconsistencies, they conducted a meta-analysis of 51 experimental or quasi-experimental studies published between November 2022 and February 2025.

The review focuses on ChatGPT used as an educational support tool in learning settings, including higher education, secondary education, and a small amount of primary education. The included studies span STEM and related courses, language learning and academic writing, and skills/competencies development, with ChatGPT deployed in personalized learning, problem-based learning, project-based learning, contextual learning, reflective learning, and mixed formats. The control conditions were required to exclude ChatGPT and rely on traditional or comparable non-ChatGPT learning methods.

The meta-analysis finds that ChatGPT has a large positive overall effect on learning performance and moderate positive effects on learning perception and higher-order thinking. Moderator analyses suggest that learning performance benefits are strongest in skills/competencies courses, problem-based learning, and 4–8 week interventions; learning perception benefits increase with longer duration, especially beyond 8 weeks; and higher-order thinking gains are strongest in STEM courses and when ChatGPT serves as an intelligent tutor. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can support learning, but its effectiveness depends on course type, instructional model, duration, and how it is used pedagogically.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-analysis of 51 experimental/quasi-experimental studies with explicit inclusion criteria, effect-size computation, heterogeneity tests, publication-bias checks, and sensitivity analyses. That makes it high-credibility evidence for the general effect of ChatGPT in education, though the included studies vary widely in context and quality.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled effects on learning performance (g=0.867), learning perception (g=0.456), and higher-order thinking (g=0.457) are all at least moderate, with learning performance large. Although this paper is not middle-school mathematics-specific, the magnitude and consistency of effects indicate substantial positive impact on educational outcomes overall.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a generative AI tutor/assistant across experimental studies, supporting students through tutoring, assessment and feedback, personalized recommendations, and conversational problem solving in varied courses.

finding.finding_summary: This meta-analysis of 44 independent studies found that ChatGPT improved learning performance with a large overall effect (Hedges's g=0.867, 95% CI [0.683, 1.052]). The included studies used post-test means/SDs or equivalent statistics from experimental vs control groups, with outcomes spanning STEM, language, and skills courses; the paper reports high heterogeneity (I²=89.243%).
finding.measure: Learning performance measured primarily by tests and exams

finding.finding_summary: Across 19 independent studies, ChatGPT had a moderate positive effect on learning perception (g=0.456, 95% CI [0.287, 0.625]). Outcomes were assessed with scales/questionnaires capturing perceptions, with moderate heterogeneity (I²=72.580%); longer interventions (>8 weeks) showed larger effects.
finding.measure: Learning perception measured by scales and questionnaires

finding.finding_summary: For higher-order thinking, 9 independent studies showed a moderate positive effect of ChatGPT (g=0.457, 95% CI [0.255, 0.650]). The outcome was measured via scales/questionnaires targeting higher-order thinking, with moderate heterogeneity (I²=55.813%); effects were strongest when ChatGPT acted as an intelligent tutor.
finding.measure: Higher-order thinking measured by scales and questionnaires

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of Gender Stereotypes on the Self-Concept of Female Students in STEM Subjects with an Under-Representation of Females
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how gender stereotypes, school experiences, and family support relate to female students’ academic self-concept in STEM fields. The authors focus on a specific group that is often underrepresented in STEM: women studying STEM subjects with 30% or fewer female students, which they label STEM-LPF. The central research question asks whether women’s own stereotypes, compared with school- and family-related factors, predict how positively they evaluate their STEM abilities.

The main empirical component is a survey of 296 female university students from German universities enrolled in STEM-LPF subjects such as mechanical engineering, computer science, physics, metal engineering, civil engineering, and electrical engineering. Students reported their STEM self-concept, internalized gender stereotypes, school-related experiences such as favorite subjects and perceived teacher behavior, and family support in mathematics and STEM. The study also includes a small qualitative interview study with 11 female STEM students to illustrate the quantitative findings.

Results from the latent regression model show that stronger gender stereotypes are associated with lower STEM self-concept. School factors are mixed: having STEM as favorite school subjects relates positively to self-concept, while perceived school support and stereotyped teacher behavior relate negatively. Family support also shows a negative relationship with STEM self-concept, which the authors interpret as potentially intrusive or stereotype-reinforcing support rather than purely helpful assistance. Overall, the paper argues that stereotypes remain influential even among women who have already chosen gender-atypical STEM pathways, and that indirect, stereotype-sensitive forms of support may be more beneficial than direct intervention.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational/latent regression study with a qualitative supplement, not an experimental test of an intervention. It provides useful evidence about associations among stereotypes, support, and self-concept, but cannot establish causal effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful associations for a priority population (female STEM students), including a moderate negative relation between stereotypes and STEM self-concept (β=-0.405). However, because it is observational and focuses on self-concept rather than direct achievement gains, the impact is indirect and not clearly generalizable as an intervention effect.

finding.finding_summary: This correlational latent regression study of female STEM-LPF university students (n=296) found that higher internalized gender stereotypes were associated with lower STEM academic self-concept (β=-0.405). The paper also found that school favorite STEM subjects predicted higher self-concept, while school support/teacher stereotypes and family support variables were negatively related to self-concept, explaining 30.4% of the variance in STEM self-concept overall (R²=0.304).
finding.measure: STEM academic self-concept; internalized gender stereotypes; school support/teacher stereotypes; family support

paper_profiles.title: Transforming Psychometrics: Integrating Technology, and Application in the 21st Century
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter presents a conceptual overview of contemporary psychometrics and its evolution from Classical Test Theory to more advanced approaches such as Item Response Theory, Bayesian psychometrics, network psychometrics, and computerized adaptive testing. The paper asks how modern psychometric methods, together with artificial intelligence, big data, and wearable technologies, are reshaping measurement in education, clinical psychology, organizational settings, and human-computer interaction.

Rather than reporting an empirical intervention study, the chapter synthesizes recent developments and illustrates potential applications with examples such as adaptive learning platforms, AI-driven assessment systems, and personalized psychometric feedback. The educational examples include adaptive learning and testing systems that tailor item difficulty and content to individual learners, including middle school math scenarios used only as illustrative examples rather than as study participants or evaluated interventions.

The authors conclude that modern psychometrics can improve precision, adaptability, and personalization of assessments, but they also emphasize major challenges involving privacy, bias, interpretability, and ethics. Overall, the chapter argues that future progress will depend on careful validation, transparent reporting, fairness-aware design, and culturally sensitive implementation of AI-enabled psychometric tools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative book chapter/review rather than an empirical study, and it does not present a clear evaluation design, comparator, or original outcome data. The paper is peer-reviewed as a chapter, but it provides conceptual discussion and examples instead of causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct impact on student outcomes is demonstrated, and no measurable effects are reported for middle school mathematics achievement or transfer. The chapter is descriptive and forward-looking, so its practical impact on the target outcome remains unsubstantiated.

interventions.use_case: conceptual overview of AI-enabled psychometrics, including adaptive testing, Bayesian psychometrics, cognitive diagnostic models, and AI-driven assessment systems in education

paper_profiles.title: Educational Applications of the ChatGPT AI System: A Systematic Review Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emerging literature on ChatGPT in education and asks what educational uses, benefits, and risks have been reported since the tool’s release in late 2022. The review is framed around broad questions about subject areas affected by ChatGPT, the results and conclusions in the existing literature, and the potential advantages and ethical challenges of using the system in educational settings.

The paper is not an intervention study; instead, it systematically reviews 40 publications identified through searches of Google Scholar and several databases, with inclusion limited to English-language works published between December 2022 and February 15, 2023. The included studies span multiple domains such as education, medical education, law, language, engineering, psychology, finance, and computer science, and they are analyzed qualitatively for themes related to ChatGPT’s educational functions.

The review identifies several positive educational applications, including summarizing and abstracting texts, generating literature, translating and paraphrasing, helping students study, producing complex exam answers, identifying learner needs, supporting personalized learning, grading and assessment, data analysis, cybercrime prevention, directing users to experts, and creating instructional materials. It also highlights negative concerns such as cheating, biased outputs, incorrect answers, legal issues, and ethical risks. The authors conclude that ChatGPT may reshape educational practice, but its use requires caution and attention to integrity, reliability, and governance.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review with a clear search and screening process, but it synthesizes heterogeneous early studies rather than evaluating a causal intervention directly. The paper is qualitative/descriptive and does not provide primary experimental evidence on student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests potentially meaningful educational uses of ChatGPT, but it does not estimate effect sizes or demonstrate direct achievement gains. Any impact claims are therefore preliminary and unclear for K-12 populations, especially middle school mathematics achievement and transfer.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of ChatGPT as a generative conversational AI used for education tasks such as helping students study, generating complex answers, translation/paraphrasing, literature review support, grading, and material generation.

paper_profiles.title: The Promises and Pitfalls of LLMs as Feedback Providers: A Study of Prompt Engineering and the Quality of AI-Driven Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how prompt quality affects the usefulness of ChatGPT-4 as a feedback provider in higher education, and whether LLM-generated feedback differs from novice and expert human feedback. The authors argue that while LLMs are increasingly used in education, there is still little empirical work comparing their feedback quality to that of real people, especially in relation to prompt engineering.

To address this, the study develops a theory-driven prompt manual for assessing prompt quality and creates three prompts of varying quality (poor, medium, good). These prompts are used to generate ChatGPT-4 feedback on a learning goal containing three known errors. The resulting LLM feedback is quantitatively coded for multiple feedback-quality dimensions such as concreteness, empathy, activation, correctness, and errors. The best prompt is then used to elicit feedback from pre-service teachers and experts in teacher education, enabling comparison between novice, expert, and AI feedback.

The study finds that prompt quality strongly shapes feedback quality: only the highest-quality prompt consistently produces strong feedback, while a superficially well-formed prompt can still produce more factual errors. Overall, ChatGPT-4 outperforms novice feedback and in some dimensions rivals or exceeds expert feedback, especially in specificity, questions, and explanation. The authors conclude that LLMs can be efficient and high-quality feedback providers in higher education, but only when guided by careful prompt design and human oversight.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical study with clear methods (coded feedback, ANOVAs, inter-rater reliability), but it is not a randomized or causal evaluation of learning outcomes. It is best classified as observational/experimental product-quality analysis of generated feedback rather than a student outcome trial.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows a clear operational benefit in feedback-generation speed, but it does not test student achievement, and no standardized effect size for learning impact is reported. The practical impact is therefore promising but still indirect and modest.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-4 used as an AI feedback provider to generate formative feedback on a learning-goal statement in teacher education, compared against novice and expert human feedback. The paper also manipulates prompt engineering quality to study how prompt design changes the quality of the LLM's feedback output.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT-4 produced feedback much faster than expert humans, with the paper stating that the LLM generated an average of 49 pieces of feedback in the same amount of time an expert produced one. This indicates a substantial efficiency advantage for AI feedback generation, although no formal effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Feedback production speed / time efficiency for generating formative feedback
finding.study_size: n=61 feedback instances for prompt comparison; n=30 LLM feedback, n=11 expert feedback, n=30 novice feedback for agent comparison

paper_profiles.title: To be with artificial intelligence in oral test or not to be: a probe into the traces of success in speaking skill, psychological well-being, autonomy, and academic buoyancy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether AI-powered tools, specifically ChatGPT, can improve EFL learners’ speaking performance and also influence related non-cognitive outcomes such as psychological well-being, learner autonomy, and academic buoyancy. The authors frame the study as addressing a gap in research on the broader effects of AI in language assessment, beyond simple test scores.

The intervention involved using ChatGPT to score and provide feedback on speaking responses in TOEFL iBT speaking tasks. Participants first completed a Michigan Language Proficiency Test to confirm upper-intermediate proficiency, then took a TOEFL iBT speaking pretest, practiced speaking with ChatGPT feedback, completed an immediate posttest, and finally a delayed posttest three weeks later. Psychological well-being, autonomy, and academic buoyancy were explored through narrative frames, making the study concurrent mixed-methods.

The sample consisted of 28 upper-intermediate EFL students from a university in Ethiopia. Quantitative results showed significant gains in speaking scores from pretest to posttest and delayed posttest, with retention of improvement over time. Qualitative findings suggested that ChatGPT reduced anxiety, increased motivation and confidence, supported self-directed learning, and helped students cope better with academic challenges. The authors conclude that AI-assisted oral assessment can support both language development and learner well-being, though they note limitations related to the small, single-site sample and reliance on self-reported qualitative data.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods study, but it is not a randomized controlled trial and uses a single intact class (n=28) without a clear comparator. The qualitative outcomes are informative, and the quantitative speaking analysis is within-subject only, so causal credibility is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The speaking outcome shows a large improvement (partial eta squared=0.770) with sustained gains at delayed posttest, which exceeds the threshold for medium/large impact. Although the sample is small and context-specific, the magnitude of the observed speaking gains is substantial.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as an AI-assisted tool for scoring and providing personalized feedback on EFL oral speaking tasks in TOEFL iBT speaking practice.

finding.finding_summary: Speaking scores improved substantially after ChatGPT-supported oral practice. In the 28 upper-intermediate EFL learners, mean TOEFL iBT speaking scores increased from 5.214 (SD=2.024) at pretest to 16.071 (SD=4.936) at immediate posttest and remained elevated at 15.357 (SD=4.676) at delayed posttest. The repeated-measures analysis showed a significant time effect (Wilks’ lambda=0.230, partial eta squared=0.770), indicating a large improvement that was largely retained three weeks later.
finding.measure: TOEFL iBT speaking section scores at pretest, immediate posttest, and delayed posttest
finding.std_deviation: Pretest SD=2.024; posttest SD=4.936; delayed posttest SD=4.676

finding.finding_summary: Qualitative narratives indicated improved psychological well-being after using ChatGPT for oral test feedback, especially reduced anxiety, increased motivation, and higher self-confidence. Participants reported that the nonjudgmental, immediate feedback created a more supportive learning environment, but the study did not provide a quantitative effect size for this outcome.
finding.measure: Narrative frame themes on psychological well-being (anxiety, motivation, self-confidence, supportive environment)

finding.finding_summary: The qualitative findings suggest that ChatGPT increased learner autonomy by promoting self-directed practice, individualized learning, confidence in independent practice, and resourcefulness. Participants described being able to practice speaking anytime and use instant feedback to manage their own learning, but the paper reports no quantitative effect size for autonomy.
finding.measure: Narrative frame themes on learner autonomy (self-directed learning, individualized learning, independent practice, resourcefulness)

finding.finding_summary: The study’s qualitative analysis also found positive effects on academic buoyancy, including greater fortitude, problem-solving, perseverance, and adaptability in speaking tasks. Learners reported feeling more able to handle speaking tests and recover from difficulties, though the study did not report a quantitative estimate for this construct.
finding.measure: Narrative frame themes on academic buoyancy (fortitude, problem-solving, perseverance, adaptability)

paper_profiles.title: The Effectiveness of Explanatory Adaptive Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether explanatory adaptive feedback in a digital educational game improves students’ fraction learning beyond corrective feedback alone. The study is motivated by persistent difficulties children have with fraction magnitude understanding, including misconceptions such as natural number bias and unit-of-reference errors, as well as the role of non-cognitive factors like math anxiety, motivation, and self-concept.

The intervention used the Number Trace Fraction game, a number-line estimation learning environment. Students received one of three conditions: a game with corrective feedback, the same game with explanatory adaptive feedback tailored to likely misconceptions, or an active control condition using non-fraction math learning tracks. The adaptive version changed textual and visual feedback based on students’ estimation accuracy and included additional scaffolds such as simplification notation and animated agents. The study was conducted with fourth graders in regular classrooms in Flanders, Belgium, over six training sessions spanning roughly 3–4 weeks, with pretest, posttest, and two-month retention testing.

Results showed that both experimental conditions improved near transfer fraction knowledge relative to the control group, but explanatory adaptive feedback did not outperform corrective feedback. Far transfer fraction knowledge improved over time across conditions, suggesting some influence of regular curriculum exposure rather than the game alone. For non-cognitive outcomes, explanatory adaptive feedback was associated with a reduction in trait math anxiety without the motivational decline seen in some other conditions, but it did not improve math self-concept. The authors conclude that adaptive feedback may have promise, but the current implementation was not fine-grained enough to yield cognitive benefits beyond corrective feedback.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a well-designed randomized intervention study with an active control group, pre/post/retention testing, and multilevel modeling. Credibility is strong, but some concerns remain about weak internal consistency for the fraction measures and limited evidence that the adaptive component was actually processed.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows clear positive effects for near transfer compared with control, but the added adaptive feedback produced no measurable gain over corrective feedback and effect sizes for the main comparative claim are not reported. Overall impact is therefore modest and somewhat unclear beyond the base game intervention.

interventions.use_case: digital educational game for fraction number line estimation with adaptive feedback and scaffolds to address misconceptions (natural number bias, unit of reference) in fourth graders
rule-based corrective versus explanatory adaptive feedback on fraction number line estimation tasks, including misconception-specific text, visual highlights, and scaffolding agents
system-adapted feedback delivered based on students' response accuracy during gameplay, with predefined thresholds and feedback areas

finding.finding_summary: In this randomized study of 288 fourth graders, near transfer fraction knowledge improved significantly from pretest to posttest and retention in both experimental game conditions, but not in the active control condition. However, explanatory adaptive feedback did not outperform corrective feedback alone on fraction knowledge; far transfer also showed only time effects, with gains from pre- to posttest for corrective feedback and from pre- to retention for all conditions.
finding.measure: Near transfer fraction knowledge (10-item number line estimation test) and far transfer fraction knowledge (10-item procedural/conceptual fraction test)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention had mixed effects on motivational and emotional outcomes. Trait math motivation decreased in the control condition and corrective feedback condition, while trait math anxiety decreased only in the explanatory adaptive feedback condition; state math motivation also decreased over time in the corrective condition, but no significant state anxiety effects were found.
finding.measure: Trait math motivation, trait math anxiety, state math motivation, state math anxiety, state math self-concept

finding.finding_summary: State math self-concept was significantly lower in both experimental game conditions than in the active control condition across five training sessions, suggesting the fraction game was experienced as challenging. The paper reports a significant condition effect for state self-concept but does not provide a standardized effect size in the text excerpt.
finding.measure: State math self-concept collected after each training session

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the structural links between peer support, psychological resilience, and exercise adherence in adolescents: a multigroup model across gender and educational stages
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how peer support, psychological resilience, and exercise adherence are related among adolescents, and whether these relationships differ by gender and educational stage. The authors start from the problem that adolescents’ physical activity levels are low, and that prior research has rarely examined how social support and resilience work together to predict sustained exercise participation across developmental subgroups.

The study combines a quantitative survey with qualitative interviews. In the quantitative component, 2,137 students from elementary, middle, and high schools in Zhejiang Province, China completed standardized measures of peer support, psychological resilience, and exercise adherence. The authors also conducted semistructured interviews with 21 students, parents, and teachers to better explain the survey patterns. The analyses included correlations, regressions, mediation testing, and multigroup structural equation modeling across school levels and gender.

The findings show that peer support, psychological resilience, and exercise adherence were all positively related. Peer support had both a direct association with exercise adherence and an indirect association through psychological resilience, indicating a partial mediation pattern. The subgroup analyses suggested that middle school students showed the strongest direct peer support–adherence link, while the resilience pathway was relatively stronger for elementary and high school students. Gender differences were also observed: peer support related more directly to exercise adherence among boys, whereas resilience played a relatively larger role for girls. Qualitative interviews supported these results by showing that peer encouragement, shared skill levels, and emotionally supportive friendships help adolescents persist in exercise. The paper concludes that strengthening peer support environments and psychological resilience may improve adolescents’ sustained physical activity, with strategies tailored to developmental stage and gender.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional correlational study with qualitative interviews, not an experimental or quasi-experimental design. It provides useful associative evidence and subgroup comparisons, but cannot support causal claims about intervention effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The observed associations are meaningful, with moderate effect sizes for some subgroup differences and a strong regression association, but the study does not test an educational intervention or demonstrate causal impact on academic outcomes. Its relevance is more about understanding social/behavioral mechanisms than producing direct instructional impact.

finding.finding_summary: This cross-sectional mixed-methods study (n=2,137 adolescents) found that peer support was positively associated with exercise adherence and psychological resilience. In regression models, peer support strongly predicted exercise adherence (β=0.586) and the indirect pathway through psychological resilience accounted for 17.586% of the total association, suggesting a partial mediation-consistent pattern.
finding.measure: Self-reported peer support, psychological resilience, and exercise adherence scales; correlation, regression, and mediation modeling
finding.effect_size: β=0.586 direct association; indirect effect proportion=17.586%

finding.finding_summary: The paper also connects peer support and psychological resilience to persistent exercise habits, emotional regulation, goal focus, and sustained effort—skills embedded within the exercise adherence construct. Exercise adherence scores differed by gender and school stage, with moderate effect sizes for gender (d=0.358 for exercise adherence) and small-to-moderate stage effects (η²=0.112), indicating meaningful developmental variation in these durable behaviors.
finding.measure: Exercise adherence scale (effort investment, emotional experience, behavioral habits)
finding.effect_size: d=0.358 (gender difference in exercise adherence); η²=0.112 (educational stage effect)

paper_profiles.title: Lessons Learned from Historical Failures, Limitations and Successes of AI/ML in Healthcare and the Health Sciences. Enduring Problems, and the Role of Best Practices
paper_profiles.venue: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Health Care and Medical Sciences, Health Informatics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book chapter reviews historical failures, limitations, and later successes in AI and machine learning, with an emphasis on lessons that can inform best practices for building and evaluating AI/ML systems in health care and the health sciences. Rather than reporting a new empirical study, it synthesizes case studies and methodological issues such as the Gartner hype cycle, AI winters, limitations of early neural networks and Bayesian learners, overfitting, model overconfidence, and mismatches between AI systems and real-world clinical needs.

The chapter is framed around the idea that many apparent AI breakthroughs were followed by setbacks, and that progress has often been non-monotonic. It discusses how later technical advances such as backpropagation, deep learning, support vector machines, random forests, Bayesian networks, and improved validation protocols addressed earlier shortcomings, while also noting that many of these methods still have important limitations, especially in low-sample or poorly designed settings.

The population and context are not an education sample; the material is entirely about health care and health sciences. The chapter argues for science-driven development, rigorous model selection and error estimation, appropriate data design, and cautious interpretation of benchmark and validation results. Its main conclusion is that many historical problems in AI/ML recur when methods are applied without proper theoretical grounding or alignment to real-world use cases, and that best practices are essential to avoid repeating past failures.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/book chapter-style review of historical AI/ML failures, limitations, and best practices in healthcare and the health sciences, not an empirical study. It does not evaluate an educational technology intervention or report a controlled design relevant to the requested topic.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct educational intervention effect is reported, and there are no student learning outcomes, comparators, or effect sizes. The chapter is not about ChatGPT-based support or middle school mathematics achievement/transfer.

paper_profiles.title: Interactive Digital Media PanPinRu as an Effort to Increase Interest in Learning Students in Linear Equations of One Variable
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an interactive digital mathematics medium, PanPinRu (Segment Moving Board), can improve junior high school students’ interest and achievement in learning one-variable linear equations. The motivation is the persistent problem of low student engagement and weak understanding of abstract algebra topics in conventional, teacher-centered mathematics instruction.

The intervention is a web-based, gamified digital application that lets students manipulate variables and constants virtually, receive automatic feedback, and complete game-like challenges. The study uses a Design-Based Research approach with iterative cycles of needs analysis, design/development, classroom implementation, revision, and evaluation, involving collaboration among researchers, a mathematics teacher, and students.

The population studied was class VII A students at SMP Darul Ulum 5 Grati in Indonesia, with teachers participating in development and implementation. Data came from observations, questionnaires on learning interest, interviews, and pretest/posttest learning outcome measures, analyzed using both quantitative and qualitative methods. The paper reports that PanPinRu increased students’ learning interest and produced learning outcomes above the achievement criterion, suggesting that interactive digital and gamified media can be an effective way to support mathematics learning in this topic and setting.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a design-based research/mixed-methods classroom study in a single class, with descriptive quantitative analysis and qualitative feedback. It is peer-reviewed, but there is no clear comparison group or randomized design, so causal evidence is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported outcomes are positive for a priority population, but the magnitude is unclear because no effect size, confidence interval, or comparison condition is provided. The evidence suggests promising impact, but it is modest/uncertain rather than clearly large.

interventions.use_case: interactive digital PanPinRu segment-moving board for one-variable linear equations, with virtual manipulation of variables/constants, automatic feedback, and gamified challenges

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports improved mathematics learning outcomes after use of the interactive digital PanPinRu media for one-variable linear equations. The average learning outcome score was 84.74, exceeding the Learning Objective Achievement Criteria (KKTP); the study describes this as a significant improvement, but does not report a formal effect size or inferential statistic in the excerpt.
finding.measure: math learning outcome test (pretest/posttest; average post-implementation score)

finding.finding_summary: Student learning interest increased after the intervention, with an average student response score of 65.57 categorized as an increased category. The study concludes that the interactive digital/gamified design significantly raised motivation and engagement, though no inferential statistics or effect size are reported.
finding.measure: learning interest questionnaire / student response score

paper_profiles.title: Effect of Bilingual Instructional Method in the Academic Achievement of Junior Secondary School Students in Mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether using a bilingual instructional method improves junior secondary school students’ achievement in mathematics compared with conventional monolingual instruction. The paper is motivated by persistent low mathematics performance and argues that language of instruction may be a barrier to understanding mathematical concepts, especially for students in multilingual settings.

The intervention was a bilingual teaching module: a mathematics teaching module originally developed in English and then translated into Igbo by a mathematics expert with Igbo proficiency. The study used a non-equivalent control group quasi-experimental design with intact classes. The target population was JSS1 students in Abia State, Nigeria, and the sample came from two public secondary schools in Ohafia Local Government Area. Students in the experimental group received bilingual instruction, while the control group received conventional instruction; both groups took a pre-test and post-test using a researcher-developed Mathematics Achievement Test.

Findings indicated that students taught with the bilingual instructional method scored higher than those taught with the conventional method on the post-test. The analysis also found no significant main effect of gender, though there was a significant interaction effect between instructional method and gender. The authors conclude that bilingual instruction is an effective and gender-fair approach for improving mathematics achievement in this context and recommend broader adoption by schools and policymakers.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental non-equivalent control group study, not a randomized trial. It has a defined intervention and outcome measure, but there are notable internal validity concerns from non-randomization and attrition, so it fits yellow rather than green or blue.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gain in mathematics achievement is positive but modest and based on a small single-study sample from one local context. No standardized effect size is reported, and the result is not directly about AI or ChatGPT, so broader impact is unclear.

finding.finding_summary: A quasi-experimental study of junior secondary school students in Nigeria (n=38 completing the study; initially 76) found that bilingual instructional method improved mathematics achievement compared with conventional instruction. Post-test MAT performance was higher for the bilingual group, with a mean difference of 4.83 in favor of bilingual instruction and a statistically significant ANCOVA result (F=50.357, p=0.000).
finding.measure: Mathematics Achievement Test (MAT) post-test scores; ANCOVA-adjusted comparison of bilingual vs conventional instruction
finding.study_size: n=38 completing the study (20 experimental, 18 control)

paper_profiles.title: Assessing English as a Second Language Middle School Students' Ability to Learn Engineering Concepts
paper_profiles.venue: American Society for Engineering Education Annual Conference & Exposition
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether English as a Second Language (ESL) middle school students can learn engineering concepts effectively through hands-on, project-based instruction delivered by engineering teaching fellows. The broader problem addressed is how to teach STEM content to limited-English-proficiency students in ways that also support English vocabulary and academic language development.

The intervention consisted of a sequence of seven one-hour classes at Sherwood Githens Middle School in Durham, North Carolina. Eight sixth-grade ESL students worked through inquiry-based lessons on electric circuits, potential, current, resistance, and motors, using highly scaffolded instruction, visuals, simplified vocabulary, demonstrations, and paired hands-on activities. The unit culminated in building and modifying model electric cars to explore how resistors change speed.

The paper also describes how undergraduate and graduate engineering teaching fellows should be trained for ESL classrooms and how such lesson materials can be prepared for the TeachEngineering digital library. Student learning was assessed with picture-based questions, cloze and multiple-choice items, and performance tasks requiring students to build circuits. The authors conclude that ESL students can make substantial progress in engineering content in a short sequence of carefully scaffolded lessons, while simultaneously practicing academic English.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/single-case study with a very small sample (n=8) and no comparison group, randomization, or statistical analysis. The evidence is peer-reviewed and reasonably detailed, but credibility is limited by the design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are encouraging, but they are based on a small ESL case study without an effect size and with outcomes that are largely descriptive. The impact is therefore modest and not clearly generalizable.

finding.finding_summary: In this case study of 8 ESL sixth-grade students, the engineering unit produced strong gains in engineering content knowledge as measured by a content-based final exam and hands-on circuit-building tasks. The class mean on the final exam was 82%, and all 8 students were able to independently build a circuit that lit a bulb and then modify it to make the bulb dimmer by inserting a resistor in series.
finding.measure: Content-based final exam; hands-on circuit-building performance

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the engineering activities also supported academic English development, especially vocabulary and oral explanation in an ESL setting. Students transitioned from shy, timid behavior to being more animated and confident in using spoken and written English, though no standardized language assessment or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Classroom participation, spoken/written English use, vocabulary acquisition

finding.finding_summary: The unit appears to have improved engagement and confidence among the ESL students. The author describes students as moving from shy and timid demeanors to vibrant, animated, and confident behaviors while participating in hands-on engineering tasks, but this is based on qualitative observation rather than a formal scale.
finding.measure: Observed student engagement, confidence, and enthusiasm

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a review and position-style article that surveys artificial intelligence in education, with particular attention to chatbots and ChatGPT. It asks how AI technologies may transform teaching and learning, what educational benefits they may offer, and what ethical or practical problems they introduce.

The article does not report a primary empirical intervention or participant study. Instead, it synthesizes prior literature on AI applications in education, including personalized learning, feedback systems, assessment, and chatbot-based support. It discusses ChatGPT as a recent generative AI system that can produce human-like responses to prompts and be used for tasks such as question answering, explanation, summarization, and writing support.

Because the paper is conceptual and literature-based, it does not focus on a specific student group, classroom, or institution. Its main conclusion is that ChatGPT and related AI tools have substantial promise for individualized learning, student support, and teacher assistance, but they also raise concerns about privacy, bias, reliability, dependency, and academic integrity. The authors argue that successful adoption requires responsible use, ethical safeguards, and adequate teacher preparation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review/opinion-style overview with no original empirical design, no comparison groups, and no new quantitative data. It is peer-reviewed, but the methodology is not systematic enough to meet higher evidence tiers.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper describes potentially important educational impacts of ChatGPT, but it provides no direct measured effects or effect sizes. Its impact is therefore unclear and best characterized as a conceptual overview with modest practical relevance.

interventions.use_case: Narrative review of ChatGPT as a conversational AI for education, including its use as a chatbot for student question answering, personalized support, feedback, and assistance in learning tasks.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT could transform education by supporting personalized learning, feedback, and assistance, but it also emphasizes substantial institutional risks. Reported concerns include privacy, bias, reliability/accuracy, over-reliance, academic integrity, and the need for teacher training and policy responses; no original effect size is reported because this is a review article.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of opportunities, ethical concerns, and implementation challenges in education

finding.finding_summary: The review states that ChatGPT and related AI tools can reduce repetitive work for teachers by automating scoring, assignment evaluation, feedback, and answering student questions. These claims are descriptive rather than experimentally tested in this paper, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of teacher workload reduction and administrative support

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests AI/chatbots may increase student motivation, engagement, confidence, and reduce anxiety, citing prior studies rather than presenting new data. It specifically notes that AI-enabled environments can create more comfortable learning conditions, but this article does not report its own effect size or sample.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of motivation, engagement, confidence, and anxiety-related outcomes

paper_profiles.title: Preserving Teacher and Student Agency: Insights from a Literature Review
paper_profiles.venue: Palgrave Studies in Creativity and Culture
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter addresses a broad question in AI in education: how AI systems may affect human agency, especially the autonomy and decision-making of teachers and students. Rather than evaluating a single tool or classroom intervention, it reviews existing literature to identify where AI supports educational tasks and where it may reduce human control or expertise.

The chapter situates the discussion in common AI-in-education applications such as intelligent tutoring, learning assessment, dropout prevention, and automated grading. It uses two conceptual lenses: technician system theory, which warns that increasingly sophisticated AI can obscure the complexity of teaching practice, and the concept of agency, drawn from both computer science and social science perspectives. The context is educational settings broadly, with examples including AI assistance for math problems at home and AI-supported assessment in schools.

The review concludes that AI can create power imbalances if it shifts pedagogical authority away from teachers toward programmers and system designers. Student agency may also be constrained, especially through task assignment and gamification. The chapter argues for designing AI tools that preserve and enhance human agency rather than restrict it, and it emphasizes ethical concerns around autonomy, decision-making, and the responsibilities of AI deployment in education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/editorial chapter introducing themes and surveying prior literature, not an empirical study with a defined sample, intervention, or measured outcomes. It does not present original research design or results relevant to the research topic beyond general discussion.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No measurable impact is reported in this chapter for middle school mathematics learning or ChatGPT use. The text is descriptive and theoretical, so there is no outcome evidence to classify as positive, negative, or mixed.

interventions.use_case: The chapter discusses ChatGPT and other generative AI/chatbot tools as emerging AI applications in education, mainly as examples of tools that could support learning interactions and human-AI collaboration.

The chapter frames much of the AI-in-education literature around classical intelligent tutoring systems that provide personalized tutoring and support learning activities, including mathematics problem help.

paper_profiles.title: Towards Responsible Development of Generative AI for Education: An Evaluation-Driven Approach
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to responsibly develop and evaluate generative AI systems for education, especially conversational tutors. The authors argue that progress in AI for education has been slowed by weak evaluation practices, unclear pedagogical goals, and the difficulty of translating learning-science principles into model behavior.

The paper introduces LearnLM-Tutor, a text-based gen AI tutor built by fine-tuning Gemini 1.0, along with a participatory development process that included learners, educators, workshops, interviews, co-design activities, and user studies. The work also proposes seven pedagogical benchmarks spanning automatic and human evaluation, and it describes several fine-tuning datasets, including human tutoring data, synthetic role-play, GSM8k-derived dialogue, and teacher-written “golden conversations.” The context is primarily higher education and programming-learning settings, with learners such as university students and adult Python learners, plus educators including STEM teachers and education researchers.

The main conclusion is that an evaluation-driven, participatory approach can improve a gen AI tutor’s pedagogical behavior relative to a prompt-tuned baseline, while also surfacing important safety and design considerations. The authors report that LearnLM-Tutor is often preferred by educators and learners on pedagogical dimensions, and they emphasize that future AI-for-education work should better align model development, pedagogical theory, and rigorous evaluation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a technical report/framework paper with participatory workshops, interviews, and benchmark design rather than a controlled impact study. It includes some empirical user feedback and model evaluations, but the evidence is primarily qualitative and developmental, not a well-designed RCT or QED.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports promising qualitative improvements in pedagogical behavior and user acceptance, but it does not provide a clear effect size on student learning outcomes. Impact is therefore plausible but still unclear and not yet demonstrated at scale, especially for middle school mathematics learners.

interventions.use_case: text-based generative AI tutor for 1:1 conversational tutoring, fine-tuned from Gemini 1.0 to provide pedagogically improved responses, hints, explanations, and adaptive feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates LearnLM-Tutor as a development and evaluation framework for education-specific conversational AI, emphasizing improved pedagogical behaviors that can reduce the burden on teachers and support more scalable tutoring. In deployment and participatory feedback, learners and educators reported that the system could provide helpful, timely support; however, the paper does not report a direct workload effect size for teachers or operational metrics like time saved.
finding.measure: teacher preferences, learner feedback, deployment interviews; pedagogical evaluation benchmarks
finding.study_size: n=60 learners, n=34 educators in workshops; n=3 learners in Wizard-of-Oz sessions; broader user-study participation not fully reported

finding.finding_summary: Qualitative workshop and interview evidence suggests learners found AI tutoring less formal and less threatening than human tutoring, making them more comfortable asking clarifying questions. Educators and learners also reported that encouraging, constructive, and kind feedback was valued, and the deployment example includes a learner taking a mental break after a supportive exchange, but no quantitative effect size is reported.
finding.measure: workshop/interview feedback on comfort, encouragement, and willingness to ask questions
finding.study_size: n=60 learners, n=34 educators, plus n=3 learner interviews/Wizard-of-Oz sessions

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly aims to improve metacognition, active learning, and learner self-explanation through tutor behaviors such as asking students to explain answers in their own words and not giving away solutions prematurely. In the example deployment, the tutor prompts the learner to explain the charAt method, reinforcing reflection and understanding, but the paper reports qualitative rather than quantitative learning-gain evidence.
finding.measure: metacognitive prompting, learner self-explanation in tutor dialogues, pedagogy rubric evaluations

paper_profiles.title: Integrating drone technology in STEM education: Curriculum, pedagogy and learning outcomes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how a Drone Technology-Enabled STEM Curriculum (DTESC) can support secondary students’ learning across cognitive, psychomotor, and affective domains. The authors frame the work around “dronagogy,” a pedagogical approach that uses drones to create interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary learning experiences. The study asks whether drone-integrated instruction can improve students’ understanding of STEM content, their hands-on technical and design skills, and their attitudes toward STEM learning.

The intervention was implemented with 16 Grade 9–10 students from one secondary school in Hong Kong. Over 10 weeks, students completed a 36-hour program outside regular school hours that included multidisciplinary lessons, interdisciplinary modules, and transdisciplinary project-based tasks such as drone coding, landscape surveying, and designing a drone-assisted water sampling system. Data sources included a knowledge test, rubric-based assessment of design and presentation tasks, reflection journals, and a course evaluation survey.

Results showed strong engagement and satisfaction, with notable gains in psychomotor and affective outcomes. Students performed well in science and social studies-related content and in collaborative engineering and presentation tasks, but mathematics and higher-order technology reasoning were weaker areas. The authors conclude that drone-based STEM curriculum can be effective for engagement and practical skill development, but that future versions should provide stronger scaffolding for mathematical reasoning, abstract conceptualization, and higher-order cognitive learning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small-sample mixed-methods pilot study without a control group or pretest-posttest inferential comparison. The evidence is useful and peer-reviewed, but credibility is limited by the absence of experimental contrast and the very small sample (n=16).
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports positive but mostly descriptive outcomes with no effect sizes and no comparison condition. The impact appears promising for a small pilot, but the magnitude and generalizability are unclear.

interventions.use_case: Drone technology-enabled integrated STEM curriculum (DTESC) using drones for interdisciplinary learning activities such as drone-assisted water sampling, autonomous navigation coding, landscape surveying, and entrepreneurial drone proposal design.
ChatGPT 3.5 used to translate students' reflection journal entries from Chinese to English for clarity during qualitative analysis, not as the instructional intervention.

finding.finding_summary: The DTESC improved students' science-domain knowledge and understanding. On the 18-item knowledge test, students scored a mean of 3.00/4 in science (75% correct; SD=0.73) and showed generally satisfactory performance on higher-order science questions, indicating strengthened scientific comprehension in authentic drone-based contexts.
finding.measure: 18-item STEM knowledge test; science domain subscore

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics was the weakest cognitive domain in the DTESC. Students scored a mean of 1.75/3 in mathematics (58% correct; SD=0.68), and the paper reports difficulty applying polygon-angle and trigonometry knowledge to real-world drone tasks. The intervention improved hands-on application overall, but mathematics transfer and higher-order reasoning remained limited.
finding.measure: 18-item STEM knowledge test; mathematics domain subscore

finding.finding_summary: Students showed strong performance in the non-STEM PSHE domain embedded in the curriculum. The PSHE subscore mean was 2.75/3 (92% correct; SD=0.45), suggesting the drone-integrated thematic curriculum successfully conveyed history/geography/social content alongside STEM activities.
finding.measure: 18-item STEM knowledge test; PSHE domain subscore

finding.finding_summary: The curriculum produced strong gains in psychomotor and collaborative competencies. All four student groups successfully completed the engineering design task; the best group achieved 40/40 on the rubric, and proposal presentations were rated as satisfactory to strong on creativity, feasibility, and teamwork. The paper reports no formal effect size, but performance evidence indicates improved hands-on problem solving, design skills, and collaboration.
finding.measure: Rubric scores for drone-assisted water sampling system; rubric/likert ratings for entrepreneurial proposal presentations

finding.finding_summary: Students reported high engagement, enjoyment, motivation, and resilience during DTESC participation. In the course evaluation, 88% strongly supported continuing the program, 81% recognized its cross-disciplinary benefits, and 75% valued the hands-on practice; qualitative journals also highlighted joyful learning, active engagement, and resilience in the face of failure.
finding.measure: Reflection journals and course evaluation survey

paper_profiles.title: A Systematic Assessment of OpenAI o1-Preview for Higher Order Thinking in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether OpenAI o1-preview can perform higher-order cognitive tasks relevant to education, with a particular emphasis on reasoning skills that are commonly taught and assessed in academic settings. The authors review prior literature on higher-order thinking and then benchmark o1-preview against human performance across 14 dimensions, including critical thinking, systems thinking, computational thinking, design thinking, metacognition, data literacy, creative thinking, abstract reasoning, spatial reasoning, quantitative reasoning, logical reasoning, analogical reasoning, and scientific reasoning.

The approach is not a student intervention study, but a broad evaluation of an AI model using established human assessment instruments. The paper adapts or reuses tests such as the Ennis-Weir Critical Thinking Essay Test, the Biological Systems Thinking Test, the Village of Abeesee, the Lake Urmia vignette, Bebras-style computational thinking tasks, and others. The tested populations used as human benchmarks include middle school students, undergraduates, graduate students, and in some cited comparisons, psychology and other university students.

Overall, the paper concludes that o1-preview often matches or exceeds human performance on several higher-order thinking tasks, especially in systems thinking, computational thinking, creative thinking, and some forms of scientific reasoning, but it is weaker on abstract reasoning and some quantitative tasks. The authors argue that human oversight remains important and that education should increasingly emphasize complementary human skills such as abstraction, creativity, and critical thinking. No middle-school student use of ChatGPT in mathematics learning is studied here; the paper instead evaluates an OpenAI reasoning model as an educational benchmark.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark-style assessment paper based on custom prompting and secondary comparisons to prior human studies, not a controlled educational evaluation. It is useful as exploratory evidence, but it does not meet RCT/QED standards and includes substantial methodological limitations and self-described need for expert interrater validation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful effects on higher-order reasoning performance, but these are model-benchmark results rather than demonstrated learner outcomes. The impact on actual educational populations is therefore unclear and likely modest until validated in classroom studies.

interventions.use_case: Systematic benchmarking of OpenAI o1-preview as a text-based AI reasoning/tutoring tool on higher-order thinking tasks, using educational prompts and assessment instruments across critical thinking, systems thinking, computational thinking, and related domains.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that o1-preview performs strongly on several durable-skills subdomains, especially critical thinking, systems thinking, computational thinking, creative thinking, and scientific reasoning. However, performance is uneven: it slightly underperforms humans on logical, critical, and quantitative reasoning in some comparisons, and it lags human psychology students on abstract reasoning.
finding.measure: Educational higher-order thinking assessments including the Ennis-Weir Critical Thinking Essay Test, Biological Systems Thinking Test, Village of Abeesee, Lake Urmia Vignette, Bebras Challenge, Algorithmic Thinking Test, creative thinking tasks, Raven’s Progressive Matrices, and quantitative reasoning datasets

finding.finding_summary: For quantitative reasoning, o1-preview performed above general crowd baselines but below expert benchmarks, with the paper describing performance as about 15–20% lower than human experts on the FINAQ dataset. The paper frames this as a limitation in expert-level mathematical reasoning despite strong overall reasoning ability.
finding.measure: Quantitative reasoning performance on the FINAQ dataset and related quantitative reasoning tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that o1-preview outperformed humans on scientific reasoning tasks, including scientific reasoning and abstract reasoning-related scientific problem solving, with the abstract noting roughly 150% relative outperformance in some higher-order reasoning categories. The results are presented as evidence that the model can handle complex scientific reasoning tasks at or above human performance on selected benchmarks.
finding.measure: Scientific reasoning assessments included in the study’s higher-order thinking battery

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence and learner autonomy: a meta-analysis of self-regulated and self-directed learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) interventions affect learners’ self-regulated learning (SRL), self-directed learning (SDL), and related learning outcomes. The authors argue that prior evidence on AI-supported learning is fragmented, especially regarding which dimensions of regulation benefit most and under what conditions. To address this, they conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic meta-analysis of empirical studies on AI and learner autonomy.

The review synthesized 32 studies with 92 effect sizes and 3,029 participants. It included AI tools such as conversational agents, intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive recommendation systems, analytics dashboards, and generative or planning tools. The included learners were predominantly undergraduates and early postgraduate students, with participants aged 18 to 37, across domains including language learning, STEM, and medical education. The analysis compared AI-based interventions against control conditions and examined effects on overall SRL, SRL dimensions, SRL phases, learning outcomes, and SDL, along with moderators such as age, duration, subject domain, and AI system type.

The main conclusion is that AI-based interventions substantially improve overall SRL and SDL, with smaller but significant gains in cognitive/metacognitive and motivational/affective regulation, forethought, self-reflection, and learning outcomes. Effects on behavioral regulation and performance-phase regulation were inconsistent and highly heterogeneous. Conversational and interactive systems showed the broadest benefits, while longer interventions, older learners, and language-learning contexts tended to show stronger effects. The paper concludes that AI can act as an adaptive scaffold for learner autonomy, but design choices and learner/context fit strongly shape impact.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic meta-analysis following PRISMA, synthesizing 32 empirical studies with 92 effect sizes and formal moderator, sensitivity, and publication-bias analyses. It meets the highest evidence tier despite some heterogeneity and publication-bias concerns in parts of the analysis.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The meta-analysis reports large effects on SRL (g=1.613) and SDL (g=1.111), plus a smaller but positive effect on learning outcomes (g=0.350). These are medium-to-large impacts on learner regulation and moderate academic benefits, so the overall impact tier is blue.

interventions.use_case: Meta-analyzes conversational and interactive AI systems, including chatbots and generative AI tutors, as supports for self-regulated and self-directed learning across educational contexts. The paper explicitly includes examples such as ChatGPT, chatbots, and Study Buddy SRL-style conversational agents as intervention types that provide prompts, explanations, and reflective support.

Synthesizes studies of instructional and adaptive systems that provide structured tutoring and adaptive guidance for learning regulation, including classical intelligent tutoring and adaptive practice systems. These systems are discussed as AI tools that support goal setting, monitoring, and feedback-driven learning.

Reviews adaptive and recommendation-based AI systems that personalize learning sequences, practice difficulty, or content pacing to support learners' regulation and autonomy. The paper treats these as supportive AI tools that scaffold planning, monitoring, and self-directed study.

Includes feedback-oriented AI systems such as analytics-enhanced feedback tools and rule-based SRL scaffolding engines that deliver prompts, explanations, or progress feedback. These interventions are evaluated for their effects on cognitive/metacognitive and motivational regulation as well as learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Across 32 empirical studies (92 effect sizes; n=3,029), AI-based interventions had a large positive effect on overall self-regulated learning, g=1.613, p=0.032. They also improved self-directed learning, g=1.111, p=0.043, with the strongest gains in forethought/planning and motivational readiness.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning and self-directed learning scales; SRL dimension and phase measures

finding.finding_summary: AI interventions produced small-to-moderate gains in cognitive/metacognitive regulation (g=0.377, p=0.0004) and moderate gains in motivational/affective regulation (g=0.505, p=0.013). Effects on behavioral regulation were inconsistent and non-significant overall despite a large mean estimate (g=0.914, p=0.284), indicating high heterogeneity rather than reliable benefit.
finding.measure: Cognitive/metacognitive, motivational/affective, and behavioral SRL subscales; planning, monitoring, evaluation, and effort/time-management indicators
finding.confidence_interval: Cognitive/metacognitive 95% CI [0.2225, 0.5308]; motivational/affective 95% CI [0.1608, 0.8494]; behavioral 95% CI [-1.0454, 2.8742]

finding.finding_summary: AI-based interventions had a small-to-moderate positive effect on learning outcomes and academic performance, g=0.350, p=0.034, across 7 studies and 9 effect sizes. The authors interpret this as evidence that AI-supported regulation translates into measurable academic gains, though heterogeneity was moderate (I2=69.04%).
finding.measure: Learning outcomes and performance; achievement and task performance measures

paper_profiles.title: Educational Reform in Algeria: Dilemmas of Globalization, Equity, and Decolonization
paper_profiles.venue: Global Agendas and Education Reforms: A Comparative Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines Algerian national education reform, focusing on the tensions between globalization, equity, and decolonization in the country’s school system. Rather than evaluating a ChatGPT-based or other AI intervention in student mathematics learning, the chapter analyzes how broad policy reforms, curriculum changes, and language policy shifts have been experienced and interpreted by stakeholders in Algeria.

The chapter draws on semi-structured interviews with 15 participants involved in the Algerian education system: parents, female teachers across primary, lower-secondary, and upper-secondary levels, and one school head teacher. The study is situated in multiple Algerian localities, including Béjaïa, Aïn Beïda, Oum El-Bouaghi, Ghardaïa, and Tamanrasset, with additional follow-up insights from Guelma Province. The author also used ChatGPT-4 only as a translation and review aid for Arabic-to-English work, not as a learning tool for students.

Findings suggest that reform efforts have produced significant concerns about curriculum overload, early introduction of multiple foreign languages, limited teacher training, resource mismatch, inequitable access, and heavy reliance on private tutoring. Participants described the curriculum as exhausting for children, teachers, and parents, and argued that reforms have disproportionately benefited stronger students while leaving average and weaker students behind. The chapter concludes that Algerian education reform needs a more holistic, context-sensitive approach that better aligns curriculum, pedagogy, resources, and student developmental needs while balancing global agendas with local identity and equity concerns.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative chapter using semi-structured interviews and interpretive analysis, which provides contextual evidence but no experimental or quasi-experimental design. It is useful for understanding stakeholder experiences, but it does not meet higher-causal-credibility criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests substantial institutional and policy concerns, but it reports no quantified intervention effects and offers no evidence of measurable impact sizes. Its contribution is important for diagnosis and critique, not demonstrated impact.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-4 was used as a translation and critical review aid for Arabic-to-English handling of interview data, not as a student-facing tutoring tool.

finding.finding_summary: This chapter is a qualitative policy analysis of Algerian education reform based on semi-structured interviews with 15 stakeholders (9 parents, 5 teachers, 1 head teacher). Participants reported that the reforms were poorly implemented, externally driven, and associated with inequity, curriculum overload, and weak alignment between policy goals and classroom realities. No effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on reform implementation, curriculum, equity, and decolonization

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models, especially ChatGPT, for education. It asks how these models may support learning and teaching, and what risks or failure modes arise when they are used in educational settings. Rather than reporting an empirical intervention study, the paper synthesizes early applications and proposes guidance for responsible adoption.

The paper describes potential uses across educational levels, including primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional learning. For students, it highlights applications such as generating practice questions, explanations, summaries, step-by-step solutions, feedback, and conversational support; for teachers, it discusses lesson planning, personalized materials, assessment support, and feedback generation. It also notes specific possibilities for middle and high school learners in subjects such as mathematics, physics, language, and literature, including math word-problem generation and solution explanations.

The paper emphasizes that these benefits are accompanied by important risks: bias, hallucinated or unverified output, overreliance by learners or teachers, plagiarism and copyright issues, difficulty distinguishing machine-generated from human-generated text, privacy and security concerns, cost and sustainability issues, and limited adaptability to diverse learners. The authors conclude that large language models can be valuable educational tools only if used with human oversight, critical thinking, fact-checking, ethical safeguards, and curriculum design that reinforces—not replaces—student and teacher expertise.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed position paper rather than an empirical evaluation. It offers a conceptual synthesis of opportunities and risks, but no experimental, correlational, or qualitative outcome data are reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has potentially high relevance for education systems and policy because it synthesizes likely benefits and failure modes of ChatGPT in schooling, including mathematics. However, it provides no measured effect sizes or direct evidence of impact, so the demonstrated impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: Position paper on ChatGPT and other large language models used as student-facing educational assistants for generating explanations, step-by-step solutions, practice questions, quizzes, and conversational tutoring, including in middle school mathematics learning.

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual position paper, not an empirical study, so it does not report direct outcome effects on student achievement. It argues that ChatGPT/LLMs could support middle and high school learning across subjects including mathematics by providing step-by-step solutions and practice problems, but also warns that inaccurate or brittle outputs may mislead learners.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes potential benefits for critical thinking and problem-solving if students use ChatGPT to generate hypotheses and compare answers against authoritative sources, but it also flags a key risk that learners may over-rely on model outputs and become less inclined to investigate independently. No quantitative effect size is reported because the paper is a position paper.
finding.measure: critical thinking, problem-solving, fact-checking/verification practices

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests LLMs can improve student engagement and interaction, but it does not provide empirical evidence. It also warns about potential dependency, reduced curiosity, and diminished motivation to do independent work if students rely too heavily on generated answers.
finding.measure: engagement, curiosity, reliance/dependency risk

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT-like systems can reduce teacher workload by supporting generation of quizzes, explanations, feedback, and teaching materials. It frames this as a potential efficiency gain for lesson planning, assessment, and personalized feedback, but provides no empirical estimate.
finding.measure: teacher workload / task efficiency

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is governance, ethics, and institutional risk: bias, copyright/plagiarism, privacy/security, cost, sustainability, human oversight, and the difficulty of distinguishing AI-generated from student-generated work. Because the paper is conceptual, it reports no effect sizes, but it strongly argues that these risks must be managed for responsible adoption in schools.
finding.measure: policy, governance, risk mitigation, ethical deployment

paper_profiles.title: Editorial: Generative AI in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial introduces a Frontiers Research Topic on generative AI in education and summarizes 11 included papers. The broad question addressed is how generative AI, including ChatGPT and other large language models, is being used across educational contexts and what opportunities and challenges it presents for learning, assessment, and support.

The editorial does not report a single intervention study; instead, it synthesizes the themes of the papers in the special issue.
