These include AI for feedback generation, adolescent use of generative AI for schoolwork, critical thinking support, ChatGPT for pre-service mathematics teachers’ proof construction, whole-learner modeling, personalized assessment, AI mentors for STEM career exploration, academic integrity, interactive listening task generation, and deception detection in educational AI robots.

One of the summarized studies involved 22 Japanese middle school students interacting with generative AI robots and examining their ability to detect lies; the editorial notes that most students were deceived and that there were no significant differences in learning effectiveness, motivation, or encouragement across conditions. More generally, the editorial concludes that generative AI shows promise for personalized learning, feedback, and engagement, but raises concerns about accuracy, emotional appropriateness, interpretability, ethics, privacy, fairness, and the risk of deceptive or harmful outputs.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an editorial/perspective piece summarizing a research topic rather than reporting a primary empirical study. It does not present a clear analytic methodology or original outcomes on student learning.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct intervention effect is estimated in this paper, so there is no measurable educational impact to classify. The article is useful as a field overview but reports no quantitative impact on learners.

interventions.use_case: Editorial overview of generative AI and chatbots such as ChatGPT used for tutoring, feedback, assessment support, and student assistance in education, including mathematics-related use cases discussed in the research topic.

paper_profiles.title: Retrieval-augmented Generation to Improve Math Question-Answering: Trade-offs Between Groundedness and Human Preference
paper_profiles.venue: NeurIPS’23 Workshop on Generative AI for Education (GAIED)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can improve the quality of AI-generated responses to middle-school mathematics questions, and whether increased grounding in a textbook necessarily makes responses better for users. The authors are motivated by concerns that LLMs used for math tutoring can hallucinate, give incorrect answers, or produce responses that are poorly aligned with a school’s curriculum.

To study this, they built a RAG-based math question-answering system using sections from the OpenStax Prealgebra textbook as the retrieval corpus and GPT-3.5 as the response model. They varied prompt guidance across several conditions: no retrieval guidance, low guidance, high guidance, and a retrieval-only condition. They first evaluated groundedness on 51 real student questions from the Math Nation discussion board, then surveyed 9 educators and education-technology designers who ranked the responses and judged whether they were grounded in the textbook. They also annotated the relevance of retrieved documents.

The paper finds that retrieval and prompt guidance can increase groundedness, but that the most grounded responses are not always the most preferred. In particular, low-guidance RAG responses were preferred over both no-guidance and high-guidance responses, while high-guidance responses were perceived as more grounded. The authors conclude that math QA systems need to balance faithfulness to source materials with student preference and conversational usefulness, and they highlight the need for future work involving real middle-school students and actual learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small, non-randomized evaluation study with human ratings rather than a causal learning experiment. It is methodologically careful for a prototype paper, but it is still primarily a qualitative/comparative system evaluation with limited external validity.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The system shows promising preference and groundedness results for a priority population context, but there is no direct evidence of learning gains or practical impact. The study suggests design value for math tutoring systems, yet the impact on student outcomes remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: retrieval-augmented conversational math tutoring for middle-school algebra and geometry question answering, using GPT-3.5 with prompts that vary the degree of textbook grounding

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure student learning directly; instead it evaluates math QA response quality for middle-school algebra and geometry questions. Humans preferred the low-guidance RAG responses over no-guidance and high-guidance responses, while high guidance produced the highest groundedness (mean groundedness 0.90 vs 0.59 low and 0.52 none).
finding.measure: Human preference rankings and groundedness judgments on generated answers to 51 middle-school math questions
finding.study_size: n=51 queries; n=9 annotators; n=153 groundedness ratings

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence, especially ChatGPT and related large language models, is reshaping education and argues that three competencies are central for responsible classroom use: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. The paper is motivated by concerns that students and teachers may use AI uncritically, misunderstand its limitations, or rely on it in ways that reduce learning and academic integrity.

The author combines a conceptual discussion with a case study from Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich, Switzerland, plus a narrative literature review. The case study describes how the university developed internal AI guidelines for student academic work, including requirements for transparency about which model was used, how it was used, and how outputs were critically evaluated. The paper also summarizes practical classroom uses of AI such as student experiments with chatbots, AI-generated case studies, curriculum support, gamification, and immersive technologies.

The main conclusion is that bans or unrestricted access are both problematic; instead, institutions should foster an AI culture built on clear rules, training, and ongoing engagement. The paper recommends workshops, regular updates, dedicated budgets, and expert positions to support teachers and students. It also proposes AI literacy content that includes technical basics, ethical issues, limitations such as hallucinations and bias, and prompt engineering as a teachable skill. The overall message is that AI should be used as a sparring partner, not a substitute for human judgment or student thinking.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual discussion and narrative literature review with an institutional case vignette, not an empirical evaluation of student outcomes. It does not use a controlled design or report original quantitative evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for potentially meaningful classroom and institutional effects of ChatGPT-related practices, but it reports no measurable impact size. The likely impact is plausible but remains unclear because the claims are not empirically tested.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual discussion of ChatGPT and other large language models as classroom tools and as a 'sparring partner' for student learning, including brainstorming, source-finding, and guided academic use under transparency rules.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI use in classrooms can support critical thinking when students are trained to evaluate outputs, craft prompts, and compare responses across models. However, it also warns that uncritical use can offload cognitive work to the machine and weaken students' own reasoning, so the net effect is conditional rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of critical thinking, prompt engineering, and AI literacy; no direct student outcome measure reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes institutional responses to ChatGPT adoption, including AI guidelines, documentation requirements, workshops, and calls for dedicated staff and budget. It presents these as necessary governance measures, but also notes implementation risks such as weak compliance, limited monitoring, and uneven educator preparedness.
finding.measure: Institutional policy discussion and case-based analysis of AI guidelines and implementation practices

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims AI tools can help teachers create curricula, case studies, and classroom materials more efficiently, and that students can use LLMs to brainstorm and refine work. These benefits are presented qualitatively rather than measured, and the paper also notes that prompting can take considerable time and may offset efficiency gains.
finding.measure: Qualitative discussion of teacher preparation and student task support efficiency

paper_profiles.title: MathVC: An LLM-Simulated Multi-Persona Virtual Classroom for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of supporting collaborative problem-solving (CPS) in middle school mathematics when real peer interaction is difficult to orchestrate at scale. The authors argue that existing tools often improve the process of collaboration, but do not adequately simulate the peer dynamics that make productive mathematical discussion possible. They ask whether large language models (LLMs) can be used to create believable virtual classmates that help students engage in authentic math talk, critique, and shared reasoning.

To study this, the authors designed MathVC, an LLM-simulated multi-persona virtual classroom in which one middle school student collaborates with multiple virtual peers. The system includes a meta-planning module that manages the stages of collaboration and a persona simulation module that gives each virtual peer a mathematical skill level and an error-injected schema so that peers can make plausible mistakes and revise their thinking. The backend uses GPT-4o and the platform was configured with teacher-specified problems, misconceptions, and peer personas.

The evaluation involved 14 U.S. middle school students who used MathVC to solve grade-appropriate math problems in sessions lasting about an hour. Data included interaction logs, exit surveys, and semi-structured interviews. Students generally reported constructive interaction, shared understanding of problems, and increased engagement, motivation, and confidence. They also found the virtual peers realistic in key ways, especially when peers made and corrected mistakes, though some noted that the language sometimes sounded too formal or adult-like. The authors conclude that LLM-based peer simulation can support collaborative mathematics learning, while also highlighting design challenges around authenticity, persona alignment, and conversational realism.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative human-subjects evaluation with 14 middle school participants, using interviews, exit surveys, and dialogue logs. It provides useful empirical evidence, but there is no randomized comparison, no pre-post achievement measure, and no causal estimate.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests promising but unquantified benefits for math collaboration, engagement, and confidence, with no reported effect sizes. Because the findings are descriptive and based on a small sample, the impact appears modest and uncertain rather than clearly large.

interventions.use_case: LLM-simulated multi-persona virtual classroom for middle school mathematics collaborative problem solving, where virtual peers generated questions, critiques, scaffolding, and peer-like dialogue to support student problem solving.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that 14 middle school participants used MathVC to collaboratively solve grade-level math problems, with 40 dialogue sessions and 695 total messages. Students and interviewees reported that the system helped them reach shared solutions and supported problem understanding, but the evidence is qualitative and descriptive rather than based on achievement tests or a controlled comparison.
finding.measure: Exit survey items about shared understanding/solution and ability to understand the math problem; interview feedback; conversational logs

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that interacting with the virtual peers increased engagement, motivation, confidence, and persistence during mathematical problem solving. In the exit survey, constructive interaction (M=4.36/5) and confidence in working in the virtual classroom (M=4.21/5) were high, and interview themes emphasized reduced cognitive burden and more enjoyable collaboration.
finding.measure: Exit survey Likert ratings; thematic interview analysis

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on collaborative problem solving and metacognitive aspects such as planning, sharing ideas, critiquing, and validating solutions. Exit survey responses were strong for planning and understanding how each action contributed to solving the problem (M=4.36/5), and students described constructive peer interaction and shared reasoning throughout the task.
finding.measure: Exit survey item on planning and contribution; interview themes; dialogue analysis of collaboration stages

paper_profiles.title: Examining Pre-service Mathematics Teachers' Purposes of Using ChatGPT in Lesson Plan Development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines why pre-service middle school mathematics teachers used ChatGPT while developing lesson plans. The study asks how ChatGPT supported lesson content creation and how it helped participants deepen their own knowledge and address gaps while planning instruction.

The intervention/approach studied was the use of ChatGPT as an AI tool during lesson plan development. Participants were 56 third-year pre-service middle school mathematics teachers enrolled at a state university in Turkey. They were asked to select mathematics curriculum outcomes, prepare a lesson plan using ChatGPT, and then respond to an open-ended questionnaire. The analysis used qualitative content analysis.

Findings showed that ChatGPT was used most often to create lesson content: generating learning activities, problems and examples, assessment tools, course flow, creative ideas, explanations of math concepts, interdisciplinary and real-life connections, and revisions to lesson plans. A second major use was helping participants deepen pedagogical knowledge and fill conceptual gaps, especially around teaching strategies, materials, classroom management, and mathematical concepts. The paper concludes that ChatGPT can be a useful support tool in teacher education, but it should complement rather than replace teachers' own expertise, and its outputs should be checked for accuracy.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative phenomenological study using open-ended questionnaire responses from 56 pre-service teachers, with content analysis and interrater agreement reported. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically clear, but it does not provide experimental or causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports perceived benefits for lesson planning and teacher knowledge, but no quantitative impact on student outcomes or workload reduction is measured. The likely impact is positive yet modest and unclear in magnitude because findings are descriptive and self-reported.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used by pre-service middle school mathematics teachers to support lesson plan development, including generating learning activities, problems/examples, evaluation tools, course flow, concept explanations, and revision suggestions.

finding.finding_summary: This qualitative phenomenology study (n=56 pre-service middle school mathematics teachers) found that ChatGPT was used extensively to support mathematics lesson planning, especially for explaining concepts, generating problems and examples, and structuring lesson flow. The paper does not report effect sizes, but participants consistently described ChatGPT as helpful for deepening mathematical content understanding and improving the quality of math instruction materials.
finding.measure: Self-reported purposes and uses of ChatGPT during mathematics lesson plan development; content analysis of open-ended questionnaire responses

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that ChatGPT supported creative thinking, idea generation, and connecting mathematical concepts to daily life, other lessons, and prior knowledge. It also helped some pre-service teachers deepen pedagogical knowledge and identify gaps in their own understanding, suggesting benefits for metacognition and instructional planning rather than direct student achievement.
finding.measure: Self-reported uses of ChatGPT for creativity, conceptual linking, and knowledge deepening in lesson planning

finding.finding_summary: The paper indicates that ChatGPT improved efficiency in lesson planning by helping participants rapidly produce course flow, assessment ideas, activities, and revised lesson materials. Teachers described it as saving time and reducing effort in planning and editing, but the study provides no quantitative workload estimates or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Self-reported lesson-planning productivity and editing support

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a review article that surveys the emerging literature on artificial intelligence in education, with particular attention to chatbots and ChatGPT. Rather than evaluating a single intervention, the authors aim to synthesize what AI technologies can do in educational settings and to highlight the ethical and practical issues that come with their adoption. The paper frames ChatGPT as part of a broader landscape of AI tools that can support instruction, feedback, assessment, and student engagement.

The article discusses how chatbots and related AI systems may be used for personalized learning, language learning, answering student questions, automated assessment, and teacher support. It positions these tools within existing AI-in-education paradigms and describes the kinds of benefits reported in prior literature, including improved motivation, individualized feedback, workload reduction for teachers, and support for diverse learners. The discussion is not based on original participant data; instead, it is a conceptual and literature-based analysis.

The paper also emphasizes risks and limitations associated with ChatGPT and similar tools, including privacy concerns, bias, deceptive or inaccurate outputs, over-reliance on technology, weak accountability, and potential threats to academic integrity. The authors conclude that while ChatGPT and other AI tools have significant promise in education, their use must be guided by responsible implementation, adequate teacher preparation, and attention to ethical safeguards.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review/opinion-style article with no original empirical design, no comparison groups, and no new outcome data. It is peer reviewed, but it does not meet criteria for experimental or quasi-experimental evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper makes broad claims about potentially meaningful impacts of ChatGPT in education, but these are not directly measured here. Because the article is largely conceptual and evidence-synthesizing, the observable impact in this paper is unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual review of ChatGPT as a conversational AI tutor and assistant for education, including answering questions, generating explanations, and supporting personalized learning and feedback.

finding.finding_summary: This is a review paper rather than an intervention study, so it does not report original effect sizes. It argues that ChatGPT and related AI tools could improve education through personalization, feedback, and efficiency, but also highlights systemic risks around privacy, bias, academic integrity, teacher training, and inequity.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of prior literature on AI in education; reported ethical/practical risks and potential applications

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI chatbots can reduce repetitive teacher work by automating scoring, assignment evaluation, and responding to student questions, thereby saving time for lesson planning and support. This is presented as a literature-based claim rather than a measured effect, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Narrative claims about automated grading, feedback, and administrative support

finding.finding_summary: The review states that AI-supported learning can increase student motivation, engagement, confidence, and reduce anxiety, citing prior studies on AI tutors and robots. However, these are secondary summaries of earlier work, not new measurements in this paper.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of motivation, engagement, confidence, and anxiety outcomes in prior studies

paper_profiles.title: LEGO-PROVER: NEURAL THEOREM PROVING WITH GROWING LIBRARIES
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents LEGO-Prover, a neural theorem-proving framework designed to improve large language model performance on formal mathematics by maintaining a growing library of reusable verified lemmas. The central problem addressed is that existing LLM-based provers often struggle with longer proofs and cannot effectively reuse previously proven intermediate results across problems.

LEGO-Prover introduces two main components: a prover that decomposes a target theorem into subgoals, retrieves relevant lemmas from a vectorized skill library, and constructs proofs in a modular block-by-block style; and an evolver that generalizes or directly solves requested subgoals to create additional reusable skills. The system uses ChatGPT as the LLM, Isabelle as the proof verifier, and is evaluated on the miniF2F benchmark of competition mathematics formalized in Isabelle. The benchmark consists of high-school competition problems, but the paper is about theorem proving infrastructure rather than human learners.

The results show that LEGO-Prover improves pass rates over prior baselines, reaching 57.0% on miniF2F-valid and 50.0% on miniF2F-test, with the growing skill library contributing to gains over an ablation without the library. The authors conclude that modular proof construction and skill accumulation can make formal theorem proving more effective and bridge the gap between informal and formal mathematical reasoning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical systems paper, but it is not an education intervention study and does not use a randomized or quasi-experimental design with learner outcomes. Evidence is mainly algorithmic evaluation on theorem-proving benchmarks plus ablations and case analysis.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports moderate benchmark gains for automated theorem proving (e.g., pass rate 48.0% to 57.0% on miniF2F-valid), but this is not direct K-12 student learning impact. Any educational relevance is indirect and confined to formal mathematical reasoning infrastructure rather than classroom outcomes.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT is used as the language model for automated theorem proving in mathematics, generating informal proofs, decomposing proofs into subgoals, formalizing Isabelle proofs, and evolving reusable lemmas/skills in a growing skill library.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: A revolutionary tool for teaching and learning mathematics
paper_profiles.venue: EURASIA Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines early perceptions of ChatGPT as a tool for teaching and learning mathematics, focusing on both stakeholder opinions and direct use of the system on mathematical tasks. The authors ask whether ChatGPT can support mathematics instruction, how accurate and useful it is, and where its limitations lie, especially for solving equations, limits, derivatives, and geometry problems.

The study uses a qualitative instrumental case study design with two components: content analysis of interviews and a user-experience investigation. For the interview component, 30 interviewees drawn from public blogs and discussions about ChatGPT in mathematics were analyzed; these included students and educators, particularly math instructors. For the user-experience component, three experienced educators used ChatGPT for one week and tested several scenarios involving algebra, calculus, and geometry. The context is mathematics education, and the paper includes examples intended for middle school mathematics, especially in geometry.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT is viewed as promising and potentially transformative, but unreliable as an autonomous mathematics tutor. Participants saw strengths in instant feedback, accessible explanations, and support for geometry instruction, yet the authors also documented multiple mathematical errors and misconceptions in ChatGPT’s responses. The paper concludes that ChatGPT may be useful as a complementary educational tool, but its outputs must be checked carefully and safer, more responsible guidelines for classroom use are needed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative case study using interview content analysis and scenario-based user experience testing. It provides useful exploratory evidence, but it is not an experimental or comparative design and does not report inferential statistics or effect sizes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful instructional support from ChatGPT in mathematics, but the evidence is mixed and primarily qualitative. Reported benefits are offset by substantial accuracy problems, so overall impact is unclear and modest at best.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a conversational AI tool for mathematics teaching and problem solving, including generating explanations, solving equations, giving geometry examples, and answering follow-up questions.

finding.finding_summary: This qualitative case study found that ChatGPT can accurately explain some middle school geometry concepts and solve simpler math problems, but it also produced multiple mathematical errors in algebra, limits, derivatives, and geometry. In the user-experience scenarios, the authors report incorrect solutions such as 3x+4(1-5x)=-9 yielding the wrong answer (13/20 instead of 13/17) and a Pythagorean theorem calculation giving 5.93 instead of 5.97; no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Accuracy of ChatGPT responses to math problems and explanatory quality across linear equations, cubic equations, limits, derivatives, and geometry prompts
finding.study_size: n=30 interviewees; n=3 educators in user-experience testing

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests ChatGPT may support problem-solving and provide step-by-step explanations that could aid understanding, but it also may reinforce misconceptions rather than improve reasoning. This conclusion is based on qualitative interview analysis and scenario-based observations rather than a quantified learning gain, so no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived support for problem-solving, understanding, and correction of misconceptions
finding.study_size: n=30 interviewees; n=3 educators in user-experience testing

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that ChatGPT can produce explanations and example solutions quickly, sometimes faster than manual drafting, which suggests time-saving potential for teachers and learners. However, the paper provides no quantitative productivity metric or effect size, and this benefit is tempered by concerns about accuracy and the need for verification.
finding.measure: Perceived speed/efficiency of generating explanations and solutions
finding.study_size: n=30 interviewees; n=3 educators in user-experience testing

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in Higher Education: The ChatGPT Effect
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book-length work addresses the rapid emergence of ChatGPT and generative AI in higher education and asks how these tools might reshape teaching, learning, assessment, and institutional policy. Rather than evaluating a single intervention on learning outcomes, it synthesizes concepts, examples, and practices to help educators and policymakers understand the opportunities and risks of GenAI in academic settings.

The book discusses AI literacy, strengths and weaknesses of using ChatGPT in curriculum design, redesigning assessment for the AI era, developing institutional AI policies, and the technical foundations of generative AI. It also includes examples, case scenarios, frameworks, and prompt-engineering guidance, with a strong emphasis on higher education. The text notes that many examples and cases are drawn from post-secondary contexts, though some ideas may be adapted to other educational levels.

Its main conclusion is that GenAI should be integrated thoughtfully as a human partner rather than as a replacement for educators. The authors argue for AI literacy, ethical and policy guidance, authentic assessment redesign, and a learner-centric approach that prioritizes feedback, integrity, and responsible use of AI in education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a book chapter/preface-style descriptive and conceptual treatment of generative AI in higher education, not an empirical study. It contains no direct evaluation, comparison, or outcome measurement relevant to the retrieved topic.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No intervention effect is reported and no student achievement outcomes are measured. The text is informative and policy-oriented rather than evidence of impact on learning.

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in intelligent tutoring systems toward sustainable education: a systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews how artificial intelligence is being used in intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs) to support sustainable education. The authors focus on broader educational challenges such as unequal access, limited teacher ICT skills, engagement and dropout risks, privacy and bias concerns, and the need for explainable, trustworthy AI in education. Rather than studying a single intervention, the paper synthesizes prior research to identify common themes, methods, and outcomes across AI-enabled tutoring systems.

The review covers 29 studies on AI and ITSs, plus additional papers on sustainable education challenges, drawn primarily from Scopus and Web of Science. The included studies span mainly higher education, with some high school and K-12 examples, and are located across Asia, Europe, the Americas, and Oceania. The systems and approaches discussed include machine learning for performance prediction, clustering for learning behavior analysis, dropout prediction, personalization, learner emotion detection, and explainable AI methods for instructor support.

The main conclusion is that AI-integrated tutoring systems can improve performance prediction, personalize learning, support instructor decision-making, and enhance engagement, but most systems remain black-box models and raise concerns about fairness, transparency, and portability. The authors argue that future work should emphasize explainable AI, human-centered design, better data quality, stronger educational theory, and broader implementation across subjects and contexts. Overall, the paper positions AI as a support tool for more student-centered and sustainable education rather than a replacement for teachers.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review, but it is not an empirical evaluation with a controlled design. The paper synthesizes prior studies rather than producing direct causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests broad positive potential for AI in tutoring systems, but it reports no pooled effect sizes or direct achievement impacts from a single study. Its impact claims are therefore informative but not quantitatively established.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of AI- and machine-learning-embedded intelligent tutoring systems for sustainable education, including performance prediction, learning behavior analysis, dropout detection, personalization, intervention recommendation, and explainable AI support.
Learning analytics and machine-learning prediction of student performance, engagement, and dropout risk from system log data, with instructor alerts and intervention recommendations.
Adaptive and personalized learning paths or training episodes within tutoring systems, based on student behavior, performance, or emotional state.
Chatbot-style natural language interaction and conversational support within tutoring systems, discussed as one AI-enabled mode of learner interaction.

paper_profiles.title: Large Language Models: A Survey
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a survey of large language models (LLMs), with a focus on major model families, training approaches, augmentation techniques, datasets, evaluation metrics, and benchmark performance. It is not an empirical study of an educational intervention, but rather a broad обзор of the LLM research landscape following the release of ChatGPT.

The paper reviews the development of LLMs from earlier statistical and neural language models through transformer-based pre-trained language models and into modern LLMs such as GPT, LLaMA, and PaLM. It summarizes key architectural choices, training stages such as pre-training, fine-tuning, instruction tuning, and alignment, and discusses how LLMs are used with external knowledge, tools, and agentic workflows.

No student population, school setting, or educational intervention is studied. The conclusions are conceptual: the paper argues that LLMs have rapidly expanded capabilities such as in-context learning, instruction following, reasoning, and tool use, while also noting ongoing challenges around efficiency, safety, ethics, and future model design. Because it is a survey, it does not report achievement outcomes, retention effects, or subgroup effects.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative survey of large language models, not an empirical study of an educational intervention. It does not present a controlled methodology or primary outcome analysis relevant to K-12 mathematics achievement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no measured educational impact and reports no effect sizes on student outcomes. It is background/overview literature rather than evidence of classroom or tutoring effects.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and risks of large language models, especially ChatGPT, for education. Rather than reporting an empirical intervention study, it synthesizes early uses of LLMs in educational settings and argues for responsible, human-centered deployment. The paper asks how such models can support learning and teaching, and what technical, pedagogical, ethical, legal, and social challenges must be addressed before they can be used at scale.

The authors discuss a wide range of possible applications for students and teachers, including generating quizzes, practice problems, explanations, personalized feedback, lesson plans, summaries, and assessment support. The discussion spans multiple educational levels and contexts, with examples relevant to elementary through university learners, as well as group, remote, and professional learning. Particular attention is given to potential uses in middle and high school education, such as language learning, mathematics practice, and problem-solving support.

The paper concludes that LLMs may become powerful educational tools, but only if they are integrated with strong human oversight, critical thinking, fact-checking, privacy protections, bias mitigation, and sustainable governance. It emphasizes that these systems should supplement rather than replace teachers, and it calls for more research on best practices, user interfaces, fairness, and reliable educational use cases.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper and narrative overview, not an empirical evaluation with a controlled design. It presents arguments, use cases, and risks without original outcome data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct learning or implementation effect is measured, so there is no empirical evidence of impact on outcomes in this paper.

interventions.use_case: Position paper on ChatGPT and other large language models as educational assistants for students and teachers, including conversational tutoring, question answering, personalized explanations, and generation of practice problems, quizzes, and feedback.

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how artificial intelligence (AI) has been studied in higher education, how the field has developed over time, what ethical issues are discussed, and what kinds of AI applications are being used. Rather than testing one intervention, it systematically reviews 146 peer-reviewed articles published between 2007 and 2018 from Web of Science, Scopus, and EBSCO Education Source.

The review organizes AI uses into four broad application areas: profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment and evaluation, and adaptive systems/personalisation. Across the included studies, the main users were undergraduate students, with a smaller number of studies on postgraduate students and institutional/administrative users. The paper notes that most studies are quantitative and that many use machine learning for prediction tasks, automated feedback, or tutoring support.

The authors conclude that AI research in higher education is growing quickly, but it is dominated by technical and quantitative work, with relatively little involvement from educators and very limited critical reflection on ethical implications such as privacy, costs, and possible workforce impacts. They also argue that many studies are short-term and often lack longitudinal evidence, so stronger pedagogical and ethical frameworks are needed for future AI applications in higher education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review of higher-education AI research, not an empirical study of an intervention’s effects on learners. It synthesizes descriptive patterns and prior studies but does not present a direct evaluation with study-level causal evidence for the target comparison topic.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct impact estimate on middle school mathematics achievement, delayed retention, or subgroup effects. paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emerging role of artificial intelligence in education, with particular attention to chatbots and ChatGPT. Rather than testing an instructional intervention, the authors synthesize existing literature to explain what these technologies are, how they work, and why they are attracting interest in educational settings. The paper frames ChatGPT as a generative AI tool capable of producing human-like responses and discusses broader categories of AI used in education, including intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, automated assessment, and educational chatbots.

The article focuses on potential educational applications across teaching, learning, assessment, and administration. It argues that AI tools may support personalized instruction, immediate feedback, learner engagement, and teacher workload reduction. The discussion also highlights ethical and practical concerns such as bias, privacy, academic integrity, over-reliance on technology, and the need for teacher preparation and institutional support.

The paper is conceptual and literature-based, drawing on examples from prior studies across K-12 and higher education but not reporting a new empirical sample or intervention context. Its main conclusion is that AI, including ChatGPT, has considerable promise for education if deployed responsibly and aligned with pedagogical goals, but further research is needed to establish effective and ethical implementation practices.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review/opinion piece about AI and ChatGPT in education, not an empirical comparison study. It does not present a primary research design, sample, or causal evidence relevant to middle school mathematics achievement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper discusses potentially meaningful educational uses of ChatGPT, but provides no measured impact estimates or direct outcome data. Any impact claims are speculative and generalized rather than demonstrated in an empirical study.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual overview of ChatGPT as a conversational AI for education, including student support, tutoring-like interaction, feedback, and question answering.

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses the growing role of artificial intelligence in education, with a particular emphasis on AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. Rather than evaluating a specific educational intervention with outcome data, it argues that these three competencies are increasingly necessary for responsible and effective AI use in academic settings. The author frames AI as both an opportunity for personalized learning and a challenge because of issues such as hallucinations, misuse, overreliance, and inadequate educator preparation.

The paper combines a case study from Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich, Switzerland, with a narrative literature review. The case study describes institutional responses to the sudden spread of ChatGPT and other large language models, including the development of internal AI guidelines for student writing. These guidelines require transparency about model use, documentation of how AI was used, and critical evaluation of outputs. The discussion then broadens to suggest workshops, curriculum integration, and institutional support structures to build a stronger AI culture among students, teachers, and administrators.

The paper concludes that simple rules or bans are insufficient and that effective integration of AI into education requires systematic training and ongoing support. It argues that AI literacy should include technical understanding, awareness of limitations and ethics, and practical use cases; prompt engineering should be taught as a pedagogical skill; and critical thinking should remain central so that students do not treat AI as a substitute for independent work. The overall contribution is conceptual and practice-oriented, focused on higher education rather than a controlled empirical evaluation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual discussion with a narrative literature review and informal case observations, not a controlled empirical study. It does not present a clear experimental or quasi-experimental methodology for causal inference.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no measurable educational impact on student achievement or other outcomes. Its contributions are normative and practical suggestions rather than evidence of observed impact.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual discussion of ChatGPT and similar large language models as classroom support tools, including using them as an 'informed conversational partner' for student academic work and as a sparring partner for brainstorming, drafting, and questioning.
AI literacy instruction and prompt engineering pedagogy, including workshops, AI-literacy courses, and guided practice in how to interact with AI systems responsibly and critically.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking are essential durable skills for students in AI-rich educational settings. It does not report an empirical effect estimate; instead, it provides a conceptual and case-based rationale that structured AI use can strengthen students' critical evaluation of AI outputs and problem-solving capacity.
finding.measure: Conceptual synthesis and case-study-informed discussion of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes institutional AI guidelines, staff workshops, dedicated budgets, and paid AI-support roles as strategies for integrating AI into higher education. No quantitative institutional outcome is reported, but the central claim is that governance and training structures are needed to manage AI use responsibly and consistently.
finding.measure: Policy and governance recommendations derived from a university case study

finding.finding_summary: The article suggests that AI tools can improve efficiency for tasks such as curriculum design, case-study creation, and brainstorming for academic writing. These claims are illustrative rather than measured, and no effect sizes or sample-based comparisons are provided.
finding.measure: Narrative descriptions of teacher workflow support and content-generation efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Reinforcement Learning: A Survey
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a survey of reinforcement learning from a computer science perspective. It introduces the central problem of an agent learning through trial-and-error interaction with a dynamic environment, and it distinguishes reinforcement learning from supervised learning and related areas such as search, planning, and adaptive control. The paper is not an empirical study; instead, it organizes the field and reviews major concepts, algorithms, and theoretical results.

A major focus is the problem of choosing actions under uncertainty when rewards may be immediate or delayed. The paper explains the standard reinforcement-learning model, models of optimal behavior (finite-horizon, discounted infinite-horizon, and average-reward), and criteria for evaluating learning algorithms such as convergence speed and regret. It then reviews classical techniques for exploration in the simple bandit setting, including dynamic-programming-based methods, Gittins indices, learning automata, greedy and randomized heuristics, and interval-based methods.

The paper further surveys delayed-reward methods for Markov decision processes, including value iteration, policy iteration, modified policy iteration, temporal-difference learning, TD(bb), Q-learning, and average-reward extensions. It also discusses model-based approaches such as certainty equivalence and Dyna. Its main conclusion is that reinforcement learning had strong theoretical foundations but remained challenged by exploration, delayed credit assignment, and scalability to large state spaces.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a 1996 survey/theoretical review of reinforcement learning, not an empirical study of an educational intervention. It contains no K-12 learner sample, no experimental design, and no measured educational outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not evaluate educational impact, only summarizes RL methods and theory. There are no reported effects on student achievement, retention, engagement, or institutional outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Review of deep learning: concepts, CNN architectures, challenges, applications, future directions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad survey of deep learning, aiming to provide a comprehensive overview of the field rather than evaluate a specific intervention. The authors argue that prior review articles were too narrow in scope, so they synthesize literature across deep learning concepts, network types, convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures, training issues, challenges, applications, computational tools, and benchmark datasets.

The review focuses on deep learning methods such as supervised, semi-supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning, with special emphasis on CNNs because of their wide use and strong performance in areas like computer vision, speech processing, natural language processing, and medical imaging. It explains key architectural components such as convolution, pooling, activation functions, fully connected layers, loss functions, regularization methods, and optimization strategies.

The paper does not study a particular population, educational setting, or outcome; instead, it synthesizes more than 300 deep learning papers published mainly from 2010 to 2020. Its main conclusion is that deep learning has become a dominant machine learning paradigm due to its ability to learn features automatically, scale to large datasets, and outperform traditional methods in many tasks, while still facing challenges such as overfitting, interpretability, data imbalance, and vanishing gradients.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review article on deep learning and CNN architectures, not an empirical study evaluating an education intervention. It does not present a clear methodology for measuring educational outcomes or intervention effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct educational impact on middle school mathematics achievement or any other student outcome. It is background/overview literature, so there is no measurable effect size or intervention impact to assess.
